In this way, the wisdom of reflection chews upon the Dharma heard, with the power of wisdom acting as its aid, just as taking excellent medicine brings about the medicinal action that eliminates illness.

Thus, possessing the wisdom of hearing and reflection, one accords with the true meaning and practices according to the Dharma, thereby distancing oneself from all afflictions and the maladies of habitual tendencies.
Just as honey is the place where swarms of bees depend upon for their pleasant dwelling and activity,

so too is the fruit of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation the basis upon which the noble ones depend, because they experience the flavor of delight and dwell in pleasure within the present life.
Having thus praised the speaker and requested the listener to speak, they next praised the benefits of the Dharma to be taught and collectively made their request.
The verse says:
“Excellent, O one of pure wisdom! Speak of the supreme stages, free from defilement.”
"Endowed with the ten powers and unimpeded, he fully expounds the path of the Sugata.

"Excellent" (sādhu) refers to the complete perfection of the Dharma taught therein. There are three kinds of excellence: [the excellence of the speaker, the excellence of the teaching, and the excellence of the audience].
First, the basis;
second, the essential nature;
third, the fruit.

The "basis" refers to pure wisdom; the "essential nature" refers to the teaching of the unprecedented doctrines of the various stages (*bhūmi*); the "superiority of the stage" refers to the comparative excellence of the stages;
and "stainlessness" refers to the teaching that does not contradict the meaning.
There are three kinds of defilements in those who speak contrary to the meaning:
first, speaking erroneously;
second, slandering the Tathāgata.
Third, deceiving those who hear [the teaching].
As for the "result," it refers to the Buddha’s bodhi, which is endowed with the ten powers and is unobstructed.
Although he had been requested in this manner, he still did not speak.
Why is it not explained?
Because it would not satisfy the request.
*Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*, Volume One: The Stage of Joy (*Pramuditā-bhūmi*).
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*, Chapter One: The Stage of Joy (*Pramuditā-bhūmi*), Scroll Two.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Maitreya;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Later Wei dynasty.
The Treatise says:

This Bodhisattva first receives an invitation from the leaders among his co-nascent assembly, followed by an invitation from the great assembly, and further awaits the formal invitation of the Buddhas, the Kings of Dharma. Why is this?
In order to increase reverence for the Dharma,
the Sūtra says:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted from the white tuft between his eyebrows a radiant flame of light called "Bodhisattva Power," with incalculable upon incalculable rays of light as its retinue.
Having emitted this light, it shone universally throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, pervading them all without exception.
Having shone, it returned and settled back in its original place; the sufferings of the three evil realms were all brought to rest, and all the palaces of Māra were obscured and no longer appeared.
It illuminated the assemblies of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, manifesting the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata’s realm.

This light shone universally upon the worlds of the ten directions, empowering all those who preach the Dharma as commissioned by the Tathāgatas, as well as the multitudes of bodhisattvas; it then formed a great cloud-net terrace of radiant light in the sky above and remained there.

The Buddhas of the ten directions do likewise; from the white tuft of hair between their eyebrows, they emit the radiant flames of the Bodhisattva’s power of light, with incalculable upon incalculable rays of light serving as their retinue.
Having emitted this light, it shone universally throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, pervading them all without exception.
Having shone, it returned and settled back in its original place; the sufferings of the three evil realms were all brought to rest, and all the palaces of Māra were obscured and no longer appeared.
It illuminated the assemblies of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, manifesting the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata’s realm.

This light pervaded the worlds of the ten directions, empowering all those who were empowered by the Tathāgatas to preach the Dharma, as well as the multitudes of Bodhisattvas, manifesting the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata’s realm; it also illuminated the assembly of Śākyamuni Buddha’s great gathering and the body of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, and further formed a great cloud-net terrace of radiant light suspended in the void above.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted a white light from between his eyebrows, which illuminated the bodies of the bodhisattvas and their lion thrones within the great assemblies of all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

This entire great assembly clearly beheld the white tuft-light rays emitted from between the eyebrows by all the Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions, illuminating this Sahā world-system of three thousandfold great thousands, the great assembly of Śākyamuni Buddha, as well as the body and lion throne of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
At that time, all those in the great assembly clearly beheld this within the pavilion of the cloud-net of great radiance; through the spiritual power of the Buddhas, they spoke these verses.
The treatise asks:
For what reason did the Tathāgata manifest his supernormal powers and emit light to issue the collective invitation?

The Tathāgata has previously bestowed empowerment through mind alone, but not yet through body or speech; this differs from other Buddhas. Therefore, he now wishes to provide the complete empowerment of both body and speech.
Why does he not employ his usual body and speech for this empowerment?
It is for the sake of honoring the Dharma and not disparaging oneself.
This light has eight kinds of functions and two kinds of bodies.
What are the eight kinds of functions?

First is the awakening to karma: after this light has illuminated the bodies of all bodhisattvas, they personally realize the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s power, as the sūtra says, "emitting the blazing radiance of the bodhisattva's power."
Second is the cause of karma: each of the *asaṃkhyeya* rays has immeasurable light as its retinue, as the sūtra states, "with *asaṃkhyeya-asaṃkhyeya* rays as their retinue."

Third is the activity of expansion and contraction: when expanded, it reaches throughout incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds; when contracted, it returns to the constant radiance. This is as the sutra says: "Having emitted this light, it universally illumines the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions without exception; having illuminated them, it returns and abides in its original place."
Fourth is the cessation of karma, which eliminates all the various sufferings and afflictions of the evil realms, as stated in the sutra: "The sufferings of the three evil realms all find rest."

Fifth is the activity of subjugation, which causes the majestic radiance of all the palaces of Māra to disappear, inducing shock and terror, so that they are unable to disrupt or confuse those beings who are ready for conversion; as the sūtra says, "The palaces of all Māras are obscured and do not appear."

Sixth is the veneration of the activity, because it manifests the inconceivable spiritual power of the Buddhas, as the sūtra says: "It illuminates the assemblies of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, manifesting the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata’s realm."

Seventh is the manifestation of activity: it causes this assembly to see the empowerment bestowed by the Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions upon the great assembly of bodhisattvas, as the sutra states: "This light shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, empowering all those who preach the Dharma and the assemblies of bodhisattvas who have been empowered by all the Tathāgatas."

Eighth is the invitation to teach: the utterance of verses, as stated in the sutra: "At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddhas within the great cloud-net pavilion, they spoke these stanzas."
What are the two bodies?
First, the body like a shooting star, because it travels to other world-systems;
second, the body like the sun, which abides in space.
This is because the sutra states that [the Buddha] "dwells upon a great cloud-net terrace of light formed in the space above," and "simultaneously illuminates all places."
In this way, all these sentient beings see one another as if they were gathered in a single assembly, and their hearing and speaking are likewise so.
This is called empowerment by body (*kāyādhiṣṭhāna*).
What is empowerment by speech (*vāgadhiṣṭhāna*)?
The verse says:
"The Buddhas are peerless among equals; their merit is like space.
Possessing the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth, they are the foremost among immeasurable multitudes."
Śākyamuni, whose clan-name is Dharmaja, Empowered by the Supreme among Gods and Humans,
And sustained by the spiritual power of all Buddhas, Has opened the treasury of the Dharma King.
The sublime practices of the various stages, And the meaning of the stages of wisdom, have been distinguished.
Through the empowerment of all these Tathāgatas, they protect all bodhisattvas;
this person is able to hear and uphold such subtle and wondrous Dharma,
whereby the stages (bhūmis) become pure and stainless, gradually reaching fulfillment.
Realizing the ten powers of a Buddha, they shall attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Even if they are within the great ocean or amidst the fires at the end of an eon,
those with resolute faith and no doubt will surely hear this sutra.
"The path of the supreme wisdom of the various stages, entering the stages and abiding therein in succession,
is explained gradually as the sphere of immeasurable practices.
The Commentary says:
These first two and a half verses clarify the one who bestows empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the purpose for which the empowerment is bestowed.
What meaning do these two empowerments manifest that they are bestowed?
If the requester were not a venerable one, or if the Dharma were not supreme, a noble being would not speak it.
How does the first verse manifest the one who bestows empowerment?
The verse says, "The Supreme among Gods and Humans bestows empowerment.
Who is this Supreme among Gods and Humans?
This refers to all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
What is the meaning of this?
It is the meaning of being the Dharma King.
How is it known that he is a Dharma King?
Because he has accomplished four kinds of excellence:
first, excellence of mastery; [and so forth].
2. superiority in power;
3. superiority in retinue;
4. superiority in lineage.
What is the supreme mastery of the Buddhas?

It is their mastery in attaining liberation from the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the hindrance to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); for therein their mental wisdom is unimpeded, and they experience at will the unsurpassed bliss that is to be realized.
How is this known?
It is because the verse says, "The Buddhas are equal to the unequaled," which means they possess all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*).
Furthermore, they are like space, for worldly phenomena cannot defile them, as their ignorance, afflictions, and habitual tendencies have been extinguished.
"Unequaled" means that when the Buddhas are compared with other sentient beings, those others are not equal to them.
"Equal" means that their *dharmakāyas* are equal to one another.
Why, then, is it not simply said to be "unequaled"?
Because they manifest equal and perfect enlightenment.
What is the superiority of the Buddhas' powers?
Because they are endowed with the ten powers, they are able to subdue all erroneous cognitions and destroy the enemies that are the Māras.
How is this known?
It is because the verse says, "The ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth.
What is the excellence of the Buddhas' retinue?
This is because it fully encompasses the assemblies of both bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
How is this known?
From the verse stating, "The leaders of immeasurable assemblies," for those bodhisattvas constitute the primary assembly.
"Infinite" means because they are incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).
"Foremost among all beings" means that the Buddha is the most supreme and exalted in the world.
In what way is the Buddha’s lineage superior?
This refers to the excellence of his family lineage.
How is this known?
It is because the verse states: "Born from the Dharma of the Śākya clan."
Why is it that only this Buddha-lineage is praised?
Because it is directly perceived.
Furthermore, one takes the Dharma as one's family, not merely a family of birth.
The Dharma-family (dharmakāya) is so called because it abides within the Dharma.
"Application" (pratyaya) is the general characteristic; there are two kinds of application:
first, bodily application, because it relies upon the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Second, the addition of possessing the fruit:
because one realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
Regarding those who are supreme among gods and humans, this applies both collectively and individually; for others, it applies only individually.
How does the second verse reveal the purpose of the empowerment?
This Bodhisattva is empowered by those Buddhas, the Kings of Dharma, for the sake of opening and revealing the treasury of the Dharma.
The verse says:
"Relying on the spiritual power of all Buddhas, I shall open the Dharma-treasury of the Kings of Dharma;
I shall distinguish the meaning of the stages of wisdom and the sublime practices of the various grounds.
This praise of the Dharma-treasury is of two kinds: [the praise of the treasury itself and the praise of its contents].
First, the accomplishment of the treasury of meaning;
second, the accomplishment of the treasury of words.
What is the treasury of meaning?
The verse says: "The sublime and excellent practices on all stages.
"Practices" refers to the practices of all bodhisattvas, namely the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
"Sublime" refers to true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*).
"Superior" means that its spiritual power is preeminent.
It is thus displayed as profound, subtle, and supreme.
What is the "matrix of syllables" (akṣaragañja)?
The verse says, "The meaning of the stage of discriminating wisdom.
"Discriminating" refers to the explanation of the distinctions among the ten stages.
Why is it revealed in this verse that [the speaker] relies on the Buddha's spiritual power to teach?
There may be sentient beings who, having conceived thoughts of contempt toward the Tathāgata, are unable to request others themselves to preach the Dharma.

To prevent this, after thus requesting the preaching of the Dharma, there follow three verses which reveal that the benefit of preaching the Dharma for the sake of others provides advantage at three distinct times.
The benefits of the three periods are:
first, the benefit at the time of hearing;
second, the benefit at the time of practice.
Third, the benefit at the time of rebirth.
What is the benefit at the time of hearing?
The verse says:
"By the empowerment of all these Tathāgatas, who protect all bodhisattvas,
this person is able to hear and uphold such a subtle and wondrous Dharma.
That a bodhisattva hears and upholds [the Dharma] through the empowerment of the Buddha's power is called the benefit at the time of hearing.
What is the benefit at the time of practice?
The verse says:
"The stages become pure and stainless, Gradually reaching fulfillment."
"Realizing the ten powers of a Buddha, one attains unsurpassed bodhi.
Because one gradually fulfills the ten stages (*bhūmi*), personally attains the ten powers, and achieves unsurpassed bodhi, this is called the benefit at the time of practice.
What is the benefit at the time of rebirth?
The verse says:
"Though one may be in the great ocean, or amidst the fires at the end of an eon,"
With resolute faith and free from doubt, one will surely hear this sutra.
Even those born in the difficult places of the evil realms or the good realms will surely hear this Dharma.
Those in the long-lived worlds of the nāgas can also hear this sutra, as the verse says, "Even though they are in the great ocean.
Even those in the Form Realm, such as the Ābhāsvara Heaven, can also hear this sutra, as the verse says, "And even amidst the fires at the end of an eon."
Regarding those who hear this Dharma, do they all obtain benefit, or are there some who do not?
Who is able to obtain it?

Those who believe in this Dharma with certainty and without doubt are the ones who can obtain it; as the verse says: "Those who have certain faith and no doubt will surely hear this sutra. Thus it is.

Having thus demonstrated the benefits of requesting the teaching, regarding the aforementioned meaning of "the stage of analytical knowledge" (*pratyavekṣaṇājñānabhūmi*), there are three successive stages in this Dharma that is being taught; the sixth verse instructs on this matter through analysis.
The verse says:
"The path of supreme wisdom of the various stages, entering the stages and abiding therein in succession,
is explained gradually as the sphere of immeasurable practices."
"What are the three gradual stages?
First, the gradual stage of contemplation;
second, the gradual stage of realization."
Third, regarding the gradual sequence of practice: the first, second, and fourth phrases all describe this gradual sequence.

"The path of supreme knowledge" refers to the path of supreme knowledge of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); it is said that by means of contemplation or reliance upon these ten stages, one is able to generate the wisdom of the various stages.
"Entering" means entering the stages (*bhūmi*).
"Abiding" means not yet turning toward other stages.
"Progressing" means moving from one stage to another within the places where one dwells.
"Practice" (*caryā*) refers to the successive accomplishment [of the stages] from entry through abiding.
"Object-sphere" (*viṣaya*) refers to the fact that this practice has various distinct objects-spheres for its range.
"Gradual" (*krama*) refers to the sequence.
"Speaker" means one who bestows [the teaching].
For what purpose is such a teaching spoken?
It is to manifest that all causes are capable of being spoken by the Tathāgata, so as to give rise to the conviction of correct meaning in the future.
The Sūtra says:

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha surveyed the ten directions; desiring to cause the great assembly to increase their exultation further and give rise to right faith, he spoke in verse:
"The subtle, difficult-to-know Path of the Sage Is beyond conceptualization and free from thought."
Difficult to attain, it is stainless and untainted; it is the sphere of activity for the wisdom of the wise.
Its intrinsic nature is eternally quiescent—neither ceasing nor arising;
its very essence is primordially empty, existing as non-dual and inexhaustible.
Distant from all realms of existence, its character is identical to nirvāṇa;
it is neither beginning, middle, nor end, and cannot be expressed by words.
Transcending the three periods of time, its nature is like empty space.
The meditative cessation practiced by the Buddhas cannot be reached by words.
The practice of the stages is likewise: difficult to explain and difficult to hear.
Transcending the path of thought and mind, wisdom arises as the realm of the Buddhas.
It is not described in terms of aggregates, elements, or sense bases; it is beyond the reach of mind and intellect.
Like the tracks of a bird in the sky—difficult to describe and impossible to see—so too is the meaning of the ten stages: it cannot be explained or heard.
I have spoken but of a single part—compassion and the power of aspiration;
Gradually, it transcends the realm of mind and intellect, Until wisdom is perfected like a pure mind.
This sphere is difficult to see, Difficult to describe, yet known by one's own mind.
I shall speak by the power of the Buddha; listen all together with reverence.
Such entry into the practice of wisdom could not be fully told even in billions of eons;
now it is briefly explained, abiding in accordance with reality and complete.
With single-minded reverence, I await; sustained by the Buddha’s power, I shall speak well.
I shall proclaim the sublime Dharma with wondrous tones, employing appropriate metaphors and excellent syllables.
Such speech is exceedingly difficult, for it relies upon the immeasurable spiritual power of the Buddhas.
"The blazing flames have entered my body; by this power, I am able to speak.
The commentary asks:
For what reason does he observe the ten directions?
This is to demonstrate the absence of self-conceit and partiality.
Desiring to cause the great assembly to increase their joy even further and give rise to profound right faith, he therefore spoke these verses to reveal the true stages.
"Augmenting learning" means being capable of receiving the meaning.
"Rejoicing" means the mind is clear and not turbid.
There are two kinds of rejoicing:
First is the great joy of the meaning, because of attaining the meaning;
second is the great joy of the teaching, because through this great teaching one is able to attain that meaning.
Among these, the first five verses manifest the great joy of the meaning.
What is meant by "greatness of meaning"?
It is because that meaning is profound.
What is this profound meaning?
The verse says:
"The subtle and difficult-to-know Noble Path / Is not conceptualization, but free from thought.
Upon what meaning is this verse based?
Regarding the basis of the stage of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*): how is it known that this is based on the stage of wisdom?

All that has been explained above is based on the stage of wisdom, and what will be explained hereafter is likewise based on the stage of wisdom; for the fourth verse states, "The arising of wisdom is the Buddha’s sphere."
Regarding "subtle": in what sense is it subtle?
The verse states, "The noble path is difficult to know.
In what way is it difficult to know?
It means that it is difficult to know when [the teaching] is being spoken.
Furthermore, why is it difficult to know?
Because the Great Sage’s Way is difficult to know.
The Great Sage refers to the Buddhas; therefore, it is called "subtle.
The Path is the cause, for by practicing this path one can reach the state of the Sages.
It is said that the Path of the Sages is difficult to know. This subtlety is of two kinds:
First, the time of its teaching is extremely subtle;
second, the time of its realization is extremely subtle.
Why, moreover, is it so difficult to know according to this sequence?
The verse states: "It is non-conceptual and free from thought.
"Non-conceptual" means it is free from the objects of conceptualization.
"Free from thought" means its very essence is devoid of mentation.
Thus, this noble path is called "extremely subtle.
Why is it extremely difficult to attain?
Because that which is difficult to attain is difficult to realize; therefore, it is called "extremely subtle."
For what reason is it even more difficult to obtain?
The verse says:
"Difficult to obtain is that which is stainless and unturbid, the sphere of activity of the wisdom of the wise."
"Self-nature is eternally quiescent; it neither ceases nor arises.
That which is "without defilement" means that within wisdom there is no ignorance (*avidyā*); where wisdom is mixed with ignorance, it is called "defiled."
The sphere of the wise’s wisdom is so called because it is known through personal realization.
Personal realization occurs because [wisdom] arises in dependence upon that [sphere].

Within this, the wise perceive the meaning of the true truths; furthermore, they possess superior skillful understanding of the Dharma, superior skillful tranquility, and additionally, worldly wisdom that clearly knows according to what has been heard.
"Self-nature is eternally quiescent" means that self-nature is free from afflictions; it is not the case that there was first defilement which was later abandoned.
"Non-extinction" means that it does not undergo a one-sided cessation, for it does not relinquish the benefit of sentient beings.
"Non-arising" refers to its supramundane nature.
Thus, this wisdom does not abide in either nirvāṇa or the mundane world.

Because its contemplative practice is extremely subtle, its basis is extremely subtle, its purity is extremely subtle, and its qualities are extremely subtle, it is said to be "extremely difficult to attain."

Among these, the first is distinct because its subtlety is unlike that of worldly samādhis; the second and third are distinct because they differ from the self-proclaimed venerables of the non-Buddhists; and the fourth is distinct because it differs from those of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
In this verse, "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) is the general term, while the two kinds of subtlety are the specific instances.

Furthermore, it reveals that [the Dharma] is difficult to attain: "attaining it at a most subtle time" is the general term, and the remaining four kinds of extreme subtlety are the specific instances.
What further characteristics does this most subtle wisdom possess?
The verse says:
“The intrinsic nature is originally empty; Existence is non-dual and inexhaustible.”
Distant from all realms of existence, it is identical to the nature of nirvāṇa.
It is neither beginning, middle, nor end; it cannot be expressed by words.
Transcending the three periods of time, its characteristic is like space.
This characteristic of wisdom is of two kinds:
namely, the common characteristic and the uncommon characteristic.
Among these, what is the characteristic of the common characteristic?
Because that is the characteristic of wisdom, the verse says: "The self-essence is originally empty," for wisdom itself is empty.
What is its common characteristic?
All phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature as has been taught; can that which is empty of intrinsic nature be apprehended in the same way as a rabbit’s horn? No.
Can it be apprehended such that there is a distinct emptiness other than this wisdom of emptiness? No.
"No. Can it be thus apprehended that there is a self-essence of 'this' and 'that,' which undergoes transformation and cessation? No."
How is this emptiness of self-nature grasped?
It is grasped as "existence that is non-dual and inexhaustible.
This phrase reveals its exclusion from being subsumed under the three types of emptiness.
First, the inclusion of being free from slander;
second, the inclusion of being free from difference;
third, the inclusion of being free from exhaustion and cessation.
There are two kinds of verses:
first, those that exist, are non-dual, and are inexhaustible;
second, those that are definitively non-dual and inexhaustible.
Although these verses differ, they equally clarify that [the object] exists substantially; if it did not exist substantially, one could not say it is "definite.
In what sense is it definite?
It is definite because it can extinguish all afflictions; this is called their common characteristic.
What are the characteristics of difference?
They are the characteristics of purity and liberation.
These, in turn, are of two kinds:
First, from where is liberation attained;
second, how is one liberated?

Regarding "from where is liberation attained," the verse states: "far removed from all realms of existence" (*gati*). This reveals liberation from the various paths of rebirth, because one is far removed from afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth.

Regarding "how they are liberated," the verse says, "identical with the characteristics of nirvāṇa. This is because they equally embrace both the mundane world and nirvāṇa, unlike the śrāvakas who exclusively turn their backs on the mundane world.
Does this wisdom that exhausts the outflows (āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna) constitute the initial abandonment of knowledge, or the middle, or the final?
It is not the abandonment of the initial knowledge, nor of the middle or the final, for the verse states: "Neither initial, nor middle, nor final."
How is it severed?
It is like the flame of a lamp; it is not merely [severed] at the beginning, middle, or end, because it is apprehended throughout the prior, middle, and subsequent stages.
Is such liberation comparable to the contemplation of another's voice? No, it is not.
How is it observed?
The verse says, "It is not that which can be expressed by words," because it is free from language.
Can it be said that it is similar to worldly knowledge and relies upon the world? No.
What is the basis?

The verse states: "Transcending the three periods of time. This is because the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) relies upon the eternal body; it is not like the consciousness-cognition of impermanent beings, which relies upon impermanent causes and conditions.

As it is definitively taught in the sūtras regarding this liberation: Is it the same as the liberation through the removal of obstacles attained by the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas? No, it is not.
What is liberation?
The verse says: "Its characteristic is like space," because it is free from all afflictions and obstructions.
Through such contemplative wisdom, such abandonment of afflictions, such observation of observation, and such reliance, one relies upon this liberation to attain liberation.
Having spoken thus, among these, the emptiness of intrinsic nature is the general category, while the three kinds of emptiness are the specific categories;
liberation is the general category, while the five kinds of liberation are the specific categories.
The verse says:
"The meditative cessation practiced by the Buddhas cannot be reached by verbal expression;
the practice of the stages is likewise difficult to explain and difficult to hear."
What does this verse mean?
That wisdom has already manifested the nirvāṇa that is sublated by skillful means; it further demonstrates the nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity, as the verse says, "definitive cessation."
"Samādhi" refers to the accomplishment of *nirvāṇa* with common characteristics (*sābhāsa-nirvāṇa*), because its intrinsic nature is quiescent.

"Cessation" refers to the accomplishment of *nirvāṇa* through the destruction of means with differing characteristics (*asābhāsa-upāya-vināśa-nirvāṇa*), because it manifests the cessation of cognitive objects through wisdom.
By whom is this wisdom realized?
Because the verse says "the sphere of the Buddha's practice.
By whom is it taught, and by whom is it heard?
There is no speaking and no listening, for the verse states, "It cannot be reached by verbal expression.
Verbal expression refers to guidance through vocal sounds; that is to say, the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables.
Why is it that you do not simply speak of the wordless?
It is to demonstrate that one seeks understanding by relying on words.
Since that wisdom is thus, what are the characteristics of the practices of the stages (*bhūmi*)?
The verse says: "The stages and practices are likewise; difficult to speak of and difficult to hear.
"Stages" refers to the objective spheres (*viṣaya*).
"Practices of contemplation" refers to the retinue of wisdom (*jñāna-parivāra*).
The retinue of wisdom refers to those who practice together.
Those who practice together refer to the various pāramitās, such as dāna (generosity) and so forth.
For what reason, then, is it said that this is difficult to explain and difficult to hear?
The verse says:
"Beyond thought and the path of the mind, wisdom arises as the realm of the Buddha;
it cannot be described in terms of the aggregates, elements, or sense bases, for it is beyond the reach of the intellect and the mental faculty."

This verse demonstrates that while the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and the consciousness-wisdom born of maturation (*vipākaja-vijñāna-jñāna*) can indeed be described, this [supreme] wisdom is not their domain because they are not of the same nature; as the verse says: "Wisdom arises within the Buddha's domain."

Just as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases can be described, this wisdom is not so; because it is free from words and letters, it cannot be described. Thus, the verse says: "It is not described by means of the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases."
It is not known by the ear-consciousness nor deliberated upon by the mental consciousness; therefore, it cannot be heard, as the verse states, "beyond the reach of mind and intellect.
This "wisdom" is the stage [of the bodhisattva].
Regarding the arising of wisdom: by what contemplation and by what concomitant factors can this wisdom be produced?
How is it that it can be realized, yet cannot be described and cannot be heard?
Now, this meaning is further established by means of a simile.
The verse says:
"Like the tracks of a bird in the sky, they are difficult to describe and impossible to see."
"The meaning of the ten stages is thus: it cannot be described or heard.
What does this verse demonstrate?
It is like a bird flying through the sky: its tracks cannot be described, nor can its form be seen.
Why is this? Because the marks of bird tracks in the sky cannot be distinguished, yet it is not that there are no traces of movement through the sky.

Likewise, the abodes of the body of sentences, the body of phrases, and the body of syllables—being subsumed within the realized wisdom of the bodhisattva stages—cannot be described and cannot be heard.
Why is this? Because its nature is not like that of sound, yet it is not that there is no wisdom regarding the earth.
Since the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables are profound herein, they reveal the great joy of the vast meaning.
For what reason have I spoken this again?
You should not grasp the meaning according to the literal sound.
There are five kinds of faults in grasping the meaning according to the literal sound:
1. Lack of correct faith;
2. Retreat from valorous effort;
3. Deceiving others.
Fourth, slandering the Buddha;
fifth, disparaging the Dharma.
The great assembly knows for themselves that they are free from these five faults.
Having already explained the profound meaning, he now speaks five verses to further clarify the greatness [of the teaching] so as to engender right faith:
"I have spoken but a single portion Of compassion, vow-power, and the gradual stages That transcend the sphere of the ordinary mind;
When wisdom is perfected, it is like the pure mind."
This realm is difficult to see; it is difficult to describe, yet known by one's own mind.
Relying on the Buddha’s power, I shall speak of it; listen all together with reverence.
Such entry into wisdom and practice could not be fully described even in billions of eons.
Now, this has been briefly explained; it abides in accordance with reality, complete and perfect.
With single-minded reverence, wait upon it as it is well-expounded through the power of the Buddha—a sublime Dharma in wondrous tones, characterized by appropriate metaphors and excellent syllables.
These words are exceedingly difficult to express;
through the immeasurable spiritual power of the Buddhas, flames of light have entered my body, and by this power I am able to speak.
The meaning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) previously mentioned was such that it could not be spoken or heard; now, when I say that I speak but a single portion, what is the meaning of these words?
That which is subsumed under this stage is twofold:
first, the causal portion;
second, the fruitional portion.
"Explaining" means providing an interpretation.
"A single portion" refers to the causal portion being a single portion of the resultant portion; thus, it is said, "I teach only a single portion.
This teaching of the Great [Vehicle] is of three kinds:
First, the greatness of the accomplishment of the cause;
second, the greatness of the gradual accomplishment of the cause;
third, the greatness of the accomplishment of cultivation through the teaching.
What is the greatness of the accomplishment of the cause?
The verse says: "Because of compassion, loving-kindness, and the power of aspiration.
Compassion (*maitrī*) consists in sharing the causes and effects of joy and happiness with others.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) consists in the shared uprooting of the causes and effects of sorrow and suffering;
aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) consists in generating the resolve to aim for great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
This cultivation of compassion, aspiration, and the long night of practice is unlike that of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
What is the greatness of the gradual accomplishment of the cause?
The verse says "gradually" (krama).

"Gradual" refers to the explanation of the sequence beginning with the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*), up to the point where it can produce the cause for supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*).
What is the greatness of the accomplishment of cultivation as taught in the scriptures?
There are two kinds:
first, cultivation through fulfillment; [second, cultivation through mastery].
2. Contemplative Cultivation.
Regarding the cultivation of fulfillment, the verse states: "It is not the sphere of the mind.

This phrase indicates that the spheres of the mind, such as those of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*), are merely causes for wisdom (*jñāna*) capable of producing supramundane wisdom; however, these cannot fulfill the ground of that supramundane wisdom. As the verse says: "Wisdom is fulfilled like the pure mind."
Regarding "the pure mind," it refers to the supramundane pure mind, which is able to fulfill the wisdom of that stage.
Regarding "contemplative cultivation," the verse says:
"This realm is difficult to see; It is difficult to describe, known only by one's own mind."
"I shall speak by the power of the Buddha; listen all together with reverence.
What meaning does this verse reveal?
This realm is difficult to see; it can be seen through the purification of one's own mind, yet this realm is inexpressible.
Having thus explained the cultivation of accomplishment, there are two kinds of faults within the teaching of the Dharma that prevent one from attaining realization:
first, the fault of the speaker;
second, the fault of the listener.
There are two kinds of faults in the speaker:
first, speaking that which the Buddha does not approve;
second, speaking that which is unequal.
There are also two kinds of faults in the listener:
first, the fault of contentious views, such as being attached to various perspectives by asserting, "My doctrine is correct and their doctrine is wrong";
second, failing to give rise to reverence for the teacher of the Dharma.

Within this, it is shown that the speaker himself is without fault; it is not that I do not rejoice in the teachings of the Buddhas, for the verse says: "Listen all, as I speak by the power of the Buddha."
Next, the listener is instructed to guard against two kinds of faults, as the verse says: "Listen with mutual respect.

Although it has been thus sequentially permitted to speak, the assembly does not yet know whether the exposition will be extensive or concise; since an extensive exposition is not possible, only a concise exposition of the meaning of the stages (*bhūmi*) is permitted for the sake of fulfillment.
As stated in the third verse:
"Such entry into the practice of wisdom could not be fully described even in billions of eons;
now it has been briefly explained, abiding in accordance with reality and in full perfection."
Regarding "entry by wisdom": this refers to the dharmas of the stages (bhūmi) here described, which sentient beings enter by means of wisdom.
How do they enter?
They enter by way of grasping them through fulfillment according to reality, because they practice in accordance with how things are.
Because the practice is fulfilled through such conduct, it demonstrates the comprehensive grasp of the meaning of the extensive teaching.
As for "abiding," I speak thus because one abides with certainty in the family of the Tathāgata.
Preface: Listen with reverence. Since it has not yet been explained what constitutes reverence, it is now demonstrated.
The verse says:
"With single-minded reverence, wait; Receive this well-spoken teaching through the power of the Buddha."

"Proclaiming the sublime Dharma with wondrous sounds, / Through metaphors, analogies, and excellent words. Regarding "waiting with single-minded reverence," there are two kinds: first, waiting with physical reverence, such as abiding in proper deportment so as to be capable of receiving the teaching of the Dharma; second, waiting with mental reverence, which means being focused on the Dharma and not distracted by other matters. Thus it is said: "With a mind free from distraction, / One should listen to the Dharma with reverence. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not arrogant, not conceited, not haughty, and not disdainful. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with a humble mind, / Without arrogance, conceit, pride, or contempt. Moreover, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not weary, not fatigued, not indolent, and not lax. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with a tireless mind, / Without weariness, fatigue, sloth, or laxity. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not agitated, not scattered, not confused, and not distracted. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undisturbed mind, / Without agitation, scattering, confusion, or distraction. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not attached, not clinging, not greedy, and not covetous. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with a non-attached mind, / Without clinging, greed, or covetousness. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not hostile, not resentful, not angry, and not malicious. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with a non-hostile mind, / Without resentment, anger, or malice. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not proud, not self-important, not arrogant, and not conceited. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with a non-proud mind, / Without self-importance, arrogance, or conceit. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not deceitful, not guileful, not flattering, and not sycophantic. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with a non-deceitful mind, / Without guile, flattery, or sycophancy. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not suspicious, not doubting, not skeptical, and not critical. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with a non-suspicious mind, / Without doubt, skepticism, or criticism. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not contentious, not disputatious, not quarrelsome, and not argumentative. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with a non-contentious mind, / Without dispute, quarrel, or argument. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by external objects, not distracted by internal states, not distracted by the five desires, and not distracted by the eight worldly concerns. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by objects, states, desires, or worldly concerns. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by gain, not distracted by honor, not distracted by fame, and not distracted by praise. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by gain, honor, fame, or praise. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by the teacher, not distracted by the teaching, not distracted by the assembly, and not distracted by the time. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by the teacher, the teaching, the assembly, or the time. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by past thoughts, not distracted by future thoughts, not distracted by present thoughts, and not distracted by thoughts of the three times. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by thoughts of the past, future, present, or the three times. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by the body, not distracted by speech, not distracted by the mind, and not distracted by the three karmas. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by body, speech, or mind, or the three karmas. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by form, not distracted by sound, not distracted by smell, not distracted by taste, not distracted by touch, and not distracted by dharmas. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by the eye, not distracted by the ear, not distracted by the nose, not distracted by the tongue, not distracted by the body, and not distracted by the mind. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by the realm of desire, not distracted by the realm of form, not distracted by the formless realm, and not distracted by the three realms. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by the desire, form, or formless realms, or the three realms. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by the world of sentient beings, not distracted by the world of vessels, not distracted by the world of afflictions, and not distracted by the world of dharmas. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by the worlds of sentient beings, vessels, afflictions, or dharmas. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by birth, not distracted by old age, not distracted by sickness, not distracted by death, and not distracted by the four marks of existence. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by birth, old age, sickness, death, or the four marks. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by the suffering of birth, not distracted by the suffering of old age, not distracted by the suffering of sickness, not distracted by the suffering of death, and not distracted by the suffering of the five aggregates. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, or the five aggregates. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by the suffering of separation from what is loved, not distracted by the suffering of meeting what is hated, not distracted by the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and not distracted by the suffering of the five aggregates. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by the sufferings of separation, meeting, non-attainment, or the five aggregates. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by the suffering of the hells, not distracted by the suffering of animals, not distracted by the suffering of hungry ghosts, and not distracted by the suffering of the asuras. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by the sufferings of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, or asuras. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by the suffering of the human realm, not distracted by the suffering of the heavens, not distracted by the suffering of the eight difficulties, and not distracted by the suffering of the five turbidities. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by the sufferings of humans, heavens, the eight difficulties, or the five turbidities. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by the suffering of ignorance, not distracted by the suffering of views, not distracted by the suffering of afflictions, and not distracted by the suffering of karma. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by the sufferings of ignorance, views, afflictions, or karma. Furthermore, one should listen to the Dharma with a mind that is not distracted by the suffering of birth, not distracted by the suffering of aging, not distracted by the suffering of dwelling, and not distracted by the suffering of death. Thus it is said: "One should listen to the Dharma with an undistracted mind, / Not distracted by the sufferings of birth, aging, dwelling, or death. Furthermore, one should listen to the D
2. Second, "with a mind of correct reverence and waiting": this is because, as the mind is determined, one is capable of recollecting and maintaining [the teaching].
This phrase exhorts two kinds of reverent waiting, namely, those of body and mind.
"Speaking well" indicates that one is without flattery and without arrogance.
"Relying on the Buddha's power" indicates that one is without overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
What does the second half of the verse demonstrate through the metaphor of the sublime sound of the supreme Dharma corresponding to excellent syllables?
By what thing? In what manner?
Upon what thing does it depend?
What is manifested is the so-called supreme Dharma.
By what means is it manifested? It is by means of sublime sounds.
In what manner is it manifested? It is through correspondence with parables.
Regarding that which is relied upon: it refers to relying on virtuous syllables (*akṣara*), whereby I have taught all that is wholesome.
Furthermore, as for "correspondence," it refers to correspondence with analogies.
There are two characteristics of virtuous syllables:
First, because it skillfully accords with local dialects and sounds;
second, because its words and phrases are complete—neither adding nor subtracting—and correspond to the underlying principle, it is said to have "excellent phrasing."
Introduction: Having received the Buddha’s spiritual power (*buddhānubhāva*), it has not yet been explained what this power is.
The fifth verse demonstrates the activity of the Buddha’s spiritual power.
The verse says:
"This discourse is extremely difficult [to expound]; through the immeasurable spiritual power of the Buddhas, flames of light have entered my body, and by this power I am able to speak.
Having thus concluded the section on the request, from hereafter begins the formal exposition of the first bhūmi.
What matters are explained in this exposition of the divisions?
There are three types of analysis:
first, abiding;
2. Explaining the names;
3. Abiding. Within abiding, there are four kinds:
By means of which body?
For what purpose? By what cause?
What are its characteristics?
When that mind arises, one immediately dwells in the First Stage; this is called "dwelling" because therein the sons of the Buddha skillfully accumulate roots of goodness.
These forty phrases describe the matters of this dwelling.
First, it is explained upon what kind of body such a mind arises.
The Sūtra says:
"O Sons of the Buddha!"

If there are sentient beings who have thickly accumulated roots of goodness; who have well-accumulated various virtuous practices; who have well-accumulated various practices of samādhi; who have made excellent offerings to all Buddhas; who have well-accumulated pure and white dharmas; who have been well-guarded by spiritual friends; who have well-purified their minds; who have entered into a profound and vast mind; who believe in and delight in the Great Dharma and love to seek the Buddha’s wisdom; and who manifest great compassion—such sentient beings are then able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The treatise says:
These ten phrases explain which body they depend upon.
This collection consists of nine types:
First is the accumulation of conduct, which consists in skillfully cultivating the retinue of ethical discipline (*śīla*), as the sūtra says, "skillfully accumulating all virtuous conducts.

Second is the accumulation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which consists in skillfully cultivating the retinue of samādhi, as the sūtra says, "skillfully accumulating all practices of samādhi."
The practitioner of samādhi is so called because their contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) is predominant.

Third is the accumulation through proximity, which refers to the thorough cultivation of the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), as stated in the sūtra: "skillfully making offerings to all Buddhas."

Fourth is the wisdom of accumulated reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), which skillfully deliberates upon all wholesome dharmas such as the *pāramitās*; this is as stated in the sutra: "skillfully accumulating pure and white dharmas."
Fifth is the accumulation of protection, which consists of practicing and realizing the truth while properly receiving instruction, as the sutra says, "well-protected by a spiritual friend.
Sixth is the accumulation of the pure mind, which consists of attaining supramundane right knowledge, as the sutra says, "the well-purified mind."
Seventh is the accumulation through extensive gathering: acting for the benefit of all sentient beings with a profound resolve, as the sūtra says, "entering the deep and vast mind.

Eighth is the accumulation through faith: seeking the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), as the sūtra says, "believing in and delighting in the Great Dharma, and loving to seek the Buddha’s wisdom."
Ninth is manifest assembly, which involves the frequent practice of compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*), as the sutra states, "manifesting great compassion.

Within this, the thought of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) relies upon the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), while the compassion (*karuṇā*) relies upon the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

Among these, the first two types of accumulation manifest the training in higher ethics and the training in higher concentration; for the accumulation of conduct consists in skillfully performing the maintenance of ethical discipline through its retinue, and the accumulation of concentration consists in skillfully performing meditative absorption through its retinue.

Next, there are four collections that manifest the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*): the collection of proximity, because it involves cultivating the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) through diligent practice; the collection of accumulation, because it involves gathering the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) by skillfully contemplating the perfections (*pāramitā*) and other wholesome dharmas; the collection of protection, because it involves practicing according to the instructions so as to properly attain realization; and the collection of purifying the mind, because it results in supramundane right knowledge (*lokottara-samyag-jñāna*).

The latter three collections are as follows: the collection of manifesting superiority over śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others; the collection of extensively cultivating a profound mind to bring benefit to all sentient beings; the collection of faith to seek the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna); and the collection of manifesting the frequent practice of compassion.
Among these ten phrases, "thoroughly accumulating roots of goodness" is the general [category], while the remaining nine kinds are the particulars.

"Accumulating" refers to their common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), while the "particulars" refer to their distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); "formation" is explained briefly, whereas "destruction" is explained extensively.
Having explained upon which body such a mind arises, next is explained for what purpose such a mind is generated.

The Sūtra says: "For the sake of attaining the Buddha’s wisdom; for the sake of attaining the power of the ten powers; for the sake of attaining great fearlessness; for the sake of attaining the equal Dharma of the Buddhas; for the sake of rescuing all the world; for the sake of purifying great compassion; for the sake of attaining the knowledge that leaves nothing remaining throughout the ten directions; for the sake of attaining unobstructed, pure knowledge regarding all worlds; for the sake of awakening to the events of the three periods of time within a single thought-moment; and for the sake of turning the great wheel of Dharma with fearlessness—for these reasons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva generates such a mind."
The Commentary states:
Regarding "the Buddha-wisdom therein," this refers to unsurpassed wisdom, because it knows [what is to be] abandoned, realized, and cultivated.
This Buddha-wisdom possesses nine distinct types of activity; it is for the sake of seeking these that such a mind is generated.

First is the power of the Buddha’s wisdom regarding the activity of answering questions. This refers to the Tathāgata’s power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), by means of which he provides answers to questions, as explained in the Sūtras; as the Sūtra says: "In order to attain the power of the ten powers."
Second is the fearless Buddha-wisdom, which performs the activity of refuting heterodox doctrines, as the sūtra states: "for the sake of attaining great fearlessness.

Third is the impartial Buddha-wisdom, which performs the activity of teaching sentient beings the realization and entry into the selflessness of persons and phenomena, as the sūtra states: "for the sake of attaining the impartial dharma of the Buddhas."

Fourth is the Buddha-wisdom of salvation, which is the activity of transforming sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), as the sutra says: "for the sake of saving all the world.
Fifth is the Buddha-wisdom of purification, which is the activity of purifying the causes for saving and gathering [beings], as the sutra says: "for the sake of purifying great compassion."

Sixth is the wisdom of no remainder: the Buddha-wisdom constantly observes the karma of sentient beings in the world with the Buddha-eye, as stated in the Sūtra for the purpose of "attaining the wisdom of no remainder throughout the ten directions."

Seventh is the undefiled Buddha-wisdom, which spontaneously manifests transformations throughout all worlds without obstruction or defilement, performing deeds that inspire faith; its wisdom-mind is unimpeded, as the sutra states: "In order to attain the unobstructed pure wisdom regarding all worlds."

Eighth is awakening to the Buddha-wisdom, which, within a single thought-moment, knows the minds, mental factors, and karmas of sentient beings across the three periods of time, as stated in the sutra: "In order to awaken to the events of the three periods of time within a single thought-moment."

Ninth is the Buddha-wisdom of turning the wheel of Dharma; because it is the skillful activity of the means of liberation, it simultaneously turns the Great Wheel of Dharma across ten billion Jambudvīpas, as stated in the Sūtra: "In order to attain the fearlessness of turning the Great Wheel of Dharma."
One who gives rise to such a mind is, as explained in the section on the fundamental nature, a son of the Buddha because their bodhisattva vow is well-determined.
Why is it said only that they "give rise to the mind," rather than saying they give rise to "wisdom" or other mental factors (*caitasika*)?
Because within the mind one encompasses and knows all the factors conducive to enlightenment—namely, those to be abandoned, those to be realized, and those to be cultivated.
Having explained for what purpose such a mind is generated, I shall next explain by what causes such a mind is generated.

The Sūtra says: This mind takes great compassion as its primary focus, is preeminent in wisdom, and is embraced by skillful means. It is characterized by a straightforward mind and a profound mind of ultimate sincerity. Possessing the immeasurable powers of the Tathāgata, it possesses the power of well-determined sentient beings and the power of wisdom. It accords with spontaneous wisdom and is able to receive all Buddha-dharmas; through the transformation of wisdom, it is as vast as the Dharma-realm and as ultimate as space, extending to the end of the future.
The treatise states:
This has great compassion as its primary focus.
Within it, there are nine types of great compassion:
First is the supremacy of increase: because the wisdom of subtle suffering arises through increase, as the Sūtra says, "wisdom is supreme.

Wisdom (*jñāna*) refers to the contemplation of cause and effect in both their direct and reverse orders, as well as defilement and purification; discernment (*prajñā*) refers to the contemplation of the distinctions between specific and general characteristics.
Second is the greatness of inclusion, which is comprised of skillful means for rescuing suffering sentient beings, as the sutra states: "comprised of skillful means.

Third is the greatness of pure devotion, wherein one previously vowed to increase the compassionate mind that benefits sentient beings until the very end of the realm of sentient beings, as the sutra states: "the purity of the direct mind and the profound mind."
Fourth is the greatness of immeasurability, which encompasses the immeasurable powers of the Tathāgata, as the sūtra says: "The power of the Tathāgata is immeasurable.

Fifth is the greatness of certainty, which consists of the supreme, wondrous certainty of faith and the superior remedial wisdom of profound insight, as the sūtra says: "The power of beings who are well-determined and the power of wisdom."
Sixth is the greatness of conformity, which conforms to the perfect awakening of bodhi, as the sūtra says: "conforming to self-arising wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*).

Seventh is the greatness of correct reception, which is able to receive the great and supreme Dharma to instruct sentient beings, as the sūtra says: "able to receive all Buddha-dharmas and transform others through wisdom."
Eighth is the greatness of supreme excellence, which encompasses superior and sublime merits, as the sutra says: "Vast as the dharma-realm.

Ninth is the greatness of abiding until the end, wherein the causes for immeasurable fruits of love persist until the limit of nirvana, as the sutra says: "Ultimate as space, reaching to the end of the future."
Having explained by what causes such a mind is generated, the following explains what characteristics arise at the moment this mind is born.
The Sūtra says:

"As soon as a Bodhisattva generates such a mind, he immediately transcends the stage of ordinary beings and enters the rank of Bodhisattvas; he is born into the family of the Buddhas, his lineage is noble and beyond reproach; he transcends all worldly paths and enters the supramundane path; he dwells within the Bodhisattva-dharma and abides in the true station of a Bodhisattva; he enters into the *tathatā* (suchness) of the three periods of time and the lineage of the Tathāgatas, becoming definitively destined for the ultimate realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
When a bodhisattva abides in such dharmas, it is called "abiding in the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy," because of the quality of immovability.
The Commentary states:
Regarding "transcending the stage of ordinary beings," because one transcends the stage of ordinary beings, it demonstrates the attainment of the supramundane noble path.
This fault is of eight kinds:

first, the fault of entering the stage (*avasthā-praveśa-doṣa*). This refers to the initial formation of the supramundane mind, which is analogous to the state of first dwelling in the womb; as the Sūtra says, "entering the bodhisattva stage."
Second is the fault of the family (*kula*), because it is analogous to being born into a family, as the Sūtra says, "born into the family of the Buddha.
Third is the fault of the lineage (*gotra*), because it is analogous to a son, for the practice of the Mahāyāna arises from it, as the Sūtra says, "the lineage is noble and beyond reproach."

Fourth is the transcendence of the path (*mārga-samatikrama*): because the mundane and supramundane paths are not subsumed [by it], yet it subsumes them; and because it gives rise to a dharma similar to other paths. As the Sūtra says: "Transcending all mundane paths, one enters the supramundane path."

Fifth is the excellence of the essential nature (*dharmatā*). Taking great compassion as its essence, it regards the affairs of others as its own; because its own nature is analogous to this quality, as the sutra says: "Abiding within the bodhisattva-dharma."

Sixth is the excellence of abiding (*sthāna-viśeṣa*): because one does not abandon worldly skillful means while dwelling in undefiled expertise; because it is a dharma analogous to the place of abiding; as the sūtra says, "abiding in the correct place of a bodhisattva."

Seventh is the transcendence of karma: because it accords with the life-like dharma of the noble wisdom that conforms to emptiness, as the sūtra says, "entering into the true suchness of the three periods of time.

Eighth is the transcendence of certainty: because the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed, and there is the ultimate attainment of nirvāṇa through the perfection of the path, as the sūtra says, "within the lineage of the Tathāgatas, one is certain to attain ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Thus it is demonstrated that the birth of an ordinary person and the birth of a bodhisattva entering the womb are dissimilar, because one possesses afflictions while the other is free from them.

Likewise, there is a sequence of dissimilarities: dissimilarity of family, dissimilarity of lineage, dissimilarity of path, dissimilarity of essence, dissimilarity of location, dissimilarity of birth-activities, and dissimilarity of accomplishment. Thus it is said that dwelling within this stage is called "dwelling," as the Sūtra states: "A bodhisattva dwelling in such dharmas is said to dwell in the Bodhisattva Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), because of the quality of immovability."
The meaning of "abiding" has already been explained; next, the explanation of the name will be given.
How is it explained?
Because there is great joy, it is designated by the name "Joyful."
With what joy? It is the joy of the bodhisattvas within this stage.
Furthermore, with what intention were the first ten phrases spoken, followed by the subsequent twenty phrases?
The Sūtra says:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When these Bodhisattvas dwell in the Bodhisattva stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they achieve abundant joy, abundant faith and reverence, abundant affection, abundant celebration, abundant pliancy, abundant exultation, abundant receptivity, abundant non-subversion of others' intentions, abundant non-affliction of sentient beings, and abundant freedom from anger and resentment."
The treatise states:
"Joy" (prāmodya) is defined as gladness of mind; its essence is the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya).
This joy is of nine kinds:
First is the joy of reverence, because of one's respectful veneration toward the Three Jewels, as the sutra says, "abounding in faith and reverence.
Second is the joy of affection, because of one's delight in contemplating the dharma of *tathatā*, as the sutra says, "abounding in love and mindfulness."
Third is the joy of celebration, which is the realization that what one has personally attained is superior when compared [to others], as the sūtra says, "much rejoicing.
Fourth is the joy of pliancy, which is the accomplishment of pervasive benefit for one's own body and mind, as the sūtra says, "much pliancy."
Fifth is leaping with joy; one’s own body and mind are universally benefited and increased to a state of supreme fulfillment, as the sūtra says, "much leaping.
Sixth is being capable of receiving joy; one perceives for oneself that awakening is near, as the sūtra says, "much capability."

Seventh is unimpaired joy: with one's own mind subdued, the mind is not disturbed when engaging in debate or explaining the teachings, as the sutra says, "for the most part, they do not impair the minds of others."

Eighth is the joy of non-affliction; when teaching and transforming others and gathering in sentient beings, one is compassionate, gentle, and harmonious, as the sutra states: "For the most part, they do not afflict sentient beings."

Ninth is being free from anger and full of joy: when seeing sentient beings who do not practice as they have been taught or whose deportment is improper, one endures them without becoming angry; thus, as the sutra says, "one is largely free from resentment."
Having already explained "much joy," it next explains by means of what mindfulness such joy is accomplished;
this is stated in the twentieth and thirtieth phrases.
This mindfulness is of two kinds:
First, mindfulness of what is to be attained;
second, mindfulness of what is presently attained.
What is mindfulness of what is to be attained?

The Sūtra says: "O Sons of the Buddha! When Bodhisattvas dwell in this Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they give rise to a mind of joy by recollecting all Buddhas; they give rise to a mind of joy by recollecting all Buddha-dharmas; they give rise to a mind of joy by recollecting all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they give rise to a mind of joy by recollecting the practices performed by Bodhisattvas; they give rise to a mind of joy by recollecting the pure characteristics of the *pāramitās*; they give rise to a mind of joy by recollecting the superior excellence of the various Bodhisattva stages; they give rise to a mind of joy by recollecting the non-retrogression of the powers of Bodhisattvas; they give rise to a mind of joy by recollecting the teaching methods of all Tathāgatas; they give rise to a mind of joy by recollecting their ability to benefit sentient beings; and they give rise to a mind of joy by recollecting their entry into the wisdom-practices of all Tathāgatas."
The treatise says:
What is mindfulness?
It is the mindfulness that thinks, "Just as the Buddha has attained it, so shall I also attain it."
This mindfulness of the Buddha has nine aspects:
first, mindfulness of the Buddha-dharma, as the sutra says, "Because one mindfully contemplates the dharmas of all Buddhas, a heart of joy arises.
Second, mindfulness of the Buddha’s bodhisattvas, as the sutra says, "Because one mindfully contemplates all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, a heart of joy arises."
Third is mindfulness of the practice of the Buddhas, as the sutra says: "Because one mindfully recollects the practices performed by all bodhisattvas, a heart of joy arises.
Fourth is mindfulness of the purity of the Buddhas, as the sutra says: "Because one mindfully recollects the pure characteristics of all the pāramitās, a heart of joy arises."
Fifth is the excellence of mindfulness of the Buddhas, as the sutra says: "Because one compares and finds the superiority of the stages of all bodhisattvas, one gives rise to a mind of joy.
Sixth is the non-retrogression of mindfulness of the Buddhas, as the sutra says: "Because one reflects on the non-retrogression of the powers of all bodhisattvas, one gives rise to a mind of joy."

Seventh is mindfulness of the Buddha’s transformation through teaching, as the sutra says: "Because one mindfully contemplates the Dharma by which all Tathāgatas transform beings, a heart of joy arises.
Eighth is mindfulness of the Buddha’s benefit, as the sutra says: "Because one mindfully contemplates his ability to benefit sentient beings, a heart of joy arises."
Ninth is the entry through mindfulness of the Buddha, as the sūtra states: "Because one mindfully enters the wisdom-practice of all Tathāgatas, one gives rise to a heart of joy.
Within this, the first two types of mindfulness are shared mindfulness of the Buddha, because [the practitioner thinks], "Just as the Buddha has attained [this], so shall I also attain it."
One contemplates the Buddha’s mind because one contemplates the minds of all Buddhas; this is because the Buddha and the Buddha’s mind are two distinct things.
One contemplates the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas because one contemplates all Bodhisattvas.
One contemplates the Buddha’s practice because one contemplates the practices of all Bodhisattvas.
In this sequence, there are six further phrases: mindfulness of the Buddha’s purity, because one contemplates the pure characteristics of the various pāramitās;
and mindfulness of the excellence of the Buddha, because one compares and evaluates the superiority of the bodhisattva stages.
They do not regress in mindfulness of the Buddha, because they do not regress in the power of mindfulness of all bodhisattvas;
they are mindful of the Buddha’s transformation through teaching, because they are mindful of the methods of transformation taught by all Tathāgatas;
they are mindful of the Buddha’s benefit, because they are mindful of his ability to benefit sentient beings.
One enters by mindfulness of the Buddha, because one enters the wisdom-practice of all Tathāgatas.
According to what is manifested, that bodhisattva practice is revealed.
By what is it revealed?
These various recollections should be understood in this way.
Furthermore, what do they reveal?
They reveal the purity of those perfections (pāramitā).
How is it manifested?
Because that Bodhisattva’s practice of the stages (*bhūmi*) is superior through its progressive advancement and because the stages are completely traversed;

therein, the remainder [of the practices] consists in attaining the methods of conversion, ensuring that the conduct for benefiting sentient beings is not in vain, and entering the practice of the Tathāgata stage.
Among these, the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is both general and specific.
Having already explained that joy arises from mindfulness of what is to be attained, it now explains that joy arises from mindfulness of what is presently attained.
The Sūtra says:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
The Bodhisattva further reflects thus:"

I give rise to a heart of joy because I have turned away from all worldly realms; I give rise to a heart of joy because I am drawing near to the state of a Tathāgata; I give rise to a heart of joy because I am far removed from the stage of ordinary beings; I give rise to a heart of joy because I am approaching the stage of wisdom; I give rise to a heart of joy because I have severed all evil paths; I give rise to a heart of joy because I act as a refuge for all sentient beings; I give rise to a heart of joy because I am drawing near to seeing all Buddhas; I give rise to a heart of joy because I am born into the realm of all Buddhas; I give rise to a heart of joy because I enter the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma of all Bodhisattvas; and I give rise to a heart of joy because I am free from all terrors such as the bristling of body hair.
The treatise states:
"I have turned away from all worldly spheres" means that I have turned away from all matters of grasping and attachment characteristic of ordinary beings.
This turning away consists of nine kinds:
First is the detachment through entry and transition, as the sūtra says: "Because they draw near to entering the realm of the Tathāgata, they give rise to a heart of joy.
Second is the detachment through distancing and transition, as the sūtra says: "Because they distance themselves from the stage of ordinary beings, they give rise to a heart of joy."
Third is the turning away through approaching, as the sutra says: "Because one has approached the stage of wisdom, one gives rise to a heart of joy.
Fourth is the turning away through severance, as the sutra says: "Because one has severed all evil paths, one gives rise to a heart of joy."
Fifth is the turning away from reliance, as the sūtra says: "Because one acts as a refuge for all sentient beings, a heart of joy arises.
Sixth is the turning away from proximity, as the sūtra says: "Because one draws near to and beholds all Buddhas, a heart of joy arises."
Seventh is the turning away from birth, as the sutra says: "Because one gives birth to the realm of all Buddhas, one gives rise to a mind of joy.
Eighth is the turning away from equality, as the sutra says: "Because one enters the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all bodhisattvas, one gives rise to a mind of joy."

Ninth is the turning away through relinquishment (*prahāṇa-vivarta*), as the sūtra says: "I have given rise to a mind of joy because I am free from all matters that cause fear and the bristling of body hair.
Within this, the turning away through entry (*praveśa-vivarta*) is shown because the matters [of the two] are dissimilar.
"Remote turning-away and proximate turning-away" are shown because one's own body is dissimilar [to others].

There are six further phrases: turning-away through abandonment, turning-away through reliance, turning-away through close observation, turning-away through birth, turning-away through equality, and turning-away through relinquishment. These follow in sequence because their modes of action are dissimilar, their mutual reliance is dissimilar, their external conditions are dissimilar, their locations are dissimilar, their karmic births are dissimilar, and their accomplishments are dissimilar.
Fear (*bhaya*) is that which is associated with a mind characterized by aversion, doubt, and anxious reflection.
Furthermore, there are physical manifestations of it, such as the bristling of body hair and so forth.
Next, it is explained what constitutes fear.
What is the cause of fear?
It is because by remaining far removed from this cause, there is no fear.
The Sūtra says:

Why is this? Once these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), all fears are immediately and completely removed—namely, the fear of lacking a livelihood, the fear of ill repute, the fear of death, the fear of falling into the evil realms, and the fear of being intimidated by great assemblies. They are thus freed from all such fears.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have abandoned the notion of a self, they do not even crave their own bodies, let alone the things they use; therefore, they have no fear of being unable to sustain themselves.

The mind harbors no desire for offerings or honor; rather, one thinks, "I should make offerings to all sentient beings and provide them with all their necessary requisites. For this reason, there is no fear of ill repute.
Being far removed from the view of self and free from the notion of a self, they have no fear of death.
