The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are those that conjoin with greed, hatred, and so forth; as the Sūtra states: "This bodhisattva, by means of the knowledge of others' minds, knows the minds and mental factors of other sentient beings as they truly are: he knows a mind possessed of greed as a mind possessed of greed, up to a mind free from delusion."
Regarding "messengers," there are those with afflictions and those free from afflictions, as the Sūtra says: "One knows truly the mind with defilement and the mind free from defilement.

Regarding "arising," it is small among humans, vast among the gods of the desire realm, great among the gods of the form realm, and immeasurable within the two liberations of the formless realm, as the Sūtra says: "the small mind, the vast mind, the great mind, and the immeasurable mind."
Regarding the practitioner of samādhi: as for the distracted mind and the non-distracted mind, it is as the sūtra says, "the concentrated mind and the unconcentrated mind.

Regarding one who has attained samādhi: during the times of entering meditative absorption and not entering it, as well as when emerging from absorption, it is as the sūtra says, "the mind abiding in absorption and the mind not abiding in absorption."
Regarding those who have attained liberation, there is the state of being bound and the state of being unbound, as the Sūtra says: "the liberated mind and the unliberated mind.

Regarding false practice and right practice, it is because within the pursuit of fame one manifests longing for what is favorable or unfavorable, as the Sūtra says: "the seeking mind and the non-seeking mind."

Other ordinary persons who possess overweening pride, because they practice coarse and subtle habitual tendencies, are as stated in the Sūtra: "One knows a superior mind as it truly is a superior mind, and one knows a non-superior mind as it truly is a non-superior mind."
Regarding the supernormal power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānābhijñā*):

who is it that can recollect? It is wisdom that is able to recollect; as the Sūtra states: "This Bodhisattva truly recollects and knows the immeasurable places of birth throughout his various past lives."
What matters does one recollect?

As the sutra states: "One is also able to recollect and know a single lifetime, up to recollecting and knowing immeasurable hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, and nayutas of kalpas."
What is mindfulness?
It is by means of the distinction of names, as the Sūtra says: "In the past, I was in such-and-such a place with such-and-such a name.
It is by means of the distinction of family, as the Sūtra says: "I was of such-and-such a clan."
The distinction between noble and base is as stated in the sūtra: "born in such a way.
The distinction between the beautiful and the ugly is as stated in the sūtra: "possessing such a form.
The distinction between fine and coarse provisions is as stated in the sūtra: "consuming such food and drink."
The distinction of karmic activities is as stated in the Sūtra: "Such is their lifespan; such is their duration of stay.

The distinction of decline and benefit, or formation and destruction, is as stated in the Sūtra: "Thus experiencing suffering and pleasure, I die there and am born here; I die here and am born there."
Among these, the distinction of family refers to the distinction between parents.
The distinction of noble and lowly refers to the distinction between Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and so forth.
The distinction of karmic conduct refers to the distinction of lifespan, due to death occurring either at the proper time or at an improper time.
Regarding the "various characteristics" herein, these refer to the distinctions among all marks, as indicated by the sūtra’s phrase "various characteristics.
Regarding the "speaker," this refers to their renown, as indicated by the sūtra’s word "speaker."
Regarding the characteristic of lineage (*gotra-lakṣaṇa*): because it pertains to family lineages and so forth, as the Sūtra states, "one is able to recollect and know all characteristics of lineage.
Furthermore, there is another meaning: one is also able to recollect and know one birth and two births.
Such as these are called "characteristics" (*nimitta*).
As for "explanation," it refers to names and so forth.
As for "signs" (*lakṣaṇa*), they are such as: "I died there and was born here."
Because one is able to recollect and know all such things as these.
As for the supernormal power of knowledge regarding birth and death (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), who is able to see?
It is seen by means of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
"Purified" means seeing with discernment.
"Surpassing that of humans" means seeing from afar, as the sūtra states: "This bodhisattva, by means of the purified divine eye-element, surpasses that of humans."
What things are seen?

They are the birth and death of sentient beings and so forth, as stated in the Sūtra: "He sees all sentient beings being born or dying, and even knows, in accordance with reality, all that they have created according to their karma."
What is meant by "seeing"?

It is as stated in the Sūtra: "He knows, in accordance with reality, that these sentient beings have accomplished evil bodily karma, and so forth, up to receiving retribution according to their karma.
The remainder is as explained previously in the second bhūmi.
The retribution of good and evil karma should be understood in this same way.

Among these, "dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas; "vimokṣa" refers to the four formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpattis); "samādhi" refers to the four immeasurables (apramāṇas); and "samāpatti" refers to the five supernormal powers (abhijñās).
Regarding "being able to enter and being able to emerge": this is because at the very moment the mind arises, its corresponding function manifests before one.
As for "not arising through the power of dhyāna or liberation," this demonstrates the accomplishment of that mind of profound, thick, and deep mindfulness.

Regarding "following what one sees to fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment" (bodhipakṣadharma), this is because one is born in the same place as all Buddhas and great bodhisattvas; as the Sūtra says: "This bodhisattva, through the power of his vows, is born therein, from the meditative absorptions and liberations up to [the higher realms]."
The Sūtra says:

When this bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva Ground of Radiance, they see many Buddhas by virtue of their great power of supernormal knowledges and their great power of vows; they see many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, many billions of Buddhas, many hundreds of billions of Buddhas, many trillions of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, by virtue of their great power of supernormal knowledges and their great power of vows.

When this bodhisattva sees the Buddhas, he makes offerings, pays homage, respects, honors, and praises them with a superior mind and a profound mind; he presents them with all requisites such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions. He also provides the Sangha with the most excellent and delightful articles of the bodhisattvas. By means of these roots of goodness, he dedicates them all toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Toward all Buddhas, they give rise to a heart of supreme reverence and listen to the Dharma with single-minded focus; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, practicing according to the teachings. These bodhisattvas contemplate that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, existing only through causes and conditions.
The treatise states:

That all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing means that within pure phenomena no increase is perceived, and within afflictions and conceptual constructions no decrease is perceived, because they arise through the gathering of causes and conditions.

Within that purity, there is not a single dharma to be added; within those afflictions and delusive thoughts, there is not a single dharma to be subtracted. Nevertheless, by virtue of the conditions of the remedial counteractive measures, one becomes free from afflictions and delusive thoughts, and the increasingly superior, pure prajñā manifests before one.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "One contemplates that all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, but exist by way of causes and conditions.
The Sūtra states:
"The bonds of all desire of this bodhisattva become even more subtle and thin; the bonds of all form, the bonds of all existence, and the bonds of all ignorance all become entirely subtle and thin."
Those bonds of various views have already been eliminated.

Once this bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), for immeasurable hundreds of kalpas, immeasurable thousands of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, immeasurable billions of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of billions of kalpas, immeasurable thousands of billions of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, they no longer manifest as accumulated;
they sever false craving; they no longer manifest as accumulated; they sever false hatred.
They no longer manifest as accumulations, having severed delusion and ignorance.
Thus, the roots of goodness of these Bodhisattvas become increasingly bright and pure.
O Sons of the Buddha!
For example, it is like pure gold that a skilled smith refines and purifies; while its weight remains constant, it becomes increasingly refined and its radiance becomes doubly superior.
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is the same for a Bodhisattva who, having dwelled in the Bodhisattva Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), does not again manifest the accumulation [of afflictions] for immeasurable hundreds of kalpas, even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, as they have severed false craving.
They no longer manifest as a collection [of afflictions], having severed deluded anger;
they no longer manifest as a collection, having severed deluded ignorance, so that those roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.

This Bodhisattva’s mind of patience and tranquility becomes increasingly bright and pure; their mind of concord, their pliant mind, their non-angry mind, their immovable mind, their unclouded mind, their mind free from the conceit of high and low, their mind that does not expect anything from the deeds of sentient beings, their mind that does not look for reward in whatever they do, their non-deceptive mind, and their mind free from the thicket of afflictions become increasingly purified.

Among the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), this bodhisattva’s excellence lies in beneficial action; among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), excellence lies in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*). This does not mean that the other perfections are not practiced; rather, they are cultivated according to his strength and capacity.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the brief explanation of the third bodhisattva stage, the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).
The treatise says:

"All fetters of desire become even more attenuated" means that all afflictions belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness—which are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation—as well as their causes and the habitual tendencies of ignorance, are all rendered thin and are completely distanced and eliminated.
The fetters of various views have already been severed at the time of the path of seeing within the first stage (*bhūmi*).
As the Sūtra states: "For this bodhisattva, all fetters of desire become even more attenuated, up to the point that the fetters of various views have already been eliminated."

Regarding the phrase "no longer manifesting the accumulation [of afflictions], thereby severing false greed and so forth": this refers to severing the unwholesome roots, their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and their active manifestations (*vṛtti*); it does not refer to severing coarse afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), as these have already been severed in the preceding stages.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "Once this bodhisattva has dwelled in the Bodhisattva Stage of Radiance, for immeasurable hundreds of kalpas, those roots of goodness become increasingly more radiant and pure."
The analogy of refined gold illustrates that it remains constant without losing its weight or measure;
likewise, when a bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), their renunciation of the world surpasses that of the preceding stage, as they do not lose their mastery.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "O Sons of the Buddha!
It is like, for example, primordial refined gold, and so forth, until those roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.
Thus, when this Bodhisattva’s mind of patience and tranquility becomes even more bright and pure, he is able to endure the malicious intent of others and skillfully protects their minds.
As the sutra states: "This bodhisattva’s mind of patience and peace becomes increasingly bright and pure.

Even when others inflict harm, he does not fail to properly protect the minds of others; he manifests through discernment as one who commits evil or harbors doubt, appearing as a companion using affectionate speech to instruct and lead them, as the sutra says: "because of a harmonious mind" and "because of a gentle mind."

To encounter evil without anger, to hear abuse without retaliation, and not to give rise to distress or affliction—this is because of the "non-angry mind," the "unshakable mind," and the "unturbid mind" as described in the Sūtra.
In the past, he was not arrogant and spoke kindly to himself, as the sūtra says, "without a mind of highness or lowness.
His mind did not hope for the respect of others, as the sūtra says, "a mind that does not hope for what sentient beings do."
In performing deeds, one does not seek recompense in the mind, as the sūtra says: "In whatever one gives or acts, there is no expectation of reward.
One does not perform beneficial actions with an insincere mind, nor with partiality and the like, as the sūtra says: "With a mind free from flattery and crookedness."
They are entirely free from subtle, concealed, and defiled states of mind, as the sūtra says: "The mind, no longer like a dense forest, becomes further purified.
The sūtra states:

When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage, they frequently become kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; having attained mastery over the Dharma, they are able to eliminate the stains of afflictions such as greed in sentient beings, and by the power of skillful means, they rescue sentient beings from the mire of their various desires.

The wholesome deeds they perform—generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation—all these merits are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of bodhisattvas, mindfulness of bodhisattva practices, mindfulness of the pāramitās, mindfulness of the ten stages, mindfulness of the indestructible powers, mindfulness of the fearlessnesses, and mindfulness of the unique buddha-dharmas, up to and including being never apart from mindfulness of the possession of all aspects of the knowledge of all modes.
One should constantly give rise to this thought:

"I shall become the foremost, the most excellent, the greatest, the sublime, the most subtle, the highest, the unsurpassed, the guide, the general, the teacher, and the venerable among all sentient beings, even unto becoming the one upon whom the wisdom of omniscience relies."

Furthermore, from this thought he gave rise to diligent practice; by the power of such diligence, in a single moment of thought he attained hundreds of thousands of samādhis, beheld hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, knew the spiritual powers of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, was able to shake hundreds of thousands of Buddha-worlds, was able to enter hundreds of thousands of Buddha-worlds, was able to illuminate hundreds of thousands of Buddha-worlds, was able to teach and transform sentient beings in hundreds of thousands of Buddha-worlds, was able to abide for the duration of hundreds of thousands of kalpas, was able to know the events of hundreds of thousands of kalpas each in the past and future worlds, was able to skillfully enter hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates, and was able to manifest a body as hundreds of thousands of forms, with each individual body manifesting hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas as its retinue.
If one considers the sovereign excellence of their power of vows, a bodhisattva’s power of vows exceeds these numbers.

They manifest various kinds of supernormal powers—whether through the body, or light, or supernormal faculties, or the eyes, or spheres of experience, or voice, or conduct, or adornments, or empowerments, or faith, or karma.
These supernormal powers (abhijñā) continue until they cannot be numbered or known even throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
The Commentary says:
These are the fruits of the retribution of the stage and the fruits of the power of the wisdom of vows, as explained in the section on the First Stage.
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*, Third Fascicle of the *Prabhākārī-bhūmi*,
and Sixth Fascicle of the *Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*.
Composed by Bodhisattva Maitreya (Sthiramati).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Later Wei Dynasty. 4.
*Jvalanābhūmi* (The Blazing Ground). The treatise states:
The fourth ground, *Jvalanā*, is so named because it manifests based on that pure samādhi through the purity of the wisdom that hears and retains [the Dharma] as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
The distinctions of this stage consist of four parts:
first, the part on the causes for the increase of the cultivation of purification and remedies;
second, the part on purification.
Third, the section on the increase of the cultivation of antidotes;
fourth, the section on their results.
Regarding the causes for the increase of the cultivation of pure antidotes, these are the ten entries into the light of the Dharma.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said:
"O Sons of the Buddha!"

If a bodhisattva, having attained the third bodhisattva stage and perfected its pure illumination, desires to attain the fourth bodhisattva stage, they should enter the fourth stage by means of ten illuminating entries into the Dharma (*dharmāloka-mukha*).
What are the ten?
First, the clear entry through contemplation of the realm of sentient beings;
second, the clear entry through contemplation of the world-realm.
3. The luminous entrance of contemplating the dharma-realm;
4. The luminous entrance of contemplating the space-realm;
5. The luminous entrance of contemplating the consciousness-realm.
Sixth, the clear entry through reflection on the desire realm;
seventh, the clear entry through reflection on the form realm;
eighth, the clear entry through reflection on the formless realm.
9. The clear entry into the realm of resolute faith through the contemplation of the superior mind;
10. The clear entry into the realm of resolute faith through the contemplation of the great mind.
By means of these ten clear entries into the realms of phenomena, the bodhisattva enters the fourth stage.
The Treatise says:

Regarding the "entry into the illumination of the Dharma" (*dharmāloka-praveśa*), it refers to attaining the light of wisdom pertaining to the stages (*bhūmi*). By relying on that illumination of wisdom, one enters into the teachings expounded by the Tathāgata; thus, that wisdom is called the "entry into the illumination of the Dharma."
One should correctly contemplate, deliberate upon, and know as they truly are the teachings he has expounded, because one practices in accordance with these two points.
This deliberation has ten types of distinctions:
the deliberation on the conceptual differentiation of the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), as in the sūtra’s statement, "deliberating on the clear entry into the realm of sentient beings."
The discrimination based on abiding is as stated in the sūtra: "the clear entry through contemplation of the world.
The defiled discrimination is as stated in the sūtra: "the clear entry through contemplation of the dharma-realm."
The discrimination of inexhaustibility is as stated in the sutra: "the clear entry through contemplation of the realm of space.
The discrimination of the basis for defilement and purity is as stated in the sutra: "the clear entry through contemplation of the realm of consciousness."

The defilements of afflictions and conceptualization are as stated in the sūtra: "by reflecting upon the clear entry into the desire realm," "by reflecting upon the clear entry into the form realm," and "by reflecting upon the clear entry into the formless realm."

Purifying discrimination is as stated in the Sūtra: "Because of the clear entry into the realm of resolute faith through the contemplation of the superior mind," and "because of the clear entry into the realm of resolute faith through the contemplation of the great mind."
In this context, "afflictions," "latent tendencies," and "the defiled" refer to the three realms;
"the pure" refers to the latter two phrases:
first, being undefiled in reliance upon afflictions.
Second, regarding the meaning of whether or not one is equal to the śrāvakas and others in terms of not abandoning sentient beings:
what constitutes the purified portion?
It is that which gains increasing power within the family of the Tathāgata.
The Sūtra says:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When these Bodhisattvas attain the Bodhisattva stage of Blazing Fire (Arciṣmatī), they gain increasing power within the family of the Tathāgatas, because they have attained those internal dharmas and because they teach and mature others through ten kinds of dharma-knowledge."
What are the ten?
First, because of the non-retrogressive mind;
second, because of ultimate and exhaustive reverence toward the Three Jewels with certainty.
3. By means of analytical contemplation on the process of arising and ceasing;
4. By means of analytical contemplation on the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena;
5. By means of analytical contemplation on the formation and destruction of the world.
Sixth, by discerning that karma gives rise to birth;
seventh, by discerning the distinction between the world and nirvāṇa;
eighth, by discerning the differences in the karma of sentient beings and their worlds.
Ninth, by means of discerning and observing the distinctions between the prior limit and the posterior limit;
tenth, by means of discerning and observing the exhaustion of non-existence.
O Sons of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva thus matures through these ten kinds of knowledge of the dharmas, they gain increasing power within the family of the Tathāgata because they have attained those internal dharmas.
The treatise asks:
In what way do they gain increasing power within the family of the Tathāgata?

Because it relies upon the ultimate wisdom of extensive learning and because it excels by subsuming the elimination of cognitive obscurations, this suchness of purity and excellence is the family of the Tathāgata; therefore, it is called "attaining that internal dharma."

All the dharmas possessed by the Tathāgata himself are manifested through these very dharmas; that is to say, because he teaches and brings others to maturity through ten kinds of dharma-knowledge, it should be understood that this entry into the illumination of these dharmas is attained simultaneously.
Furthermore, because they are transformed and matured through four kinds of wisdom, this is called "transformation and maturation through the wisdom of the Dharma.
The four kinds of wisdom are:
first, the ultimate wisdom of abiding in one’s own place, as the sutra says, "because of the non-retrogressive mind."
2. Ultimate wisdom that equally reveres the Three Jewels, as the Sūtra says: "Because one definitively reveres the Three Jewels until they are ultimately exhausted.

3. Wisdom of True Suchness (*tathatā*), as the Sūtra says: "Because one analytically contemplates the process of arising and ceasing," and "because one analytically contemplates that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is non-arising."

Fourth, the wisdom that discriminates what is taught, as stated in the Sūtra: "because of discriminating the observation of the formation and destruction of the world," "because of discriminating the observation of the arising of karma," "because of discriminating the observation of the world and nirvāṇa," "because of discriminating the observation of the differences in the karma of the world of sentient beings," "because of discriminating the observation of the distinctions between the prior limit and the subsequent limit," and "because of discriminating the observation of the exhaustion of non-existence."
The Bodhisattva’s own abiding place refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Regarding the first two dharmas therein: it is the non-retrogressive mind that maintains definitive reverence toward the Three Jewels with ultimate sincerity.
These first two wisdoms are the ultimate wisdom of abiding in one’s own place and the ultimate wisdom of equal reverence for the Three Jewels, because they bring about transformation and maturation.

The next two involve the analytical contemplation of the processes of arising and ceasing, and the analytical contemplation that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-arising; this is the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness), namely, the contemplation of the selflessness of sentient beings and phenomena.
One should understand that this sequence of distinctions is to be known accordingly; the remainder are the wisdoms spoken of as being subject to conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, because they depend upon the defilement and purification of the afflictions (*kleśa*), they follow the defilement of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
By what afflictions is it defiled?
It is defiled by all that is pure, according to that which is purified.
How is it defiled by secondary afflictions?
Because it accords with the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), as the Sūtra says: "discerning the formation and destruction of the world.
Because it accords with the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) in terms of taking birth through common causes, as the Sūtra says: "discerning that there is birth due to karma."
What is defilement by afflictions?
It is the mundane world.
What is that which is pure?
This refers to nirvāṇa, as it is said in the sūtra: "Discerning and contemplating the world and nirvāṇa.
How does one follow that which is purified?

Because sentient beings are transformed within the worlds of the Buddhas through the maturation of their own karma, as stated in the Sūtra: "He discerns and contemplates the differences in the karma of the world of sentient beings."

Defilement and purification refer to the past limit (*pūrvānta*) and the future limit (*aparānta*), as stated in the Sūtra: "One discerns and contemplates the distinctions between the past limit and the future limit.

Regarding those past and future limits, there is neither loss nor gain, as stated in the Sūtra: "One discerns and contemplates the exhaustion of non-existence," because within defiled phenomena one does not see a single dharma that can be diminished, and within purified phenomena one does not see a single dharma that can be increased.
What is the antidote?
There are two ways in which cultivation increases:
first, cultivation that guards against the defilement of afflictions; [second, cultivation that increases wholesome qualities].
2. Second, the practice of protecting against the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
What constitutes protecting against the defilement of afflictions?
It is the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
The Sūtra says:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When these Bodhisattvas have dwelled in this Bodhisattva stage of Blazing Flames (Arciṣmatī), they contemplate the body internally, observing the body with diligence and single-mindedness, removing worldly greed and anxiety."
Contemplating the external body, he dwells observing the body, diligent, with a focused mind, removing worldly greed and sorrow.
Contemplating both the internal and external body, he dwells observing the body, diligent, with a focused mind, removing worldly greed and sorrow.

In this way, one contemplates internal feelings, external feelings, and both internal and external feelings; likewise, one contemplates the internal mind, the external mind, and both internal and external minds; and in this way, one contemplates internal phenomena by observing phenomena in accordance with the Dharma, exerting oneself with single-mindedness to eliminate worldly greed and sorrow.
Contemplating external phenomena through the contemplation of phenomena, one practices with diligence and single-mindedness to eliminate worldly greed and sorrow.
Contemplating both internal and external phenomena through the contemplation of phenomena, one practices with diligence and single-mindedness to eliminate worldly greed and sorrow.
This bodhisattva, for the sake of preventing the arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states, generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, and applies right abandonment.
For the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, and applies right abandonment.
For the sake of producing all unarisen wholesome dharmas, he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, and applies himself with right conduct.

For the sake of maintaining, not losing, cultivating to fulfillment, increasing, and expanding all arisen wholesome dharmas, he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, and applies himself with right conduct.
This bodhisattva practices the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), accomplishing the application of energy through concentration of desire.
He cultivates these bases of psychic power by relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, dedicating them toward equanimity.

Accomplishing the formative acts of abandonment through the concentration of energy, one cultivates the factor of the bases of psychic power, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, and dedicates it toward equanimity.

With concentration and the accomplishment of the formative forces of abandonment, one cultivates the bases of psychic power, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating them toward relinquishment.

With reflection and the accomplishment of the formative forces of abandonment, one cultivates the bases of psychic power, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating them toward relinquishment.
This bodhisattva practices the faculty of faith, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, dedicating it toward equanimity.
He practices the faculty of diligence, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, dedicating it toward equanimity.
One cultivates the faculty of mindfulness, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One cultivates the faculty of concentration, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
He cultivates the faculty of wisdom, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
This bodhisattva cultivates the power of faith, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One cultivates the power of energy, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One cultivates the power of mindfulness, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One cultivates the power of concentration, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One cultivates the power of wisdom, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
This bodhisattva practices the awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward equanimity.
He practices the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward equanimity.
One cultivates the awakening factor of energy, relying on disenchantment, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One cultivates the awakening factor of rapture, relying on disenchantment, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One cultivates the awakening factor of tranquility, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One cultivates the awakening factor of concentration, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
The bodhisattva cultivates the awakening factor of equanimity, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, dedicating it toward equanimity.
This bodhisattva cultivates right view, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, dedicating it toward equanimity.
One practices right intention, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One practices right speech, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One practices right action, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One practices right livelihood, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One practices right effort, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One practices right mindfulness, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment.
One practices right concentration, relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, dedicating it toward equanimity.
The treatise asks:
How does one practice the protection against the Lesser Vehicle?
Because he does not abandon any sentient being, he practices the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyadharma*).

The Sūtra says: This bodhisattva practices because his mind does not abandon any sentient being; because he gives rise to pure devotion through his original vow; because he takes great compassion as his foremost principle; because he accomplishes great loving-kindness; because he contemplates the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*); because he seeks to adorn the Buddha-lands; because he seeks to be fully endowed with the Buddha’s powers, fearlessnesses, unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*), and the wondrous voice; because he seeks the most supreme and excellent practices; and because he practices in order to accord with the hearing and liberation of the profound Buddha-dharma, and to contemplate great skillful means (*mahopāya*).
The Treatise says:
Regarding the mind that does not abandon any sentient being, this mind of non-abandonment has four aspects:
first, the initial; second, the beneficial; third, the aspirational; and fourth, the practical.
"Beginning" refers to the original vow, as the sutra states: "arising through the purity of the original vow.
"Benefiting" refers to compassion, as the sutra states: "taking great pity as the foremost" and "accomplishing great kindness."
"Hope" refers to seeking the wisdom of the Buddha, as in the sūtra’s "contemplating the knowledge of all modes" and "the practitioner’s cultivation.
There are five kinds of cultivation:
first, the cultivation of pure land practices, as in the sūtra’s "for the sake of giving rise to the adornment of the Buddha-land."

Second is the practice of cultivating the qualities of a Buddha, as stated in the sutra: "In order to give rise to the powers of a Tathāgata, the fearlessnesses, the unique Buddha-qualities (āveṇika-buddhadharma), the adornment of the marks and signs, and the possession of the wondrous voice."
"Exquisite sound" refers to the sound of the Dharma-conch.
Third is the practice of tireless application of the skillful means for that stage, as the sutra states: "in order to seek the ever-higher, superior practices."
Fourth is the cultivation of the practice for entering the stage of non-retrogression, as the sūtra says: "In order to accord with the hearing of the profound Buddha-dharma and liberation.
Fifth is the cultivation of the practice for teaching and transforming sentient beings, as the sūtra says: "One practices in order to contemplate great skillful means."
This is called the section on the increase of the cultivation of remedies.
What is the section on the fruit of the increase of the cultivation of remedies?
The Sūtra says:

This bodhisattva contemplates and extensively observes all matters arising from the view of a self-body as the foremost—including the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span, as well as the emergence and subsidence of the conceit of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—for the sake of their remediation, for the sake of the "I," for the sake of protection, and because they are objects of attachment.
This Bodhisattva completely eradicates all such matters as these.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the fruit that increases through the cultivation of remedies, [the Bodhisattva] extinguishes all such matters as arising and ceasing, including thoughts such as "I know," "I know greatly," "I practice," and "this is what I practice. Thus, all such things are entirely extinguished.
"Emerging" means the sense of arising from samādhi.
"Subsiding" means the sense of ceasing from samādhi.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of this:
There are five points: first, the root; second, arising; third, practice; fourth, protection; and fifth, faults.

Regarding these, "the root" refers to taking the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as the foundation. Based upon this, there arise the various distinctions of the conceit of a living being (*sattvāsmimāna*) and the conceit of phenomena (*dharmāsmimāna*). As the Sūtra states: "For this bodhisattva, all matters such as the arising and ceasing of the conceits of a self, a person, a living being, a life-span, and the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, have the view of a self-body as their primary cause."
"Arising" refers to the arising of improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), as the sutra says "reflection.
"Practicing" means making others know, as the sutra says "frequently observing."
"Guarding" (ārakṣā) means observing repeatedly, giving rise to the notion of self, and upholding; as the sūtra says: "because of healing, because of self, and because of guarding."
Regarding "transgressions," it means that the mind remains equanimous amidst all matters, as the sūtra states: "because of being attached to objects.
Thus, one completely distances oneself from arising and ceasing within the context of practicing these activities, as the sūtra states: "This bodhisattva completely eliminates all such matters."
This refers to the fruit of detachment arising from the defilement of afflictions.
The Sūtra says:
"Whatever actions this bodhisattva ought not to perform, and whatever defilements of the afflictions rebuked by the Tathāgata, he does not engage in any of them."
All actions that are to be performed in accordance with the bodhisattva conduct and all correct practices praised by the Tathāgata.
The treatise states:
Regarding all actions that are not to be performed, there are two reasons why they should not be done:
First, because they do not revere the Tathāgata, whom the Buddha does not praise.
Second, because they fear ill repute and give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*).
As the Sūtra says: "Whatever actions are improper for this bodhisattva, he does not perform them at all."
Regarding all deeds that ought to be performed, there are two reasons why they should be done:
first, because one perceives no ill reputation or profit [in them], as they accord with the bodhisattva practice.
2. Reverence for the Tathāgata, because the Buddha has praised it.
As the sūtra states: "All that is to be done, up to all correct practice."
This is the fruit of detachment arising from the defilement of karma.

Furthermore, as the Bodhisattva repeatedly engages in the factors conducive to enlightenment through the practice initiated by skillful wisdom, his mind becomes increasingly moistened and beneficial in this very manner.
These forty phrases demonstrate four kinds of fruits:
first, the arising of a superior desire for sublime qualities;
second, the performance of acts of gratitude toward those venerable ones who preach the Dharma.
Third, one arouses diligent effort within those skillful means;
fourth, one fulfills the fundamental mental continuum of that superior desire.
How does one give rise to a mind of superior desire toward excellent qualities?
The Sūtra says:

"This Bodhisattva further, according to each and every skillful means and wisdom that give rise to the factors conducive to the path of cultivation, in such and such ways accomplishes a mind that is moistening and beneficial, a pliant mind, a disciplined mind, a mind of peaceful happiness, an unstained mind, a mind that increasingly seeks higher and more excellent practices, a mind that increasingly seeks supreme wisdom, a mind that rescues all the world, a mind that reveres all teachers and receives their instructions in accordance with them, and a mind that practices in accordance with the Dharma as it has been heard."
The Commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "the practice initiated by the wisdom of skillful means as it applies to each respective case," this refers to the practice of not abandoning any sentient being, as previously explained.
The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) refer to all the factors of enlightenment and the limbs of the path.
"In this way and that way, one accomplishes a moistening and beneficial mind" means because of a profound desire for affection and reverence.
That moistening and benefiting mind has three aspects:
first, excellence in joyful practice, as the sutra says "a supple mind";
second, excellence in mastery over samādhi, as the sutra says "a disciplined mind."
Third, the excellence of the remedy that abandons faults, as stated in the Sūtra: "with a mind of peace and happiness.
There are six kinds of such faults:
first, the fault of food, or the fault of a jealous mind regarding the teaching of the Dharma.
This is the antidote, as stated in the sūtra: "because of the unstained mind.
Second, regarding the fault of the merit of having few desires: it is the lack of delight in extensive giving, the dhūta practices, and so forth.
The remedy for this is as stated in the Sūtra: "the mind that seeks ever higher and more excellent practices.
Third, the fault of the wisdom of few desires is not being inclined to seek superior wisdom.
This is the remedy, as stated in the sutra: "the mind that seeks ever-superior wisdom.
Fourth, the fault of indolence, which results in a lack of diligence in transforming sentient beings.
This is the remedy, as stated in the sutra: "the mind that rescues all the world."
Fifth, due to the fault of clinging to one's own views, the mind does not accord with the sublime teaching.
As an antidote to this, as stated in the Sūtra: "The mind that reveres all teachers and accords with their instructions."
Sixth, the fault of being dominated by equanimity (*upekṣā*) and failing to act in accordance with what has been taught.
Its remedy is as stated in the Sūtra: "a mind that practices according to the Dharma as it has been heard.
In this way, one accomplishes a mind of moistening benefit.
These ten phrases are called the fruit of generating a mind of superior aspiration toward supreme qualities.
How does one perform acts of gratitude toward that Honored One who expounds the Dharma?
The Sūtra says:

Thus, this bodhisattva achieves a mind that recognizes kindness and repays kindness; his mind becomes increasingly gentle, and he dwells in peace and harmony with others. With a straightforward and supple mind, he is free from the thicket of afflictions, devoid of flattery and crookedness, and free from pride. He properly receives instruction and grasps the intent of the teacher.
"Thus the accomplishment of a virtuous mind, thus the accomplishment of a tranquil mind, and thus the accomplishment of a perfectly tranquil mind.
The Commentary states:
"He performs acts of gratitude toward that Honored One who expounds the Dharma; this is demonstrated by the twentieth phrase, which reveals his mind of gratitude."
In this context, those who have accomplished the mind of gratitude practice the conduct of repaying kindness in accordance with it.
There are nine kinds of such conduct for repaying kindness, which arise based on the Honored One, as stated in the Sūtra: "knowing how to repay kindness."
Relying on fellow practitioners, one gives rise to a mind of protection, as the sūtra says, "the mind becomes supple" and "dwelling together in peace and happiness.
By practicing in accordance with the Dharma and following the teachings, one develops the capacity for endurance, as the sūtra says, "a straightforward mind" and "a gentle mind."

In reliance upon the consumption of food, one does not conceal one's own faults before the donor nor falsely proclaim one’s own virtues, as stated in the Sūtra: "because there is no conduct like a dense thicket" and "because there is no guile or crookedness."
One does not give rise to arrogance based on one’s own superior virtues, as the sūtra says, "there is no conceit.
One correctly receives verbal instructions based on the teaching, as the sūtra says, "skillfully receiving instruction."
Receiving the teaching without inversion means, as the sūtra says, "grasping the intention of the speaker.
In this way, the bodhisattva cultivates the practice of repaying the kindness toward that venerable one.
The accomplishment of such a virtuous mind is due to the increase of the cultivation of remedies.
The accomplishment of such a mind of quiescence is due to the power of the initial remedy and the increase of its cultivation.

For one who has thus accomplished the well-peaceful mind, that fruit is manifested by the first two lines; this is called the fruit of performing acts of gratitude toward the Honored One who teaches the Dharma.
How does one exert diligent effort within those skillful practices?
The Sūtra says:

This bodhisattva thus accomplishes unceasing diligence, undefiled diligence, non-retrogressive diligence, extensive diligence, boundless diligence, luminous diligence, incomparable diligence, indestructible diligence, diligence in transforming all sentient beings, and diligence in skillfully discerning what is the path and what is not the path.
The treatise states:
Within those preparatory practices (*prayoga*), one exerts diligent effort (*vīrya*) and achieves uninterrupted effort (*anikṣiptadhura-vīrya*), as indicated by the thirtieth phrase.
There are nine kinds of uninterrupted effort:
First, that vigor proceeds with an even flow, as the Sūtra states: "vigor free from defilement.
Defilement refers to being associated with laziness and attachment, or to falling into either excess or deficiency.
2. Immovability in one’s own vehicle, as the sūtra says, “non-retrogressive diligence”;
3. Vast mindfulness, as the sūtra says, “vast diligence.”
Fourth, because of the vow to gather in and benefit immeasurable sentient beings, as the sutra says, "boundless diligence" (*anantavīrya*).
Fifth, because of constant practice in accordance with the true mind, as the sutra says, "luminous diligence" (*prabhāsvaravīrya*).
Sixth, his cultivation of diligence surpasses all others, as the sutra states, "unequaled diligence.
Seventh, no demonic activities or afflictions can destroy it, as the sutra states, "indestructible diligence."
8. Because of inclusion, as the sūtra says: "the diligence of transforming and teaching all sentient beings.

9. Because of being able to sever doubt and confusion, subduing the words of others through correct cultivation, as the sūtra says: "the diligence of skillfully discerning what is the path and what is not the path."
This is called the fruit of exerting diligent effort within those skillful practices.
What is the fulfillment of that fundamental realm of mind?
The Sūtra says:
The realm of this bodhisattva’s profound mind becomes increasingly pure, and the realm of his profound mind is never lost.

The realm of his faith and understanding becomes increasingly sharp and keen; his production of roots of goodness increases, and he remains far removed from worldly defilements. He severs all doubt, and being free from the net of uncertainty, he becomes fully endowed with it in the present, accomplishing joy and bliss.
The Tathāgata bestows his presence, and immeasurable profound resolve is manifested and accomplished.
The Commentary states:
"That realm of mind becomes transformed and purified; this is demonstrated by the fortieth phrase."
Regarding the "mind-element" (*cittadhātu*), it is first indicated by the initial phrase concerning the mind of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
There are nine kinds of purity of the mind-element:
first, the increase through the cultivation of that path-mind, as the Sūtra says, "the profound mind-element is not lost."
2. Generating a mind of certainty regarding the superior realization, as the sūtra says: "The realm of faith and understanding becomes increasingly clear and sharp. 3.
Increasing the counteractive factors to those [obstacles], as the sūtra says: "The production of roots of goodness increases."
Fourth, the elimination of all obstacles, as the sūtra says: "being far removed from worldly defilements.
Fifth, the removal of secret doubts regarding this stage, as the sūtra says: "severing all doubting minds."
Sixth, because of the severance of doubt, there is certainty regarding other matters, as the sūtra says: "There is no web of doubt; it is fully present.
Seventh, by relying on the practice of supreme bliss, as the sūtra says: "One accomplishes joy and bliss."
8. Based on the power of transforming sentient beings, as stated in the sutra: "The Tathāgata bestows manifest empowerment. 9.
Based on the manifestation of immeasurable samādhis and the purification of the cognitive hindrances of the mind, as stated in the sutra: "Immeasurable minds are manifested and accomplished."
This is called the fruit of the fulfillment of the fundamental mind-realm.
The Sūtra says:
"When this bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva stage of the Radiant (Arciṣmatī), he sees many Buddhas by virtue of his great power of supernatural faculties and his great power of vows."

They see many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, many billions of Buddhas, many hundreds of billions of Buddhas, many trillions of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, by virtue of their great power of supernormal knowledge and the power of their great vows.

When this bodhisattva sees the Buddhas, with a superior mind and a profound mind, he makes offerings, pays respect, honors, and praises them; he presents all requisites—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and every other article of offering—and offers the most exquisite articles of pleasure used by bodhisattvas to the Saṃgha. By means of these roots of goodness, he dedicates them all toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Toward all Buddhas, they give rise to supreme reverence and listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, practicing according to their capacity, and leave the household life to cultivate the path within the teachings of the Buddhas. Thus, the Bodhisattva’s profound mind of resolute faith and understanding becomes increasingly clear and pure.

This bodhisattva, dwelling in this Bodhisattva Ground of Blazing Radiance for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of eons, possesses a profound resolve of certain faith and understanding that is impartial and pure; thus, those roots of goodness become increasingly superior, luminous, and pure.
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is like pure, genuine gold that a skilled craftsman refines and fashions into ornaments; once accomplished, they remain intact, and no other genuine gold that has not been made into ornaments can equal them.
O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas thus abide in this Bodhisattva stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*), those roots of goodness become accomplished and non-regressive, such that they cannot be surpassed by the roots of goodness of the lower stages.
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is like a mani-jewel that produces light; its pure circle of radiance can emit brilliant beams, achieving an indestructible state that cannot be eclipsed by the light of other jewels, nor can its brilliance be extinguished even when buffeted by all winds, drenched by rain, or soaked by water.
O Sons of the Buddha!

Thus, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva stage of Blazing Radiance (*Arciṣmatī*), they cannot be surpassed by Bodhisattvas of the lower stages, and all Māras as well as all afflictions (*kleśa*) are unable to destroy them.

Among the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), this bodhisattva excels particularly in "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*); among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*) is predominant; yet he does not fail to cultivate the remaining perfections, according to his strength and capacity.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the fourth bodhisattva stage, the Bodhisattva Stage of Radiance (*Arciṣmatī*).

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become the king of the Suyāma heaven, exercising sovereign mastery. They destroy such things as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) among sentient beings, and through skillful means, they cause sentient beings to abide in right view and other such qualities.

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—all such merits never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the bodhisattvas, mindfulness of the bodhisattva practices, mindfulness of the pāramitās, mindfulness of the ten stages, mindfulness of the indestructible powers, mindfulness of the fearlessnesses, and mindfulness of the unique qualities of a buddha, up to and including mindfulness of the possession of all aspects of the knowledge of all modes.
One should constantly give rise to this thought:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the greatest, the sublime, the most subtle, the highest, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, the teacher, and the honored one, even unto becoming the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge."
Again, he forms this thought and exerts himself with diligent practice.

By the power of diligence, in a single moment of thought, he attains a hundred million samādhis; he is able to see a hundred million Buddhas, know the spiritual powers of a hundred million Buddhas, shake a hundred million Buddha-worlds, enter a hundred million Buddha-worlds, illuminate a hundred million Buddha-worlds, transform sentient beings in a hundred million Buddha-worlds, abide for a lifespan of a hundred million kalpas, know the events of a hundred million kalpas each in the past and future worlds, skillfully enter a hundred million Dharma-gates, and manifest a hundred million bodies, in each of which he can manifest a hundred million bodhisattvas as his retinue.
If one considers the sovereign supremacy of the power of their vows, the bodhisattvas' power of vows exceeds this number.

They manifest various kinds of supernormal powers—whether through the body, or light, or supernormal faculties, or the eyes, or spheres of experience, or sounds, or conduct, or adornments, or empowerments, or faith, or karma.
These supernormal powers (abhijñā) are such that they cannot be calculated or known even throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
The Commentary says:

These bodhisattvas possess a profound mind of resolute faith and understanding that is equal and pure; those roots of goodness of theirs become increasingly superior, bright, and pure, just like those of bodhisattvas in other pure stages (bhūmi).

The analogy of using refined gold to create ornaments illustrates how the wisdom of realization (*sākṣātkāra-jñāna*) serves as an adornment manifested through the *āgama* (scriptural transmission), demonstrating the attainment of realized wisdom. As the sutra states: "It is like when a skilled smith refines and treats pure gold to fashion ornaments; they are accomplished and do not perish."

Regarding the analogy of the maṇi jewel producing light: from within the light of the maṇi jewel of the illumination of the Dharma of realized wisdom (adhigama-jñāna), the light of the Āgamas is emitted; it enters the sphere of the wisdom of the light of meaning within immeasurable dharma-gates, universally illuminating and manifesting them.
For this reason, the name of this stage is explained as "Blazing" (*Arciṣmatī*).
As the Sūtra says: "O Sons of the Buddha!
It is like a mani-jewel that produces light; its pure circle of radiance emits brilliant light that is indestructible and cannot be eclipsed by the light of other jewels."
"Producer of light" means that it is endowed with radiance.
"Pure circle of light" means that the radiance is perfect and stainless.
"Mastery over what is done" means that it destroys the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other such afflictions of all sentient beings.
In this context, "agent" refers to that which performs an action;
"sovereign" refers to capacity.
The remainder should be understood as previously explained.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Chapter Sixty:
The *Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*; Chapter Five: The *Sudurjayā-bhūmi*.
Composed by Bodhisattva Maitreyanātha.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Later Wei Dynasty. Chapter Five:
The Discourse on the Difficult-to-Conquer Ground (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*). It is said:
Within the fifth ground, there are three types of discernment.
1. The antidote to the pride of superiority;
2. The excellence of practicing the path of non-abiding;
3. The excellence of its fruit.
What is the antidote to the pride of superiority?
The sutra says:
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva has fully perfected all practices in the fourth bodhisattva stage and wishes to enter the fifth bodhisattva stage, they should enter the fifth stage by means of ten kinds of profound, pure, and equal minds.
What are these ten?
First, because of a profound and pure mind of equanimity toward the Buddha-dharma of the past;
second, because of a profound and pure mind of equanimity toward the Buddha-dharma of the future;
Third, because of the profound and pure mind of equality regarding the Buddha-dharma of the present;
fourth, because of the profound and pure mind of equality regarding the purity of ethical discipline;
fifth, because of the profound and pure mind of equality regarding the purity of the mind.
Sixth, because of the pure, equal, and profoundly pure mind that eliminates views, doubt, and regret;
seventh, because of the pure, equal, and profoundly pure mind of the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path;
eighth, because of the pure, equal, and profoundly pure mind of the knowledge of the abandonment of conduct.
Ninth, because of the profoundly pure mind of supreme purity and equanimity regarding the contemplation of all factors conducive to enlightenment;
tenth, because of the profoundly pure mind of purity and equanimity regarding the transformation and deliverance of all sentient beings.
O Sons of the Buddha!
By means of these ten kinds of equal, profound, and pure minds, a bodhisattva enters the fifth bodhisattva stage.
The commentary says:
The antidote to pride regarding superiority consists of the ten profound and pure minds of equality, because they involve the non-retrogressive mind of shared mindfulness.

While the antidote to pride regarding the understanding of phenomena was explained previously, it is now in this stage that the antidote to pride regarding the discrimination of the purity of the body is explained.
Regarding the "equanimous, profound, and pure mind" herein, it refers to attaining purity within equanimity.
This profound and pure mind is distinguished into ten types.
These ten types of profound and pure minds are the qualities of all Buddhas and that which accords with the qualities of all Buddhas; they should be understood through these distinctions.
What are the qualities of the Buddhas?

They are the powers of the three times and so forth, as stated in the Sūtra: "Because of the mind of equality, profundity, and purity regarding the Buddha-dharmas of the past; because of the mind of equality, profundity, and purity regarding the Buddha-dharmas of the future; and because of the mind of equality, profundity, and purity regarding the Buddha-dharmas of the present."
Thus, the powers of the Buddhas of the three periods of time have been explained. Next, the conformity to the teachings of all Buddhas will be explained.
How are those Buddha-dharmas accomplished?
It is through the causes of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the transformation of sentient beings.
In this regard, based on the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*), it is as the sutra says: "Because of the pure, equal, and profoundly pure mind.
Based on the purity of meditative concentration (*samādhi-viśuddhi*), it is as the sutra says: "Because of the pure, equal, and profoundly pure mind."

Based on the purity of wisdom, as the sūtra states: "Because of the pure, equal, and profoundly pure mind that eliminates views, doubt, and regret; because of the pure, equal, and profoundly pure mind regarding the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path; because of the pure, equal, and profoundly pure mind regarding the knowledge of practice and abandonment; and because of the pure, equal, and profoundly pure mind that contemplates all factors of enlightenment in their successive stages of excellence."

Regarding the wisdom of the abandonment of practice within this context: because one contemplates all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) as progressively superior and more excellent, it relies upon the transformation of sentient beings, as the Sūtra states: "Because of purifying the profound, pure mind of equality in order to transform and deliver all sentient beings."
The Sūtra says:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When these Bodhisattvas have already dwelled in the fifth Bodhisattva stage, because they skillfully practice the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), because their minds are well-purified and profound, because they further seek superior practices, because they act in accordance with the path of suchness, because they have attained the power of great vows, because they do not abandon any sentient beings due to their heart of compassion, because they cultivate the practices of merit and wisdom, because they do not cease their various activities, because they give rise to skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), because they illuminate and perceive the higher and highest stages, because they correctly receive the empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) of the Tathāgata, because they have attained the power of mindfulness, intention, and knowledge, and because they accomplish a non-retrogressive mind."
The Commentary states:

Among these, the thorough cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), up to and including practicing in accordance with the path of reality (*yathābhūtamārga*), constitutes the correct cultivation of all practices. Regarding the "thorough cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment":

this refers to the fourth Bodhisattva stage (*bhūmi*), where one cultivates the factors conducive to enlightenment through the complete purification of the profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*). Because that profoundly pure mind and so forth aspire for superior practice, one thus does not abide in the practice of the path; this is because it destroys that pride (*māna*).

One who practices in accordance with the path of suchness, because they manifest the accomplishment of a profoundly pure mind and a non-retrogressive mind within that equality, abides in that pure dharma of equality; thus, the profound mental abiding of such a bodhisattva is called practicing in accordance with the path of suchness.
Within this, there are eight kinds of practice that accord with the Way:
first, cultivating the bodhicitta, as the sūtra says, "because of attaining the power of great vows";
second, being free from weariness, as the sūtra says, "because of not abandoning any sentient beings through a heart of compassion."
Third, attaining the power of the roots of goodness, as the sūtra says: "Because of cultivating the practices of merit and wisdom.
Fourth, not abandoning various practices, as the sūtra says: "Because of never ceasing all practices."
Fifth, correct practice, as the sūtra says: "Because of the arousal of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Sixth, lack of satiety, as the sūtra says: "Because of clearly perceiving the progressively higher stages (*uttarottarabhūmi*)."
Seventh, attaining the power of others' supremacy, as the sūtra says: "Because they correctly receive the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata.

Eighth, because their own person attains supreme power and the three types of wisdom beginning with supreme mindfulness, as the sūtra says: "Because they have attained the powers of mindfulness, mental range, and knowledge (*jñāna*), and have accomplished the non-retrogressive mind."
"Departing" refers to the cultivation of wisdom-insight, because it has the sense of being without obstruction.
What is the excellence of the practice of the non-abiding path?
There are two kinds of contemplation regarding the excellence of the practice of the non-abiding path:
First, the excellence of the purity of wisdom regarding all knowable phenomena;
second, the excellence of diligent skillful means for benefiting sentient beings.
By virtue of these two dharmas, one dwells neither in the mundane world nor in nirvana.
What is the excellence of the purification of wisdom regarding the phenomena that are objects of knowledge?
The Sūtra says:

"This bodhisattva knows as it truly is: 'This is the noble truth of suffering,' 'This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering,' 'This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering,' and he knows as it truly is: 'This is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.'"

This bodhisattva is skilled in knowing the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), skilled in knowing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), skilled in knowing the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*), skilled in knowing the truth of distinctions (*viśeṣa-satya*), skilled in knowing the truth of established discourse (*vyavahāra-siddhi-satya*), skilled in knowing the truth of phenomena (*vastu-satya*), skilled in knowing the truth of arising (*utpāda-satya*), skilled in knowing the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna-satya*), skilled in knowing the truth of the knowledge that leads one into the path (*mārgāvatāra-jñāna-satya*), skilled in knowing the truth of the successive accomplishment of all bodhisattva stages (*bodhisattvabhūmi-krama-samudāgama-satya*), and skilled in knowing the truth of the accumulation of the Tathāgata’s wisdom (*tathāgata-jñāna-saṃbhāra-satya*).
Because this bodhisattva causes beings to rejoice according to their inclinations, they skillfully know the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);

because they have penetrated the single characteristic of all phenomena, they skillfully know the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), having awakened to the specific and general characteristics of phenomena.
One skillfully knows the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasatya*) because of awakening to the differentiation of phenomena.
One skillfully knows the truth of differentiation (*vibhāgasatya*) because of awakening to the analysis of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).
One skillfully knows the truth of the accomplishment of teaching (*deśanā-siddhisatya*) because of awakening to the suffering and affliction of body and mind.
They skillfully know the truth of phenomena (*vastu-satya*), because they awaken to the characteristics of the continuity of all paths.
They skillfully know the truth of arising (*utpāda-satya*), because they ultimately extinguish all feverish afflictions.
They skillfully know the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna-satya*), because they give rise to non-dual practice.
He skillfully knows the truth of the wisdom that causes entry into the path, because he has perfectly awakened to the characteristics of all phenomena.

He skillfully knows the truth of the successive accomplishment of all bodhisattva stages, as well as the truth of the accumulation of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, by means of the power of faith and understanding.
It is known through the knowledge that does not attain all-encompassing ultimate wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The treatise states:
Within the objects of knowledge, there are two superior forms of purity of wisdom:

First, the discrimination of real dharmas (*bhūta-dharma-vikalpa*): knowing the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, as the Sūtra states: "This bodhisattva knows the Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is, up to knowing the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering as it truly is."

Second, the distinction of skillful means for transforming sentient beings: the wisdom of skillful means regarding the distinctions of the ten truths, as stated in the sutra: "This bodhisattva skillfully knows the conventional truth, up to and including skillfully knowing the truth of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of accumulation."

Regarding the discrimination of real dharmas herein: whether a Buddha exists or not, the distinct entities of the cause and fruit of the two truths of suffering and origination are defiled by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); whereas the distinct entities of the cause and fruit of the two truths of cessation and the path are pure dharmas.

Regarding the distinctions in the skillful means for transforming sentient beings: one should know that because the sentient beings to be transformed are distinct, the skillful means are likewise distinct.
There are seven types of sentient beings to be transformed; among them, there are six types of those who can be transformed by the Hīnayāna:
first, for the sake of sentient beings whose faculties are not yet matured, there is the skillful means of knowing conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
2. For the sake of sentient beings whose faculties are mature, he knows the skillful means regarding the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
3. For the sake of sentient beings who harbor doubts regarding profound dharmas, he knows the skillful means regarding the truth of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-satya).
4. For the sake of sentient beings who are deluded by erroneous interpretations of the profound Dharma, he knows the skillful means of the truth of differentiation (*vibhāga-satya*).
5. For the sake of sentient beings who have strayed from right mindfulness, he knows the skillful means of the truth of accomplishment through teaching (*deśanā-siddhi-satya*).

Sixth, for the sake of clarifying the meaning for sentient beings with right view, one knows the skillful means of the truth of phenomena (*vastu-satya*), the skillful means of the truth of arising (*utpāda-satya*), the skillful means of the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna-satya*), and the skillful means of the truth of the knowledge that leads to entry into the Path (*mārga-praveśa-jñāna-satya*).
The truths of phenomena (*vastu-satya*) and so forth are subsumed within the Four Noble Truths, such as the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Seventh, for the sake of sentient beings who are to be converted through the Mahāyāna, one must skillfully know the truth of the sequential accomplishment of all bodhisattva stages, as well as skillfully know the truth of the accumulation of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

As the sutra states: "Because this bodhisattva causes beings to rejoice according to their inclinations, he skillfully understands conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), up to and including that which is not yet known by the ultimate wisdom (sarvajñajñāna)."

Regarding the sequence of the bodhisattva stages therein, it should be understood that one enters each stage in succession according to its own order; for in every place of birth, the body and mind undergo suffering and affliction.
Knowing the truth of suffering means that all that is felt is of the nature of suffering.
Engaging in non-dual practice means practicing with a single mode of conduct.
Perfectly awakening to all aspects means possessing skillful knowledge of the five fields of learning (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-bala*).
Regarding "knowledge," this refers to the power of wisdom through the contemplation of mirror-images, rather than the power of wisdom through the contemplation of non-attainment.

Thus, the excellence of the purity of wisdom regarding the dharmas to be known has already been explained; how, then, is the excellence of the skillful means of diligent application for the benefit of sentient beings described?
Because they know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) have the characteristic of being false and illusory, they give rise to thoughts of compassion for sentient beings.
The Sūtra says:

"When this bodhisattva has thus well-aroused the knowledge of the truths, he knows as it really is that all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are entirely false, deceptive, and delusive toward ordinary people."

At that time, the Bodhisattva’s great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) further manifests with increasing intensity toward sentient beings, and the light of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) arises. The Commentary states:

Regarding the passage from "this Bodhisattva, having thus well-aroused the knowledge of the truths" up to "the light of great loving-kindness arises," herein [it is explained that] they are "false" (*mṛṣā*) because things such as permanence are non-existent and do not correspond to reality; they are "constant" (*nitya*) because one constantly engages in the conceit of a self (*ātman-māna*); they are "delusive" (*vañcana*) because worldly phenomena are utterly destroyed; they are "deceptive" (*pralobhana*) because they entice foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*); they are "fraudulent" (*kūṭa*) because characteristics such as permanence are non-existent yet appear to exist; they are "vain" (*tuccha*) because the mind correctly grasps at the conceit of a self within these vain matters; they are "erroneous" (*vitatha*) because the benefit of worldly phenomena, which are afflictions, is exhausted; and they are "deceptive" (*visaṃvādaka*) because they entice the mind, as foolish ordinary beings are led away by worldly phenomena.
Because deceptive phenomena appear, it is said that they delude ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); the meaning of these phrases should be understood as follows.
"Ordinary persons" refers to those who rely upon and grasp at that body characterized by the conceit of self (*asmimāna*).
The one of great compassion and great kindness feels pity for those sentient beings.

Because he manifests superior benefit that surpasses the compassion of the preceding stage, it is called "great compassion" (mahākaruṇā); because his practice on the path is superior, he does not abide [in the mundane].
Because they have accomplished the skillful wisdom for saving sentient beings, it is called the "light of great compassion. The Sūtra says:

This Bodhisattva, having attained such power of wisdom, does not abandon any sentient being and constantly seeks the wisdom of the Buddha. He contemplates, according to reality, the prior and subsequent limits of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). He knows that all sentient beings arise from ignorance and craving regarding the prior limit, transmigrating through the world and returning to the home of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). They are unable to stir themselves free; instead, they increase the accumulation of the aggregates of suffering. Within this, there is no self (*ātman*), no life-span (*jīva*), and no sentient being (*sattva*); it is devoid of "I" and "mine" (*mamakāra*); he knows all of this as it truly is.
The same applies to the future limit (*aparānta*).
This non-existence, false attachment, and the exhaustion of the divisions [of existence] transcend both being and non-being; all are known as they truly are.
The Treatise says:
That these bodhisattvas attain such power of wisdom is as previously described.
That they do not abandon any sentient beings is because the radiance of their great compassion and great loving-kindness is also as previously described.
Those who seek the wisdom of a Buddha do so for the purpose of saving all sentient beings.

To contemplate, according to reality, the prior and posterior limits of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) involves demonstrating two aspects in accordance with that great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*):

first, contemplating the accumulation of the causes and conditions of suffering according to reality, as the Sūtra states: "Knowing that all sentient beings are born from ignorance and craving regarding the prior limit, up to knowing, according to reality, that both existence and non-existence are likewise."
