In this context, "arising from ignorance and craving since beginningless time" refers to the birth of ordinary beings, not the birth of bodhisattvas; for bodhisattvas arise through skillful means.
Why are other causal factors not mentioned?
It is because ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) are the roots of the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
Regarding those who are born, it is said that there are three kinds of sentient beings:

Sentient beings who seek sensual pleasures, sentient beings who falsely seek the holy life, and sentient beings who seek existence—even up to the mass of suffering consisting of the five aggregates at the peak of existence—these are matters of non-self;
herein, one's own person is without self.
Furthermore, that which is the matter of selflessness is non-existent from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Subsequently, although there is no self, it abides by the power of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and undergoes birth again and again; because the continuity of the sentient being’s body and mind is neither eternal nor annihilated, it is said that there is life and there are sentient beings.
To shatter the grasping of pride and conceptualization, it is said that there is no life and no sentient beings.
Because one is far removed from the conceit of a grasper and a grasped, as well as from the mind of selfhood, it is said that one is free from "I" and "mine" regarding the prior limit.
For what reason does one follow all sentient beings and engage in all forms of ascetic practice?
Having observed this correctly, he likewise observes the future limit as following from the causes of that suffering.
The exhaustion of ignorance, craving, and their objects is called cessation, because it is a cessation superior to that of the world.
That which issues forth is called the Path.

To know non-existence as it truly is, and to know existence as it truly is—this is called the first kind of great compassion: the correct contemplation of the causal conditions of the collection [of aggregates], based on the reality of suffering.
Next, the second type of great compassion is explained: the correct contemplation of profound and heavy suffering that pursues one through immeasurable lifetimes and its various manifestations.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the Bodhisattva forms this thought:

These ordinary worldlings are truly most strange; deluded and lacking wisdom, they have had immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable bodies that have already perished, are now perishing, and will perish.

Even after such total exhaustion and cessation, they are unable to conceive a sense of revulsion toward the body; instead, they further increase this mechanical body of suffering, constantly drifting with the world without being able to turn back. They cannot abandon their return to the house of the five aggregates, do not fear the four great poisonous snakes, cannot pull out the arrow of the view of self-conceit (*asmimāna*), cannot extinguish the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, cannot shatter the darkness of ignorance, and cannot dry up the great river of craving and attachment. Failing to seek the Great Sage Teacher endowed with the ten powers, they constantly enter the dense forest of Māra’s intent and are perpetually driven within the ocean of birth and death by various evil thoughts and observations.
The treatise states:
Great Compassion correctly contemplates profound and heavy suffering because it pursues various forms of suffering throughout immeasurable lifetimes.
It involves the extinction of immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodies because it pursues them throughout immeasurable lifetimes.
What is the contemplation on various kinds of suffering?
It is because of the suffering of birth, its origination, and the path leading to its cessation through separation from it.
One contemplates old age, sickness, and death in the same way: as suffering, their origination, and the path leading to their cessation through separation from them.
In this context, the statement that "this body is a machine-like body of suffering existing dependent on causes and conditions" is a manifestation of the suffering of birth.
The statement that "it constantly drifts with the world and cannot return" is a manifestation of the accumulation of craving.
"Those who cannot abandon or leave the house of the five aggregates" refers to the manifestation of the path of cessation that brings about detachment from them.
"Not fearing the four great poisonous snakes" refers to the suffering of illness, because they arise through increase or decrease [of the elements].
Sentient beings who falsely seek the holy life, sentient beings who seek sensual desires and indulge in them, and those who practice evil deeds—these are the sentient beings who possess seeking;
they are unable to extract the arrows of the view of self-conceit that have been manifested.
It cannot extinguish the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion; it cannot shatter the darkness of ignorance; and it cannot dry up the great river of craving and attachment.
In this manner, their accumulation is sequentially demonstrated.
They proceed toward the state of fearlessness, yet they do not seek the Great Holy Teacher endowed with the Ten Powers; they manifest as being far removed from that cessation.
They constantly enter the dense forest of Māra’s intent and follow the path of enmity, yet they manifest as being far removed from that path.

One who is constantly driven by various evil thoughts and observations within the ocean of birth and death should understand that these are all the false discriminations of the mind and mental factors throughout the three realms.
Next, the practice of contemplation on the radiance of supreme great compassion is explained.
The Sūtra says:

“I see those sentient beings undergoing such suffering and affliction—lonely and without rescue, without one to rely upon, without a shelter, without an island, without a final refuge, blind and sightless, entangled by the cataracts of ignorance and shrouded by delusion.”
For the sake of these sentient beings, one should give rise to this thought:

"May I alone, without equal or peer, cultivate and accumulate the merit, wisdom, and factors conducive to enlightenment; and by means of these provisions of merit, wisdom, and factors conducive to enlightenment, may I cause all sentient beings to abide in ultimate purity, even unto the attainment of the Buddha’s ten powers and unobstructed knowledge."
The treatise says:
Those who undergo such suffering and affliction are as previously described.
They are "solitary" because there is no one to rescue them from that suffering.
Furthermore, "the solitary" refers to those who have already experienced suffering or are yet to experience it.
"Without rescue and without reliance" means being separated from virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
"Without a shelter" means being separated from hearing the true Dharma.
To say they have no island means they are devoid of tranquil contemplation.
To say they have no ultimate goal means they are devoid of right view.

To say they are blind and sightless means that, being obstructed by both innate afflictions and adventitious afflictions, they constantly give rise to false thoughts and do not hear the True Dharma and so forth.
The statement that he is "enveloped by the cataracts of ignorance and shrouded by delusion, such that I alone am solitary and without equal" demonstrates his heroic and preeminent qualities.

The phrase "having cultivated and accumulated the merits and wisdom that assist the Path" demonstrates the growth of his practice, because by relying on those [merits and wisdom], he teaches and transforms sentient beings, acting as the cause for their becoming humans or devas, and even the cause for their attainment of nirvana.
"Ultimately pure" means that it is superior to worldly purity.
"Attaining the ten powers of a Buddha" means that one subdues all demonic adversaries.
"The exhaustion of unobstructed wisdom" means that it is superior to the pure wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Sūtra says:

“In this way, the Bodhisattva skillfully contemplates and gives rise to the power of wisdom; he cultivates all virtues and makes vows for the sake of rescuing all sentient beings, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, out of compassion for all sentient beings, for the sake of causing all sentient beings to be free from suffering and affliction, for the sake of causing all sentient beings to attain liberation, for the sake of gathering in all sentient beings, for the sake of purifying the minds of all sentient beings, for the sake of taming all sentient beings, and he makes vows for the sake of leading all sentient beings into Great Nirvāṇa.”
The Commentary states:
Regarding "skillfully contemplating therein to give rise to the power of wisdom," this is because one tames sentient beings through the wisdom of correct contemplation.
Regarding "all for the sake of rescuing and delivering all sentient beings," this is because one uproots all their suffering and affliction.
There are nine kinds of salvation:
first, causing sentient beings dwelling in unwholesome states to dwell in wholesome dharmas, as the sūtra says, "for the sake of bringing benefit to all sentient beings."
2. To cause sentient beings who abide in wholesome dharmas to obtain the fruits of happiness, as the sūtra says: "For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings. 3.
To provide all necessities of life to sentient beings who abide in poverty, as the sūtra says: "Out of compassion for all sentient beings."

Fourth, to cause all sentient beings who dwell in the suffering of illness and are afflicted by various external conditions to eliminate them entirely, as stated in the sutra: "In order that all sentient beings may be free from suffering and affliction."
Fifth, to cause sentient beings bound and confined in the world to attain liberation, as the sūtra says: "In order to bring about the liberation of all sentient beings.
There are four aspects by which one causes non-Buddhists to have faith and understanding in the True Dharma, as the sūtra says: "In order to gather in all sentient beings."
To decisively sever the doubts of sentient beings who are in a state of uncertainty, as the sutra says: "For the sake of purifying the minds of all sentient beings.
To encourage those who already abide in certainty to cultivate the three trainings, as the sutra says: "For the sake of subduing all sentient beings."

Sentient beings who have already established themselves in the three trainings are led to attain *nirvāṇa*, as the sūtra states: "He makes a vow for the sake of all sentient beings so that they may enter great *nirvāṇa*.
Among these nine ways of rescuing from suffering, the first two phrases rescue those of the future, while the remaining phrases rescue those of the present and also rescue those of the future.
This is called the excellence of practicing the path of non-abiding.
Next, the excellent fruits of practicing the path of non-abiding are explained;
they consist of four aspects:
First, superiority in the gathering of merit;
second, superiority in spiritual practice;
third, superiority in the teaching and transforming of sentient beings.
4. The superiority of giving rise to wisdom that accords with the world.
What is the superiority of encompassing merit?
It is due to the superiority of encompassing learning, ethical discipline, and wisdom.
The Sūtra says:
"When this bodhisattva has dwelled in this fifth bodhisattva stage, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā), he is called 'one who possesses mindfulness' because he does not forget any dharmas;
he is called 'one who possesses intention' because his wisdom is well-determined."
They are called "those who go" because they understand the meaning and sequence of the sūtras.
They are called "those with a sense of shame and dread of blame" because they protect themselves and protect others.
They are called "those of firm mind" because they do not abandon the practice of upholding the precepts.
He is called "the Awakened" because he skillfully contemplates what is possible and what is impossible.
He is called "one who follows knowledge" because he does not follow others.
He is called "one who follows wisdom" because he skillfully discriminates the phrases and sentences of all dharmas as to whether they are meaningful or meaningless.
They are called "those who have attained supernormal powers" because they have skillfully cultivated meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
They are called "those with skillful means" because they act in accordance with worldly dharmas.
The treatise says:
Regarding the excellence of gathering what has been heard, it is because of the excellence of gathering the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
How is there excellence of wisdom?
As the Sūtra says: "He is called one who possesses mindfulness, because he does not forget any dharmas."
That which is called "mind" (manas) is so named because it possesses well-determined wisdom.
That which is called "going" (gati) is so named because it knows the sequence of the meaning of the scriptures.
Among these, "recollection" (smṛti) is so named because the wisdom derived from hearing (śruta-mayī-prajñā) is preeminent.
"Intention" (mati) refers to the preeminence of wisdom derived from reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā).
"Departure" (yāti) refers to the preeminence of wisdom derived from cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).
There is another sequential interpretation for these terms as follows:

One is called "mindful" because of the excellence of hearing and retaining; one is called "intentional" because of the excellence of the profound knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*); and one is called "one who goes" because of the excellence of the profound knowledge of intention. This is a brief explanation of the accomplishment of two kinds of skillfulness: skillfulness in the phenomena (*dharma*) and skillfulness in their meaning (*artha*).
Regarding the excellence of being subsumed by ethical discipline (*śīla*), there are two kinds:
excellence in patience and gentleness, and excellence in the absence of defects in ethical discipline.
As the Sūtra says: "They are called those possessed of shame and dread, because they protect themselves and protect others."
"One who is called 'steadfast in mind' does not abandon the practice of upholding the precepts.
There are five kinds of excellence in the gathering of wisdom:

first, the wisdom that gathers causes and conditions, which serves as the antidote to causelessness, inversion, and false views; as the sūtra says: "One is called 'awakened' because of skillfully reflecting upon what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*)."
Second is the wisdom of realization, which serves as the antidote to the deeds of Māra, as the sūtra states: "One is called a follower of knowledge because one does not follow others.

Third is the wisdom that discerns false teachings, which serves as the antidote to divergent doctrines; it skillfully understands what constitutes a meaningful phrase, what does not, and what constitutes a confused phrase, as the sūtra states: "One is called a follower of wisdom because one skillfully discriminates between the phrases and syllables of all dharmas, distinguishing their true meaning from what is not the meaning."

Fourth is the wisdom of supernormal powers (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*), which serves as the antidote to the practice of taking refuge in what is false, as the sūtra states: "They are called those who have attained supernormal powers because they have skillfully cultivated meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)."

Fifth is the wisdom that transforms sentient beings, because it gathers them in through skillful means; as the sutra says: "He is called one of skillful means, because he acts in accordance with the ways of the world."
This is called the excellence of encompassing merit.
What is the excellence of cultivation?
The Sūtra says:
They are called "those who are never satiated" because they skillfully accumulate meritorious deeds that aid the path.
They are called "those whose diligence is unceasing" because they constantly seek the practice of wisdom that aids the path.
They are called "those who are untiring" because they gather the practices of great compassion that assist the path.
They are called "those who constantly mind the Buddha-dharma" because they seek the Buddha's ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
They are called "practitioners of virtuous mindfulness" because they give rise to the adornment of Buddha-lands.
They are called "those who fully practice various virtuous deeds" because they accumulate the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
They are called those who constantly practice diligence because they seek to adorn the Buddha’s body, speech, and mind;
they are called those who delight in the dharma of great reverence because they draw near to and make offerings to all bodhisattvas and Dharma masters.
They are called "Masters of the Sovereignty of Skillfully Arising Vows," because they skillfully enter the world through great expedient means.
They are called "Those Who Constantly Distance Themselves from Other Minds Day and Night," because they always delight in teaching and transforming all sentient beings.
The Commentary states:
Within this, there are ten superior modes of practice.
First is the practice of increasing the causes, as the Sūtra says: "He is called one who is never satiated, because he skillfully accumulates meritorious practices that assist the path."
2. Practice based on causal conduct: As the sutra says, "He is named 'One of Unremitting Diligence,' because he constantly seeks the practice of wisdom that aids the path.

3. Practice of not becoming weary in transforming sentient beings: As the sutra says, "He is named 'One Without Weariness,' because he accumulates the practice of great compassion that aids the path."

Fourth, initiating the practice of the Buddha-dharma, as the sutra says: "Those who are called 'constantly mindful of the Buddha-dharma' do so because they seek the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."

Fifth, the practice of purifying the Buddha-fields, as stated in the sutra: "They are called those who practice with wholesome mindfulness, because they give rise to the adornment of the Buddha-fields.
How do they adorn them?
One attains firm wisdom free from the defilements of affliction, because sentient beings dwell therein and it is adorned by the Buddha-dharma.

Sixth, one initiates practice based on the Buddha’s Dharma-body, as the Sūtra says: "It is called being fully endowed with the practice of various wholesome deeds, because of the accumulation of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics."

Seventh, practicing in reliance upon what the Buddha has done, as the sutra says: "He is called one who constantly practices diligence, because he seeks to adorn the body, speech, and mind of the Buddha."

8. Reverence for the practice of the Dharma, as stated in the Sūtra: "He is called one who delights in great reverence for the Dharma, because he draws near to, honors, and makes offerings to all Bodhisattvas and Dharma teachers."
9. The practice of vowing to take up existence, as the sūtra says: "He is named 'One Who Has Well-Arisen Mastery over Vows,' because he skillfully enters the world through great expedient means.

10. The practice of abandoning the mind of the Lesser Vehicle, as the sūtra says: "He is named 'One Who Is Day and Night Far Removed from Other Minds,' because he constantly delights in teaching and transforming all sentient beings."
This is called the excellence of spiritual practice.
What is the excellence of teaching and transforming sentient beings?
The Sūtra says:

When this bodhisattva accomplishes such practices, they transform sentient beings through the giving of gifts; they also transform sentient beings through kind words, beneficial conduct, and cooperation. They transform sentient beings by manifesting their physical body, and they transform sentient beings by preaching the Dharma. They transform sentient beings by extensively demonstrating the supernatural powers and deeds of the bodhisattva path; they transform sentient beings by explaining the great matters of the Buddhas; they transform sentient beings by revealing the faults and evils of the world; they transform sentient beings by explaining the benefits of the Buddhas' wisdom; and they transform sentient beings by manifesting the marks of great supernatural power and adornment while also teaching various modes of practice.

This bodhisattva thus achieves mastery in the skillful means of teaching and transforming sentient beings; their body and mind constantly incline toward the Buddha-wisdom without ever falling back, for they constantly and diligently cultivate various practices of roots of goodness, thereby advancing upon the increasingly superior path.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the excellence of teaching and transforming sentient beings herein, it is by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). As the Sūtra says: "When this bodhisattva accomplishes such practices, he teaches and transforms sentient beings through generosity, and further teaches and transforms sentient beings through kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation."

To act in concert with sentient beings by manifesting in accordance with them for their transformation, as the sutra says: "Furthermore, he manifests in a form-body to teach and transform sentient beings.
To bring about the accomplishment of the Dharma for sentient beings who harbor doubts, as the sutra says: "Furthermore, he teaches and transforms sentient beings through the preaching of the Dharma."

It is for the sake of sentient beings who lack skillful means regarding bodhi, as the sūtra states: "Furthermore, it extensively demonstrates the supernatural powers and deeds of the bodhisattva path to teach and transform sentient beings.
It is for the sake of sentient beings who have become weary of the Mahāyāna, as the sūtra states: "Furthermore, it speaks of the great matters of all Buddhas to teach and transform sentient beings."
It is for the sake of sentient beings who delight in the world, as the sūtra states: "Furthermore, he demonstrates the faults and evils of the world to teach and transform sentient beings.

It is for the sake of sentient beings who do not believe in the Mahāyāna, as the sūtra states: "Furthermore, he speaks of the wisdom and benefits of all Buddhas to teach and transform sentient beings."

For the sake of sentient beings who lack wisdom, he manifests the adornment of supernatural powers and displays various modes of conduct; by manifesting infinite bodies through a single body and so forth, he causes them to give rise to resolute faith, as the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, he manifests the marks of the great adornment of supernatural powers and also teaches various modes of conduct to transform sentient beings."
That this bodhisattva thus accomplishes the skillful means for teaching and transforming sentient beings is as previously explained.
That their body and mind always incline toward the wisdom of the Buddha is because they seek supreme power in order to teach and transform sentient beings.
"Not falling away from the practice of the various roots of goodness" means that whatever merit and wisdom one has attained, none of it is ever lost.
"Constantly and diligently practicing the increasingly superior path" means that one desires to cause those practices being cultivated to increase and become more excellent.
This is called the excellence of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
What is the excellence of giving rise to wisdom that accords with the world as an antidote to the defiled obstacles?
The Sūtra says:

For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, this bodhisattva skillfully knows all worldly scripts and treatises, seals, arithmetic, treatises on mineralogy and the like, and medical prescriptions for treating various diseases—namely, treatments for wasting diseases, treatments for insanity, treatments for possession by spirits, and treatments for venomous poisons—and is able to cure all those things that harm sentient beings, such as through incantations and medicines.

They manifest as treatises, scriptures, music, laughter, and amusements; as lands, cities, towns, villages, houses, rivers, springs, ponds, streams, gardens, groves, flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, forests, and trees; as the various precious substances such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mani-jewels, pearls, coral, amber, musaragalva, and agate; as the sun, moon, stars, earthquakes, dreams, and the entry into signs of good or bad fortune throughout the body; and as the observance of precepts, meditative concentrations, supernormal powers, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments. All these things—which do not afflict sentient beings and which are able to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings—are manifested out of compassion for them, in order to gradually cause them to have faith and enter the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the wisdom that accords with the world, it is the antidote to the afflictive hindrances, as the Sūtra says: "This bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, skillfully knows all the books and treatises in the world," and so forth.
Among these, writing and so forth serve as remedies for four kinds of obstacles.
These four kinds of obstacles are:

first, the obstacle of forgetfulness regarding matters to be undertaken—such as taking, giving, or entrusting; hearing the Dharma and reflecting on its meaning; and matters that have been done or not yet done, as well as matters that ought or ought not to be done. Writing serves as the remedy for this.
2. The obstacle of wrong views and weak intelligence: this treatise is expounded as an antidote to these two through the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*) and the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*).
3. The obstacle of failing to protect the objects of appropriation: the seal (*mudrā*) serves as the antidote to this.
Fourth, there is the obstacle of doubt arising regarding grasping; as an antidote to this, one employs counting.
Counting means: one becomes two, two twos become four, and so forth.
"Calculation" refers to such things as one vertical and ten horizontal lines.
"Treatises on the nature of stones and so forth" are for the purpose of counteracting obstacles related to poverty.

"Prescriptions for treating various diseases" are for the purpose of counteracting the obstacle of illness—the toxic manifestations of sentient beings arising from the disharmony of the four great elements.
Those suffering from wasting, emaciation, or insanity possess the characteristics of the disharmony of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Diseases such as possession by spirits (*bhūtagrasta*) are the characteristics of sentient beings (*sattvalakṣaṇa*).

Diseases caused by *gūḍha* poisons likewise involve the disharmony of the four great elements and are also characteristics of sentient beings; they are both causes of illness and causes of death. Their remedies consist of mantras, medicinal herbs, and the like.

Regarding the various signs pervading the body, such as the sun, moon, stars, earthquakes, dreams, and omens of good and bad fortune: these are included here because they consist solely of the perception of signs such as the sun and moon, and are subsumed under the category of solar and other celestial luminaries.
"Entering" refers to entering into the eight fruits of karma.
"The various marks throughout the body" refers to the practice of results that are either desirable or undesirable.

Regarding "the spheres of conduct for maintaining the precepts" and so forth: herein, the spheres of conduct for maintaining the precepts, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*) are explained in this sequence to counteract, respectively, the defilement of breaking the precepts, the defilement of sensual desire, the defilement of false refuge, the defilement of falsely practicing meritorious deeds, and the defilement of falsely cultivating liberation. Thus they are taught in successive order.
As stated in the Sūtra: "The discourse on the nature of stones, and so forth, up to spells and medicines.
Regarding the composition of treatises, scriptures, music, theater, laughter, and amusements, these serve as remedies for the obstacles of sorrow and affliction.
Regarding "the lands, cities, towns, and even the medicinal herbs, forests, and trees," this is the antidote to the obstacle of lack of joy.
Regarding "gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and even the nature of various jewels," this is the antidote to the obstacles of confinement and so forth.

Regarding "the sun, moon, stars, and even all the various marks throughout the body," this refers to the remedial factors for the obstacles caused by past misdeeds that obstruct the portion of karmic retribution one has obtained.
Regarding "the spheres of ethical discipline up to the formless attainments," these are the remedies for the five types of defilement.
What are the five kinds of defilement?
They range from the defilement of breaking the precepts to the defilement of falsely practicing for liberation.
This gives rise to mundane wisdom, which possesses four characteristics:
First, because there is no obstruction within the midst of various obstructions, as the sūtra says: "All matters that do not afflict sentient beings.
Second, because it bestows faultless happiness, as the sūtra says: "Matters capable of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings."
Third, purity of motivation, as the sūtra says: "He emerges out of compassion for sentient beings.
Fourth, purity of application, as the sūtra says: "In order to gradually cause them to have faith and enter the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma."
The Sūtra says:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

Once these Bodhisattvas have dwelled in this Bodhisattva stage of Difficult to Conquer (sudurjayā), they see many Buddhas by virtue of their great power of supernormal knowledge and their great power of vows."

They see many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, many billions of Buddhas, many hundreds of billions of Buddhas, many trillions of Buddhas, many hundreds of quadrillions of Buddhas, and many hundreds of quintillions of nayutas of Buddhas, by virtue of their great power of supernormal knowledge and the power of their great vows.

When these bodhisattvas see the Buddhas, they make offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise with their superior mind and profound mind; they present all requisites—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal elixirs, and every other article of offering—and provide the most excellent and delightful articles of enjoyment for the Saṃgha of bodhisattvas. They dedicate all these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Toward all Buddhas, they give rise to supreme reverence and listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, practicing according to their capacity. They go forth into homelessness within the Buddha-dharma, and having gone forth, they receive and hear the sutras and teachings from all Buddhas to become Dharma-preachers. By benefiting others through preaching the Dharma, they attain the accomplishment of a Dharma-preacher who possesses an even more excellent dharani of extensive learning.

At that time, as this bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Ground of Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), those roots of goodness become increasingly superior, bright, and pure for immeasurable hundreds of kalpas; they become increasingly superior, bright, and pure for immeasurable thousands of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, immeasurable billions of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of billions of kalpas, immeasurable trillions of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas. This bodhisattva accomplishes such methods for teaching and transforming sentient beings.
O Sons of the Buddha!
It is like pure, original gold which, when polished and refined with musaragalva, becomes increasingly brilliant, radiant, and pure.
O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Ground of Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), those roots of goodness become increasingly brilliant and pure by virtue of the power of skillful means, wisdom, and reflection; those roots of wisdom and goodness achieve non-retrogression through superior reflection, such that they cannot be equaled by the roots of goodness of the lower stages.
O sons of the Buddha!

It is, for example, like the sun, moon, stars, and the celestial palaces of the devas, whose circles of light are perfectly complete, accomplished, and indestructible, such that the winds cannot move them.
In the same way, O sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Ground of Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), those roots of goodness, through the power of skillful means, wisdom, and contemplation, achieve non-retrogression; they cannot be equaled by any of the roots of goodness of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or worldly beings.

Among these ten pāramitās of the bodhisattva, the dhyāna-pāramitā is predominant; yet it is not that the remaining pāramitās are not cultivated, for they are practiced according to one's power and capacity.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the fifth Bodhisattva stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become the King of the Tuṣita Heaven; acting with sovereign mastery, they subdue all external paths and false views, enabling sentient beings to abide within the True Reality (*satya*).

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—all such merits never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the bodhisattvas, mindfulness of the bodhisattva practices, mindfulness of the pāramitās, mindfulness of the ten stages, mindfulness of the indestructible powers, mindfulness of the fearlessnesses, and mindfulness of the unique buddha-qualities, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of all-aspect omniscience.
One should constantly give rise to this thought:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the greatest, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the general, the teacher, and the honored one, even unto becoming the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge."

Furthermore, from this thought he gave rise to diligent practice; by the power of diligence, in a single moment of thought, he attained ten billion samādhis, beheld ten billion Buddhas, knew the spiritual powers of ten billion Buddhas, was able to shake ten billion Buddha-worlds, was able to enter ten billion Buddha-worlds, was able to illumine ten billion Buddha-worlds, was able to transform the sentient beings of ten billion Buddha-worlds, was able to abide for a lifespan of ten billion kalpas, was able to know the events of ten billion kalpas each in the past and future worlds, was able to skillfully enter ten billion Dharma-gates, and was able to manifest ten billion bodies, in each and every body manifesting ten billion bodhisattvas as his retinue.
If one considers the sovereign supremacy of their power of vows, the bodhisattvas' power of vows exceeds these numbers.

They manifest various kinds of supernormal powers—whether through the body, or light, or supernormal faculties, or the eyes, or spheres of experience, or sounds, or conduct, or adornments, or empowerments, or faith, or karma.
These various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) cannot be fully enumerated even throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* eons.
The Commentary states:

"One who has attained the *dhāraṇī* of superior and abundant learning and is accomplished as a Dharma-preacher does not merely attain the *dhāraṇī* of meaning, because a mind of equal purity is exceedingly difficult to obtain."
Furthermore, because it is most difficult for supramundane wisdom to manifest mundane wisdom, one attains the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining.
On this stage, the light of wisdom manifests the reality of *tathatā*, as the Sūtra says: "O Sons of the Buddha!"
It is said: "For example, it is like original, pure gold that cannot be matched even by the roots of goodness of the lower stages.

Regarding the "orb of the sun and moon," this refers to the increase of the light of wisdom based upon the *āgamas*, as its knowledge surpasses that of the preceding stage; as the sutra states: "O Sons of the Buddha!"
"For example, it cannot be reached even by the sun, moon, stars, or the roots of goodness of the world.
Thus ends the fifth fascicle, the seventh of ten, of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* on the "Difficult-to-Conquer" Stage (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*),
and the eighth of eight on the sixth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra* on the "Manifest" Stage (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
Composed by Bodhisattva Maitreya;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Later Wei Dynasty. 6.
The Treatise on the Stage of Presence (*Pratibhāna-bhūmi-śāstra*) states:

Just as in the fifth stage there are three distinct types of excellence— the excellence of the antidote to pride, the excellence of the practice of the path of non-abiding, and the excellence of its fruit—
it should be understood that the sixth stage is likewise so, because it is even more superior.
What is the superiority?

In the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), the antidote to the pride of conceiving oneself as superior to sentient beings and the pride of conceiving oneself as superior in understanding the Dharma was explained. In the fifth stage, the antidote to the pride of conceptualizing the purity of the body was explained. Now, in this sixth stage, the antidote to the pride of conceptualizing the grasping at phenomena as either defiled or pure is explained by means of the ten dharmas of equality.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said:
"O Sons of the Buddha!"
If a bodhisattva has already fully perfected the path of the fifth stage and wishes to enter the sixth bodhisattva stage, they should enter the sixth stage by means of the ten dharmas of equality.
What are the ten?
First, because all phenomena are equal in being signless;
second, because all phenomena are equal in being thoughtless; [and so forth].
Third, because all phenomena are equal in being unarisen;
fourth, because all phenomena are equal in being unestablished;
fifth, because all phenomena are equal in being quiescent.
Sixth, because all phenomena are equal in their fundamental purity;
seventh, because all phenomena are equal in being free from conceptual proliferation;
eighth, because all phenomena are equal in being without grasping or rejection.
9. Because all phenomena are equal to illusions, dreams, reflections, echoes, the moon in water, images in a mirror, and magical apparitions;
10. Because all phenomena are equal in the non-duality of existence and non-existence.

As this bodhisattva thus contemplates the characteristics of all phenomena—due to the removal of defilements, due to conformity, and due to non-conceptualization—they enter the sixth bodhisattva stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), attaining the sharp and clear "conformity-patience" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), though they have not yet attained the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Commentary states:
Regarding the antidote to the discrimination of defiled and pure phenomena through grasping, it refers to the ten dharmas of equality.

Among these, "the equality of all phenomena being signless, up to the non-duality of all existence and non-existence," is because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena within the twelve bases (*āyatana*) is equal in being signless.
Furthermore, there are nine kinds of antidotes for the discrimination of characteristics:
first, the perception of the specific characteristics of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), as stated in the Sūtra: "Because all phenomena are equal in being signless."
2. The aspect of successive arising, as the sūtra says: "Because all dharmas are equal in being unarisen.
3. The aspect of successive production, as the sūtra says:
"Because all dharmas are equal in being unestablished."
4. The characteristic of defilement (*saṃkleśa-lakṣaṇa*), as stated in the sūtra: "Because all dharmas are equal in their quiescence. 5.
The characteristic of purity (*viśuddhi-lakṣaṇa*), as stated in the sūtra: "Because all dharmas are equal in their primordial purity (*prakṛti-viśuddha*)."
Sixth, the characteristic of differentiation, as the sūtra says: "Because all phenomena are equal in being free from conceptual proliferation.
Seventh, the characteristic of emergence and disappearance, as the sūtra says: "Because all phenomena are equal in being without grasping or abandoning."

8. I am not characterized by existence, as the Sūtra states: "Because all phenomena are equal to illusions, dreams, reflections, echoes, the moon in water, images in a mirror, and magical apparitions."
9. The characteristic of formation and destruction, as stated in the Sūtra: “Because all phenomena are equal in the non-duality of existence and non-existence.
As for "removing defilements," it means being far removed from the stains of hindrances.
"Conformity" means conforming to the dharma of the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*).
"Non-conceptualization" means not giving rise to conceptual thoughts.
"Clarity and sharpness" refers to the antidote to subtle pride, whereas in the two preceding stages, it served as the antidote to coarse and medium pride.
Those who have attained the "mild" or "medium" levels of patience (*kṣānti*) are so called because they accord with the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

As for those who have not yet attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, this patience accords with that patience, but it is not itself the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
This is called the antidote to the pride of discriminating between defiled and pure phenomena.
What is the excellence of not abiding in the practice of the path?
The Sūtra says:

This bodhisattva thus contemplates the characteristics of all phenomena and attains conformity with them; furthermore, because he takes supreme great compassion as his foremost priority, because great compassion is predominant, because he brings great compassion to fulfillment, and because he contemplates the arising and ceasing of the world.
The Commentary says:

When it is said that this bodhisattva thus contemplates the characteristics of all phenomena and attains conformity with them, it is because they attain the excellence of the practice of the non-abiding path (*apratisthita-mārga*).

As for the excellence of the practice of the non-abiding path, it is due to the excellence of the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that encompasses sentient beings of the past, present, and future without abandoning them; due to the purity of wisdom regarding all knowable phenomena (*jñeya-dharma*); due to the contemplation of the subtle accumulation of causes and conditions in all their aspects; and due to not abiding in either the mundane world or nirvāṇa.
As the sutra says: "Furthermore, with great compassion as the foremost, up to observing the arising and ceasing of the world.
The sutra states:
Having observed the arising and ceasing of the world, this bodhisattva forms this thought:

All the various places of birth where bodies are received in the world arise solely from attachment to a self; if one were free from attachment to a self, there would be no place of birth in the world.

The Bodhisattva further reflects: "These ordinary beings are blinded by ignorance and attached to a self. Obstructed by the darkness of lack of wisdom, they constantly seek existence and non-existence. Always following wrong thoughts, they perversely practice the wrong path, accumulating perverse actions—actions of demerit, merit, and imperturbability. Because of these actions, they give rise to the seeds of the mind, due to the presence of outflows and the perception of grasping."

Arising as the body of future birth, aging, and death, it further produces subsequent existence; with karma as its soil, covered by ignorance, moistened by the water of craving, irrigated by the mind of self, and made to grow by the various nets of views, it produces the sprout of name-and-form.

Once born, it grows; as name-and-form grow, the sense-faculties are formed. Once the sense-faculties are formed, contact arises through their mutual confrontation. From the confrontation of contact, feeling arises. Following feeling, craving arises from what is desired. Because craving exists, grasping arises. Once grasping has grown, becoming arises. Once becoming is established, the body of the five aggregates is produced.
Once the body of the five aggregates has grown, its gradual decline and transformation within the five realms of existence is called "aging"; its decay and cessation is called "death.
After death, various fevers and afflictions arise; because of these fevers and afflictions, there arises a mass of all manner of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress.
This is the gathering of causes and conditions; there is no gatherer, yet it gathers spontaneously. There is no extinguisher, yet it extinguishes spontaneously.
Thus does the bodhisattva contemplate the gathering of causes and conditions in accordance with reality.
The Treatise says:

Regarding the distinctions among all places where bodies are received and births occur within this world, the various differences in birth and death throughout the five destinies are what are called the distinctions existing within the world.
Regarding this collection of causes and conditions, one should know that there are three types of contemplative gateways:
first, the differentiation of the characteristics of the formulated response;
second, the differentiation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); [and third, the differentiation of conventional truth].
3. The Distinctions of the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
How are these distinctions established?

First, it is clarified that there is only the collection of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*), which explains the meaning of non-self (*anātman*). This establishes that all places of birth where sentient beings receive a body in the world exist solely because of attachment to a self; if one is free from attachment to a self, there will be no place of birth in the world. Thus, the meaning of non-self is established.

If, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there were truly a characteristic of a self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*), then the mind that clings to a self would itself be the wisdom of the ultimate truth, and it should not take birth in the various places of rebirth within the mundane world.

Furthermore, if there were truly a characteristic of self within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), then even those who are free from attachment to a self would still constantly be born into the world.

To demonstrate this point, the Sūtra states: "All the various places of birth where bodies are received in the world exist because of craving and attachment to a self; if one is free from attachment to a self, there will be no place of birth in the world."
What is the response to this distinction?
If there truly is no self, how can one be attached to a self?
This is the objection that should be raised here.
He then answers himself, saying: "Blinded by ignorance, they are greedily attached to a self.
This is a demonstration, as the sutra states: "The Bodhisattva further reflects:
'These ordinary people are blinded by ignorance and greedily attached to a self.'"
In this way, since there is truly no self, what sequence could there be for becoming attached to a self such that one obtains a worldly body and a place of birth?

This demonstration is established because, as the sutra says, "those obscured by the darkness of ignorance constantly seek existence and non-existence. Thus, the difficulty is answered through these distinctions.

In this regard, those who possess ignorance regarding existence and non-existence long for permanence and annihilation; this demonstrates that ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*) are the roots of these two links of existence (*bhavāṅga*). Consequently, they constantly follow wrong mindfulness and erroneously practice the wrong path, accumulating and giving rise to erroneous conduct: meritorious actions (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*), non-meritorious actions (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*), and immovable actions (*āneñjyābhisaṃskāra*).
"Constantly following erroneous thoughts" indicates the cause of ignorance.
"Frivolously practicing erroneous paths" indicates improper conduct regarding the state of liberation.

"Accumulating and giving rise to frivolous practices" indicates the ultimate meaning of the Bodhisattva; for although a Bodhisattva acts within the realm of existence, it is not called frivolous practice.
By means of these practices, the seeds of the mind arise; there is that which is with outflows and grasping, up to the contemplation that accords with the accumulation of causes and conditions.
In this context, "the arising of the seeds of the mind" indicates the essential nature of birth, old age, and death.

Furthermore, regarding the arising of future existence (*punarbhava*): it follows from the adoption and accomplishment of actions such as demerit and merit; because karma serves as the ground; because, as previously stated, one is shrouded by the darkness of ignorance due to a lack of wisdom; and because one is moistened by the water of craving for existence and non-existence. Thus abiding and thus generating the mind—such as "I" and "mine," the conceit of "I" and "mine," and "I am born" or "I am not born"—these and other such various nets of views arise.
That which ceases spontaneously does so because its nature is inherently subject to cessation; it is not a cessation through the condition of wisdom.
Thus, having answered the objection regarding the collection of causes and conditions, the explanation of the meaning of non-self is established.
What is the distinction of characteristics?
If causes and conditions do not exist, by what characteristic would I abide in the practice of the collection of causes and conditions?
The Sūtra says:
This bodhisattva further reflects:
"Not knowing the ultimate truth of the various realities as they truly are is called ignorance (*avidyā*); the karma and its fruits produced by ignorance are called formative activities (*saṃskāra*);
based on these activities there arises the initial consciousness (*vijñāna*); and co-arising with this consciousness are the four types of sensation (*vedanā*)."
The aggregates (*skandha*) are called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); as name-and-form increases, there arise the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

The conjunction of these three factors—the sense organ, the object, and consciousness—gives rise to tainted contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*). Because contact arises together [with other factors], there is feeling (*vedanā*).

Because feeling involves attachment, it is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Because craving increases, it is called grasping (*upādāna*). The arising of tainted karma from grasping is called becoming (*bhava*); when there is karma, there is its fruit.
Birth is the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*); the growth and transformation of these aggregates is called aging; the disintegration of the aggregates after aging is called death.
At the time of separation from death, the feverish mind of the foolish person attached to it is called sorrow (*śoka*); the wailing and weeping that arise is called lamentation (*parideva*).
The contact of the five sense-faculties with their objects is called suffering (*duḥkha*); the contact of the mental faculty with its object is called grief (*daurmanasya*). Grief...
The transformation of suffering through various names is called affliction (*upāyāsa*).
Thus, there is only the growth of the tree of suffering, and no agent exists.
The Bodhisattva reflects in this way:
If there is an agent, then there is an action; if there is no agent, then there is no action. In the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is neither agent nor action.
The Treatise says:
Among these, that which is the fruit of karma produced by ignorance is what is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Within this context, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is so designated because it is its support, because name-and-form and consciousness arise together, and because consciousness and name-and-form are mutually dependent upon one another.

If there is no agent, then within that [process], the performance of an action is likewise non-existent; this explains the existence of the factors through the gathering of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*).
Since there is no activity of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this should be understood as the contemplation of the sequential gathering of causes and conditions regarding the existence of factors.
What is the differentiation of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)?
It is because by thus realizing the ultimate truth, one attains liberation through that contemplation.
The Sūtra says:
This Bodhisattva forms this thought:
"The three realms are illusory; they are created solely by the single mind.
The Commentary says:
However, it is created by the single mind, for all that exists within the three realms is but the transformation of the mind.
What are the distinctions of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)?
By observing conventional truth in accordance with reality, one immediately enters the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This contemplation has six aspects:
first, the contemplation of what constitutes defilement and its basis;
second, the contemplation of causes; [and so forth].
3. Contemplation of encompassing faults;
4. Contemplation of guarding against faults;
5. Contemplation of non-disgust.
Sixth, profound contemplation.
Regarding the contemplation on the basis of defilement therein: it is because the constituent parts of causes and conditions depend upon the one mind.
The Sūtra says:
All the twelve links of dependent origination taught by the Tathāgata are based upon the one mind.

Why is this so? Following after objects, craving arises together with the mind; this very object is consciousness (*vijñāna*), and this is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*). Because volitional formations delude the mind, they are called ignorance (*avidyā*). When ignorance arises together with the mind, it is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The growth of name-and-form is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The differentiation of the six sense bases is called contact (*sparśa*). That which arises together with contact is called feeling (*vedanā*). Having felt without satiety is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Clinging and not relinquishing is called grasping (*upādāna*). The conjunction of these factors of existence gives rise to becoming (*bhava*). That which arises from becoming is called birth (*jāti*). The maturation of birth is called aging (*jarā*), and the decay of aging is called death (*maraṇa*).
The Treatise says:
This is the contemplation of the collection of causes and conditions for the defilement of the single mind through the differentiation of the two truths.
There are two kinds of contemplation regarding the causes:
First, contemplation of external causes;
second, contemplation of internal causes.
What is contemplation of external causes?
The Sūtra says:
"In this regard, ignorance has two functions:
first, it causes delusion within the objects of perception, thereby confusing sentient beings."
Second, it acts as the cause for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Volitional formations also have two functions:
first, they produce the retribution of future lives; [second, they serve as the basis for consciousness].
Second, it acts as the cause for consciousness.
Consciousness, moreover, has two functions:
first, it enables the continuity of existence; [second, it serves as the basis for the manifestation of objects].
Second, it acts as the cause for name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Name-and-form also has two functions: first, they mutually assist and bring each other into being;
[second, they serve as the basis for the six sense bases].
Second, it acts as the cause for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The six sense bases also perform two functions:
first, they are able to take the six objects as their objective conditions (*ālambana*); [second, they serve as the basis for contact].
Second, it acts as the cause for contact (*sparśa*).
Contact also has two functions:
first, it is able to contact the object of perception (*ālambana*); [second, it serves as the cause for feeling].
Second, it acts as the cause for sensation (*vedanā*).
Sensation also has two functions:
first, it perceives matters such as aversion and attachment; [second, it serves as the cause for craving].
Second, it acts as the cause for craving.
Craving also performs two functions:
first, it gives rise to a mind of greed toward objects that provoke attachment; [second, it leads to rebirth].
Second, it acts as the cause for grasping (*upādāna*).
Grasping also performs two functions:
first, it increases the defilement of the bonds of affliction (*kleśa*); [second, it serves as the cause for becoming].
Second, it acts as the cause for existence (*bhava*).
Existence (*bhava*) also has two kinds of functions:
first, it is able to bring about birth in other realms of existence.
Second, it acts as the cause for birth.
Birth also has two kinds of functions:
first, it causes the five aggregates to increase; [second, it causes them to arise].
Second, it acts as the cause for aging.
Aging also performs two functions:
first, it causes the sense faculties to mature; [second, it causes the appearance to decline].
Second, it acts as the cause for death.
Death also performs two functions:
first, it destroys the body of the five aggregates; [second, it causes rebirth].
Second, because of non-perception and non-cognition, the continuity [of existence] is not severed.
The Treatise says:

Regarding this, as for how the destruction of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) leads to the continuity being not severed through non-perception and non-cognition—this destruction of the five aggregates acts as the cause for future birth; because it acts as the cause for future birth due to non-perception and non-cognition, this is called the contemplation of other-causality (parapratyaya-vipaśyanā).
What is the contemplation of its own causes?
It is the contemplation of the conditions for the self-arising causes of ignorance and so forth.
What are the causal conditions for ignorance and so forth that lead to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)?
Because it continuously assists and brings [the process] to completion.
The Sūtra says:
"In this context, 'ignorance conditions volitional formations' means that the causal condition of ignorance causes volitional formations not to cease, as it assists in bringing them to completion."
Regarding "volitional formations condition consciousness": the causal condition of volitional formations causes consciousness not to cease and assists in the formation of consciousness.
Regarding "consciousness conditions name-and-form": the causal condition of consciousness causes name-and-form not to cease and assists in the formation of name-and-form.
Regarding "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases": the causal condition of name-and-form causes the six sense bases to be uninterrupted and assists in their formation.
Regarding "the six sense bases condition contact": the causal condition of the six sense bases causes contact to be uninterrupted and assists in its formation.
Contact conditions feeling: through the causal condition of contact, feeling is made to continue without interruption, as it assists in the formation of feeling.
Feeling conditions craving: through the causal condition of feeling, craving is made to continue without interruption, as it assists in the formation of craving.
Regarding "craving conditions grasping": through the causal condition of craving, grasping is made to continue without interruption, as it assists in the formation of grasping.
Regarding "grasping conditions becoming": through the causal condition of grasping, becoming is made to continue without interruption, as it assists in the formation of becoming.
Regarding "conditioned by existence there is birth": it is because the causal condition of existence causes birth to continue without interruption, thereby assisting in the accomplishment of birth.

Regarding "conditioned by birth there is old age and death": it is because the causal condition of birth causes old age and death to continue without interruption, thereby assisting in the accomplishment of old age and death.
Because ignorance ceases, formations cease; because the causal condition of ignorance is absent, formations cease, as they are no longer brought to completion.
Because formations cease, consciousness ceases; because the causal condition of formations is absent, consciousness ceases, as it is no longer brought to completion.
Because consciousness ceases, name-and-form cease; because the condition of consciousness is absent, name-and-form cease, as they are no longer assisted in their formation.
Because name-and-form cease, the six sense bases cease; because the condition of name-and-form is absent, the six sense bases cease, as they are no longer assisted in their formation.
With the cessation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*) ceases; because the causal condition of the six sense bases is absent, contact ceases and is not further sustained.
With the cessation of contact, feeling (*vedanā*) ceases; because the causal condition of contact is absent, feeling ceases and is not further sustained.
With the cessation of sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*) ceases; because the causal condition of sensation is absent, craving ceases and is no longer sustained.
With the cessation of craving, grasping (*upādāna*) ceases; because the causal condition of craving is absent, grasping ceases and is no longer sustained.
Because grasping ceases, existence ceases; since the causal condition of grasping is absent, existence ceases, as it is no longer supported.
Because existence ceases, birth ceases; since the causal condition of existence is absent, birth ceases, as it is no longer supported.
With the cessation of birth, old age and death cease; with the absence of the causal condition of birth, old age and death cease because they are no longer assisted and brought to completion.
The Treatise says:

Regarding the statement here that "ignorance conditions volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskārāḥ*), and that the causal condition of ignorance causes volitional formations not to be interrupted by assisting their completion—there are two kinds of ignorance:
First, the time of the seed;
second, the time of the fruit.
Among these, the "time of the seed" refers to the manifestation of conditions and phenomena through two kinds of meanings, which cause practice to proceed without interruption.
In this way, one should understand the two meanings of the remaining factors of causal conditions and self-arising causes through their functional application.
Regarding the contemplation of self-causes: it is because they are contemplated as being inseparable, and because there is no contemplation of a subsequent factor apart from its preceding factor.

If one does not depart from ignorance, then the contemplation of formations (saṃskāra) is established; if formations existed without departing from ignorance, one could not say that "formations have ignorance as their condition.
If formations were to be established by departing from ignorance, then because they would be distinct, they could not be established [as dependent].
Therefore, the verse says:
"Phenomena produced by various conditions are neither identical to their causes nor different from their causes;
they are neither annihilated nor eternal."
The contemplation on the causes and conditions of self-arising is as previously explained.
Ignorance is of two kinds:
first, the time of the seed; [second, the time of the sprout].
2. At the time of the fruit:
the same applies from volitional formations up to old age and death.
Since the prior limit and the subsequent limit are extinguished, the middle limit also does not exist; therefore, it is not mentioned.
What is the contemplation that subsumes the faults?
It refers to the subsumption within the three paths, because they constitute the cause of suffering and the fruit of suffering.
As the Sūtra says:
Among these, the non-interruption of the three factors—ignorance, craving, and grasping—constitutes the path of afflictions.
The non-interruption of the two factors—formative action and existence—constitutes the path of karma.
The uninterrupted continuity of other causal conditions is the path of suffering.
Because there is an uninterrupted succession from the prior limit to the posterior limit, these three paths are uninterrupted.
Thus, these three paths are devoid of "self" and "what belongs to self," existing merely as arising and ceasing, like a bundle of bamboo.
The treatise says:
What is the contemplation that guards against errors?
If one asserts that things arise from causes and conditions, there are three kinds of errors in such conceptualization:
First, there is the fault that all bodies would arise simultaneously.
Why? Because there is no distinct cause [for their sequential arising].
Second, there is no fault of experiencing the retribution of one's own karma. Why is this?
Because there is no agent.
Third is the fault of the loss of karma. Why is this?
Because the karma that has not yet produced its fruit has already ceased.
These three kinds of faults are answered by demonstrating that there are distinct causes for the past life and so forth, and by the distinctions among the retributions of birth and so on.
The Sūtra says:
"Ignorance conditions volitional formations" refers to the phenomena of the past life.
Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—these are views concerning the phenomena of the present life.
Craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age and death—these are views concerning the phenomena of future lives.
Thus, one perceives the turning of the three periods of time.
Because ignorance ceases, the formative forces cease; this is called the teaching on the severance of the continuity of causes and conditions.
The treatise says:
That "ignorance conditions volitional formations" refers to seeing the phenomena of the past, because the present birth is the result of what was done in the past.
That the present fruit is the future [cause] means seeing the sense of the causes of the past.

Regarding the statement that "from consciousness up to feeling, one perceives the phenomena of the present life": whatever karma existed within past lives, that karma obtains its retribution in the form of present consciousness and so forth, and it is further able to obtain future retribution.
Craving, grasping, and becoming are views concerning future existences, because there is also the arising of birth as a single, fixed progression.
Furthermore, regarding the view that there is a transmigration through the three periods of time, this is because there is also the transmigration of birth in future lives.
What is the meaning of this statement?
It is because there are three kinds of meanings:

past karma does not receive its retribution either because it was not yet performed, or because it was already performed but its retribution has not yet been obtained, or because it has been severed through the attainment of an antidote.
Among these, ignorance as the condition for volitional formations is the manifestation of "activity";
volitional formations as the condition for consciousness, up to contact and feeling, is the manifestation of "having already obtained the retribution" once activity has occurred;
and the non-interruption of craving, grasping, and existence is the manifestation of "not having obtained the antidote."
If craving and grasping are severed, then although karma is performed, the condition of ignorance for volitional formations cannot produce existence.

Therefore, among various karmas, there are those already performed and those not yet performed; there are those that have yielded their fruit and those that have not; and there are those that have been abandoned and those that have not.
If this were so, there would be no fault of all bodies arising simultaneously.
If that is the case, it is not that all karma is necessarily experienced in the future, nor is it that it is not experienced at all, nor is it experienced all at once.
If the fruit of one's own karma is never lost because it is not experienced by another body,
then there is no fault of failing to experience the retribution for one's own karma, since that karma was not performed by another.
If one is free from those three types of activity, the fruit will certainly be attained without fail.
If this is so, then there is no fault of losing [the fruit].
This is called the demonstration of protecting against the three faults.
What is the contemplation of disenchantment through non-disenchantment?
It is the disenchantment with the various subtle sufferings of discrimination, because all sensations are suffering, as well as the disenchantment with the various gross sufferings.
The Sūtra says:
"The twelve links of dependent origination are explained as being comprised of the three types of suffering.

Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkha*)."
Contact and feeling are called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
the remaining causal factors are called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).

Because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease, and so on, until because birth ceases, old age and death cease; this is called the teaching on severing the continuity of the three types of suffering.
The Treatise says:
What is profound contemplation?
The Sūtra says:
With ignorance as a condition, volitional formations arise; conditions are able to give rise to volitional formations, and the same applies to the rest.
With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; when volitional formations are absent, the same applies to the rest.
"With ignorance as a condition, volitional formations arise"—this is the teaching on the bondage of arising; the rest is likewise.
"With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease"—this is the teaching on the bondage of cessation; the rest is likewise.
"Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations" is a teaching that accords with the contemplation of existence; the others are likewise so.
"With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" is a teaching that accords with the contemplation of the exhaustion of non-existence; the others are likewise so.
The treatise states:
There are four kinds of profound observation:
first, that which possesses constituent parts is not created by another, because it arises from its own causes.
Second, they are not self-created, because they arise dependently.
As the Sūtra says: "Conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise; conditions can give rise to volitional formations, and the same applies to the rest."
"Because with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; when volitional formations are absent, the rest likewise follow.
Third, it is not produced by two factors, because it arises in accordance [with conditions], because there is no knower, and because at the time of its production, it does not abide.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; this is the teaching on the bondage of birth. The same applies to the rest.
With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; this is the teaching on the cessation of bondage. The same applies to the rest. Therefore.
Fourth, it is not produced without cause, because it conforms to existence (*bhava*).
As the Sūtra says: "Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); this is taught as an observation conforming to existence; the rest are likewise."
"The cessation of ignorance leads to the cessation of volitional formations; this is taught as a contemplation that accords with non-existence and exhaustion, and the same applies to the rest.
Therefore, if things were produced without a cause, they would be produced eternally and never cease to be produced.
Because there is no fixed cause, it could also never arise.
Why? Because it would be produced without a cause.
This is not what is favored in the Buddha’s teaching.
If that were so, because it would conform to existence through having a cause rather than being without a cause, then if it were without a cause, one could not say it conforms to existence.
This concludes the explanation of the ten kinds of contemplations on the characteristics and distinctions of the truth regarding the accumulation of causes and conditions.
The Sūtra says:
"In this way, that bodhisattva contemplates the dharma of the accumulation of causes and conditions in these ten ways, both in direct and reverse order, namely:"

Because of the sequential order of causes and conditions; because they are subsumed within a single mind; because they are accomplished through one's own karma; because they are inseparable from one another; because the three paths are uninterrupted; because of observing the prior and posterior limits; because of the accumulation of the three types of suffering; because of arising through causes and conditions; because of being bound by the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions; and because of conforming to the contemplation of the exhaustion of existence.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, there are two kinds of distinct contemplations:
first, the contemplation that accords with great compassion; [second, the contemplation that accords with great joy].
2. The analytical contemplation of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Regarding the contemplation that accords with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), there are four types:
first, delusion and perversion;...
2. Seeking liberation elsewhere;
3. Seeking liberation through heterodox paths;
4. Seeking a different form of liberation.
What is meant by delusion and perversion?
It is because one observes this matter of delusion and perversion according to the point of attachment; it is because of clinging to a self.
Since birth occurs in all places due to the absence of a self, there is then no birth.
What is delusion? It is due to the darkness of ignorance.
As the sutra says: "Having observed the arising and ceasing of the world, this bodhisattva forms this thought:"
"All the various distinctions among the places where sentient beings receive bodies and are born in the world arise from attachment to a self.
If one is free from attachment to a self, there will be no place of birth in the world. Thus it is said.

Blinded by ignorance and attached to a self, they thus possess the inversion of perverted views and the inversion of doubt regarding the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*). As the Sūtra states: "The Bodhisattva further reflects:
'These ordinary worldlings are blinded by ignorance and attached to a self; obscured by the darkness of lack of wisdom, they constantly seek after existence, non-existence, and so forth.'"
How can one seek liberation elsewhere?

Such ordinary persons are thus deluded and inverted; they ought to constantly seek liberation within the *ālayavijñāna* and the *ādānavijñāna*, yet instead they seek liberation elsewhere, within a self and what belongs to a self.
This remedy is as stated in the sutra: "This bodhisattva reflects:
'The three realms are illusory; they are produced solely by the mind,' up to 'the decay and destruction of old age is called death.'"
How do those of other paths seek liberation?
They seek liberation within the causes of inversion.
There are three kinds of causes of inversion:
One should not seek [the cause] in terms of primal nature (*prakṛti*), the Lord (*īśvara*),
asceticism (*tapas*), or the absence of cause (*ahetu*). Why is this?

The members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) have two kinds of functions that can give rise to the phenomena of dependent origination. As the Sūtra states: "In this regard, ignorance has two functions:
first, it causes delusion within the conditions, leading sentient beings to confusion;
second, it acts as the cause for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)," and so forth.

Because they are self-arisen causes, as the Sūtra states: "In this regard, 'ignorance conditions volitional formations' means that the causal condition of ignorance prevents volitional formations from being severed and assists in their formation," and so forth.

Because they are caused by afflictions, karma, and conceptualization, and because they are not causes of happiness—as stated in the Sūtra: "In this regard, the non-cessation of the three factors of ignorance, craving, and grasping constitutes the path of affliction," and so forth.

Because of the cause for the middle limit, because of the cause for both the middle and the subsequent limits, and because of both the preceding and subsequent limits relative to the middle limit—as stated in the Sūtra: "In this regard, that 'conditioned by ignorance there are volitional formations' refers to seeing the phenomena of the past," and so forth.
If such things did not exist, then various sentient beings would also not exist; how then could one seek diverse liberations?
True liberation possesses four characteristics:

the characteristic of being free from all suffering, the characteristic of being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the characteristic of being remote from defilement, and the characteristic of being supramundane.

Those various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are accompanied by suffering even up to the bondage of the formless existence (*ārūpyabhava*), as stated in the Sūtra: "The twelve links of dependent origination are said to consist of the three types of suffering;
