ignorance, formations, and so forth up to the six sense bases are called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkha*)," and so on.

Because they arise through such causes and conditions, as the Sūtra states: "In this regard, with ignorance as a cause and condition and formations as a cause and condition, formations are produced; the rest are likewise," and so forth.

In this way, further defilement gives rise to bondage, as the Sūtra states: "Among these, ignorance conditions volitional formations; this is explained as the bondage of birth, and the others are likewise," and so forth.

In this way, there is liberation through the pursuit of formless existence (ārūpyabhava) by means of conformity; as the Sūtra says: "Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations (saṃskāra); this is taught in accordance with the contemplation of existence, and the rest is likewise," and so forth.
Thus, the observation of dependent origination in accordance with great compassion has been explained.
Regarding the analytical observation of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), there are nine types therein:

first, the analytical observation of defilement and purification. This refers to the defilement and purification of attachment to the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) and the departure from that conceit, as the Sūtra says: "After this Bodhisattva has observed the arising and ceasing of the world, he forms this thought:"
"All the various places where bodies are born in the world arise from attachment to a self;
if one is free from attachment to a self, there will be no place of birth in the world. Thus it is said.
2. Relying on contemplation (*vipaśyanā*): Upon what phenomena does this collection of causes and conditions depend?
As the Sūtra states: "This Bodhisattva further reflects:
'Because one does not know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of the truths as they truly are, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*),' and so forth."

Third is the contemplation of skillful means (*upāya*). Because the two types of karma within the links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are able to give rise to the phenomena of dependent origination, as the Sūtra states: "In this regard, ignorance has two functions:
first, it causes delusion in sentient beings through its object;
second, it acts as the cause for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)," and so forth.

Fourth, the contemplation of the characteristics of causes and conditions (*nidāna-lakṣaṇa-vipaśyanā*): because the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādāṅga*) are without agency (*nirvyāpāra*). As the Sūtra says: "In this regard, ignorance conditions volitional formations (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*); the causal condition of ignorance causes volitional formations not to cease, as it assists in their formation," and so forth.

Fifth, entering the contemplation of the truths: because the three paths constitute the truths of suffering and its origin, as the Sūtra says: "In this regard, the non-cessation of the three factors—ignorance, craving, and grasping—is the path of afflictions."
"Because it is said: 'The non-interruption of the two divisions of *saṃskāra* (formative forces) constitutes the path of karma;
the non-interruption of the remaining causal factors constitutes the path of suffering.

Sixth, regarding the contemplation based on the entry into faith through power and lack of power: because of the excellence of transformation across the prior, middle, and subsequent limits [of time], as the Sūtra says: "That 'conditioned by ignorance are the *saṃskāras*' refers to the phenomena of the past life," and so forth.

Seventh, the contemplative entry of faith regarding overweening pride and the absence of overweening pride: because one does not know subtle suffering and the conceit of "I am" as they truly are, as stated in the Sūtra: "In this context, ignorance, formations, and so forth, up to the six sense bases, are called the suffering of formations," and so on.

8. Contemplation of the Beginningless: Because there is the production of causes and conditions in the middle limit, and because there is the arising of subsequent bondage in accordance with that in the future limit, as the Sūtra says: "With ignorance as a condition, volitional formations arise; the rest are likewise."
"Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; this is taught as the bondage of birth, and the rest are likewise.

Ninth, "various contemplations," because they accord with the contemplation of existence (*bhava*); thus, craving for the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, etc., as the Sūtra says: "Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; this is taught as the contemplation of existence, and the rest are likewise."
Thus, having already explained the excellence of the practice of non-abiding on the path,
next the fivefold excellence of its fruit is explained: first,
the excellence of attaining the counteractive practices and the excellence of being free from hindrances;
2. Attaining excellence in practice;
3. Attaining excellence in samādhi;
4. Attaining excellence in an indestructible mind;
Fifth, the excellence of attaining the power of mastery.
What is the excellence of attaining the practice of the remedies?
It refers to the three gates of liberation.
The Sūtra says:

"When this bodhisattva has thus contemplated the collection of causes and conditions in these ten ways, there is no self, no life-span, and no sentient being; it is empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of an agent or a recipient."
When observing in this manner, the liberation door of emptiness manifests before one.
Because that bodhisattva observes the extinction of the intrinsic nature of those links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), constant liberation manifests before them.

Seeing that within the conditions of dependent origination there is not even the slightest mark of a dharma that can arise, and because they do not perceive the mark of even the slightest dharma, the gate of liberation of signlessness manifests before them.

Thus, this bodhisattva enters emptiness and enters signlessness, yet does not give rise to longing or aspiration, except for the foremost purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings through great compassion.
In this way, the liberation door of wishlessness manifests before him.

As this bodhisattva practices these three doors of liberation, he is free from the marks of self and other, free from the marks of agent and recipient, and free from the marks of existence and non-existence.
The treatise says:
Within this, the gate of liberation of emptiness is explained through three aspects:
first, seeing that sentient beings lack a self; [the second is seeing that phenomena lack a self; and the third is seeing that both are non-existent].
2. Seeing the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*);
3. Seeing the non-existence of those two [agent and action], because there is no agent. As the Sūtra says:

"When this bodhisattva has thus contemplated the collection of causes and conditions in these ten ways, he sees that there is no self, no life-span, and no sentient being; it is empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of an agent or a recipient."
"When one contemplates in this manner, the gate of liberation of emptiness manifests before one. Thus it is said.
The phrase "seeing that sentient beings have no self" demonstrates that there is no self, no life-principle, and no sentient being.
The phrase "seeing that phenomena lack self-nature" indicates that their intrinsic nature is empty.

Regarding the phrase "the non-existence of those two agents," this indicates that one sees that sentient beings and phenomena lack agency; since there is no agent, the action is likewise non-existent. Because one does not perceive an agent, one is free from both agent and experiencer—this is what the phrase demonstrates.
The liberation door of signlessness is also explained through three aspects:
first, the cessation of obstacles;
second, the attainment of the antidote.
Third, the non-arising of the characteristics of recollection.
As the Sūtra says: "Because this Bodhisattva contemplates that the self-nature of those links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) is extinguished, constant liberation is ever-present.

Seeing that in the locus of causes and conditions there is not even the slightest characteristic of a dharma that can arise—because he thus does not perceive even the slightest characteristic of a dharma—the gate of signless liberation (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) manifests."
Regarding the cessation of obstacles therein, this phrase indicates that one contemplates the extinction of the intrinsic nature of those links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
Regarding the attainment of the antidote, this phrase indicates the constant manifestation of liberation.

Regarding "the characteristic of mindfulness does not function": this phrase demonstrates that when one perceives the locus of causes and conditions, there is not even the slightest characteristic of a dharma that can arise.
The door of liberation through wishlessness is also explained by way of three characteristics:
first, its basis; [and so forth].
Second, its essence;
third, its excellence.

As the Sūtra states: "This bodhisattva thus enters emptiness and enters signlessness, yet does not give rise to aspiration or delight, except for making great compassion the foremost principle to transform sentient beings; in this way, the liberation door of wishlessness manifests before him. Thus it is said.
Among these, entering emptiness and entering signlessness is called "reliance.
Because one relies on entering emptiness and entering signlessness, one is able to accomplish wishlessness and not give rise to longing or desire.
The absence of the aspiration for [rebirth] is called the essence of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
That which takes great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as its foremost principle to teach and transform sentient beings is called "superior.

Śrāvakas also possess the essence of wishlessness in that they do not give rise to such aspirations; however, because they are devoid of great compassion and take no pleasure in teaching and transforming sentient beings, they are not superior.

Regarding the "Victor who Overcomes Obstructions," this is because he is free from three kinds of marks, as the Sūtra states: "This bodhisattva practices these three gates of liberation, being free from the mark of self and other, free from the mark of agent and recipient, and free from the mark of existence and non-existence."
In this manner, they are progressively removed throughout the five stages because of the mind that is equanimous, profound, and pure.
In the fourth stage, signs such as arising and ceasing are removed; in these sixth stages, they are removed because of the equality of all phenomena.
How does one attain excellence in practice?
The Sūtra says:

"The great compassion of this bodhisattva increases further; because of this profound compassion, he exerts himself with diligence, desiring to bring to fulfillment those factors conducive to enlightenment that are not yet fulfilled."
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"Because conditioned phenomena arise through conjunction; because formations cease through separation from conjunction; and because formations do not occur when the various conditions are incomplete, they do not proceed when these are not present."

Only I know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) have many faults; they should not be fully brought together through causes and conditions, nor should one ultimately extinguish conditioned phenomena, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva thus understands that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) abound in faults and are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they contemplate their intrinsic nature as neither arising nor ceasing.

Having performed this contemplation, because they give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and do not abandon any sentient beings, they immediately attain the manifestation of the gateway to unobstructed wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna-mukha*), which is called the manifestation of the light of the practice of *prajñāpāramitā*.

When this bodhisattva has accomplished such practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* and the light of its manifestation has shone forth, they do not dwell together with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) in order to fulfill the causes and conditions for the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyadharma*). Although they contemplate the nature of conditioned phenomena as having the characteristic of quiescence (*śāntalakṣaṇa*), they do not abide therein, because they desire to be fully endowed with the factors conducive to unsurpassed enlightenment.
The treatise states:
Regarding those who have attained superior practice, there are two kinds of practice:
first, the practice of exerting heroic vigor; [second, the practice of skillful means].
2. Cultivating Practice with the Resolve of a Great Man.

One who initiates courageous practice recognizes that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) abound in faults; thus, they distance themselves from worldly occupations and the afflictions (*kleśa*) that bind one equally to existence, and instead act for the supreme benefit of sentient beings.

As the Sūtra says: "The great compassion of this bodhisattva increases further; because of this profound compassion, he practices with diligent vigor, desiring to fulfill those factors conducive to enlightenment that are not yet fulfilled."
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"Because conditioned phenomena arise through conjunction, and because formations cease through disjunction; because they do not proceed when various conditions are incomplete, and because they do not proceed when conditions are not assembled."

"Only I know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) have many faults; they should not be fully brought together through causes and conditions, nor should one ultimately extinguish conditioned phenomena, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings."

Regarding those who arouse the aspiration of a great man and engage in practice, they do so because they observe many faults through the contemplation of opposition, because they eliminate opposition, and because there is no further observation regarding the common characteristics of intrinsic nature.
As the Sūtra says: "O Sons of the Buddha!"

Because the Bodhisattva thus knows that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) have many faults, are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and are characterized by the contemplation of an intrinsic nature that is neither arising nor ceasing.

As for the excellence of practice, it is because wisdom and great compassion are excellently concordant; by relying on the practice of the non-abiding path (*apratiṣṭhita-mārga*), the gateway of unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇajñāna*) manifests, and the light of the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) manifests. This is because one realizes the equality of conditioned phenomena and *nirvāṇa*, because one does not dwell together with them, and because those practices conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣika-dharma*) have not yet been fully perfected.

As the Sūtra says: "When this bodhisattva has performed such contemplation, because he gives rise to great compassion and does not abandon any sentient beings, he immediately attains the gateway of unobstructed wisdom that manifests before him; this is called the manifestation of the light of the practice of prajñāpāramitā."

When this bodhisattva has accomplished such practice of the prajñāpāramitā and its radiance has manifested before him, he does not dwell together with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) for the sake of fulfilling the causes and conditions of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣikadharma*); yet, while observing that the nature of conditioned phenomena is characterized by quiescence (*śāntalakṣaṇa*), he does not abide therein either, because he desires to fully perfect the factors conducive to unsurpassed enlightenment.
Unobstructed wisdom refers to the wisdom of the Tathāgata; however, when this has not yet been fully accomplished, it is termed "the manifestation of light.
How does one attain the excellence of samādhi?
There are ten gates of emptiness samādhi that serve as the primary leaders, together with their retinues.
The Sūtra says:

"When this bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Stage of Manifestation, they attain the samādhi of faith in emptiness, the samādhi of emptiness of nature, the samādhi of emptiness of the ultimate truth, the samādhi of supreme emptiness, the samādhi of great emptiness, the samādhi of combined emptiness, the samādhi of arising emptiness, the samādhi of emptiness as it truly is without discrimination, the samādhi of non-abandonment of emptiness, and the samādhi of attaining detachment from both detachment and non-detachment."
This bodhisattva, having attained these ten primary samādhi-doors of emptiness, brings before him hundreds of thousands of millions of samādhi-doors of emptiness.
Likewise, having attained these ten primary samādhi-doors of signlessness, he brings before him hundreds of thousands of millions of samādhi-doors of signlessness.
In this way, with these ten gateways of the wishless samādhi as the foremost, hundreds of thousands of millions of wishless samādhi gateways manifest before one.
The treatise says:
This emptiness samādhi has four kinds of distinctions:
First, contemplation;
second, non-negligence;
third, attaining supremacy.
Fourth, the basis for the practice.
Excluding the fourth samādhi, there are five samādhis which are termed "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).
First, contemplating that sentient beings are without self, as the Sūtra states: "One attains the samādhi of faith in emptiness."
2. Contemplating the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), as in the sūtra’s mention of the "samādhi of the emptiness of intrinsic nature" (*prakṛtiśūnyatā-samādhi*).
3. Grasping that contemplation of emptiness, as in the sūtra’s mention of the "samādhi of the emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārthaśūnyatā-samādhi*).
4. Contemplating based on that ālayavijñāna, as in the sūtra’s mention of the "samādhi of great emptiness" (mahāśūnyatā-samādhi).
5. Contemplating the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna), as in the sūtra’s mention of the "samādhi of combined emptiness" (saṃyukta-śūnyatā-samādhi).

Regarding "heedfulness": it is because one skillfully practices the fourth samādhi through its various distinctions and because one practices without satiety, as stated in the sūtra: "the foremost emptiness samādhi."
Regarding "attaining supremacy," the seventh samādhi attains supreme merit, as the sūtra states: "arising from the emptiness samādhi.

Regarding "the causal matter," the other three kinds of samādhis are the causal matters for purifying the cognitive obscurations, as the sūtra states: "the emptiness samādhi that does not conceptually differentiate according to reality."
The matter of the cause for teaching and transforming sentient beings is as stated in the sutra: "not abandoning the samādhi of emptiness.
The matter of the cause for vowing to take up existence is as stated in the sutra: "attaining the samādhi of emptiness that is neither separated from nor not separated [from existence]."
Taking up such vows, because one remains free from the defilement of afflictions while yet conforming to the various realms of existence, it is called "detached yet not detached.
How does one attain the excellence of an indestructible mind?
The Sūtra says:

When this Bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva stage of the Manifest (Abhimukhī), he further fulfills the indestructible mind, the resolute mind, the true mind, the profound mind, the non-retrogressive mind, the tireless mind, the pure mind, the boundless mind, the mind seeking wisdom, and the mind that fulfills the practice of skillful means and wisdom.
The treatise states:
"That which does not destroy the mind" refers to being firm and non-retrogressive.
There are nine kinds of this indestructible mind:
First, faith that is unshakable through contemplation, as the sutra says, "a resolute mind.
Second, receptivity and pliancy that are unshakable, as the sutra says, "the true mind."
Third, not being startled or terrified by secret matters and remaining unimpaired, as the sūtra says, "because of the profound mind" (*adhyāśaya*).
Fourth, being immovable and unimpaired regarding one's own vehicle, as the sūtra says, "because of the non-retrogressive mind" (*avaivartika-citta*).
Fifth, the non-destruction of the arousal of diligence, as stated in the sutra through the phrase "unresting mind.
Sixth, the non-destruction of being free from the stains of envy and broken precepts, as stated in the sutra through the phrase "pure mind."
7. The indestructibility of extensively benefiting sentient beings, as the sūtra says, "because of the mind of boundlessness.
8. The indestructibility of seeking supreme liberation, as the sūtra says, "because of the mind that seeks wisdom."
Ninth, the practice of transforming sentient beings is indestructible, as stated in the sutra: "The mind that fulfills the practice of skillful means and wisdom.
How does one attain the excellence of the power of mastery?
The Sūtra says:

This Bodhisattva’s various bodhicittas are accomplished through conformity; they incline toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* because they are established through non-regressive diligence, being unshakable by any heterodox arguments of external paths;
they are accomplished through conformity because they enter the stages of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*).
It is accomplished through detachment, because it transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
it is accomplished through single-mindedness, because it resolutely proceeds toward the wisdom of the Buddha;
it is accomplished through non-retrogression, because all māras and afflictions cannot destroy it.
It is accomplished by being firmly established, because of the clear wisdom of the bodhisattva;
it is accomplished by being correctly established, because of skillfully cultivating the practices of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and it is accomplished by assisting correct practice, through the contemplation of the wisdom of skillful means.
The practice of non-abandonment is accomplished because he gathers the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

While this bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), his practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is preeminently accomplished, and he attains the third sharp conformative patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*), because he accords with the dharmas as they truly are without any contradiction.
The treatise says:

These bodhisattvas, whose minds are compliant with and accomplished in the direction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, attain the superior power of the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* because they are able to penetrate deeply into it.
Within this, there are nine kinds of superior power:
first, the power capable of subduing others, as the sutra states: "It is accomplished through non-regressive diligence, for all heterodox arguments and discourses of outsiders cannot shake it."
2. The power to sever doubt, as the sūtra says: "Accomplishment through conformity, because of entering the stages of all-knowledge.
3. The power of the immovability of one's own vehicle, as the sūtra says: "Accomplishment through distancing, because of transcending the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Fourth, the power of firm conviction regarding the secret place, as the sūtra says: "It is accomplished exclusively, because it resolutely proceeds toward buddha-wisdom.
Fifth, the power of non-disintegration, as the sūtra says: "It is accomplished without regression, because no māras or afflictions can destroy it."

Sixth, by means of the firm power that serves as the antidote for purifying the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), as the sūtra says: "It is firmly established because the bodhisattva’s illumination of wisdom is well-established."
7. The power of extensive counteraction, as the sūtra says: “Because one correctly abides and accomplishes the well-cultivated practice of the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
8. The power of transforming sentient beings, as the sūtra says: “Because one assists the accomplishment of correct practice through the observation of skillful means and wisdom.”

9. The power of purifying the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as stated in the Sūtra: "The practice is accomplished without abandonment, because one gathers the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

When this Bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is preeminently accomplished, and they attain the third benefit, the "patience in accordance with reality" (*anulomikī kṣānti*), which accords with the dharmas as they truly are without opposition.
These dharmas are as described above, being comprised within the superior powers.
The Sūtra says:
"O Sons of the Buddha!"

Once this bodhisattva has established themselves in this Bodhisattva Stage of Manifestation (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), they see many Buddhas by virtue of their great power of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) and their great power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).

By virtue of their great power of supernormal knowledge and their great power of aspiration, they see many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, many billions of Buddhas, many hundreds of billions of Buddhas, many trillions of Buddhas, many hundreds of quadrillions of Buddhas, and many hundreds of quintillions of nayutas of Buddhas.

When this bodhisattva sees the Buddhas, he makes offerings, pays homage, respects, honors, and praises them with a superior mind and a profound mind; he presents them with all requisites, including robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal elixirs, and every other article of offering. He also provides the Sangha with the most excellent and delightful articles of enjoyment belonging to bodhisattvas. With these roots of goodness, he dedicates them all toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Generating supreme reverence toward all Buddhas, he listens to the Dharma with single-minded devotion; having heard it, he receives and upholds it; having heard and upheld it, he attains the light of wisdom of the samādhi of reality; and having practiced in accordance with it, he maintains it in memory.
The wisdom of this bodhisattva becomes increasingly superior, and they further attain the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas.

Abiding in this Bodhisattva Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), for immeasurable hundreds of kalpas, those roots of goodness become increasingly superior, bright, and pure. For immeasurable thousands of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, immeasurable billions of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of billions of kalpas, immeasurable thousands of billions of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, those roots of goodness become increasingly superior, bright, and pure.
O Sons of the Buddha!
It is like pure gold that, when polished with lapis lazuli, becomes even more brilliant and pure in its luster and color.
O Sons of the Buddha!

In this way, when a bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Stage of Presence, those roots of goodness—observed through the wisdom of skillful means—become increasingly bright and pure, and they become ever more tranquil, attaining an indestructible perfection.
O Sons of the Buddha!
It is like the bright orb of the moon, which illuminates the bodies of sentient beings and brings them refreshing coolness, such that it cannot be destroyed by the four winds.
O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva thus dwells in this Bodhisattva Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī*), those roots of goodness are able to extinguish the fires of affliction of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of sentient beings, and cannot be destroyed by the four types of demonic paths.

Among these ten pāramitās of the bodhisattva, the prajñāpāramitā is predominant; however, it is not that the remaining pāramitās are not cultivated, for they are practiced according to one's strength and capacity.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the sixth Bodhisattva stage, the Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī*).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven. They possess sovereign skill in means to eliminate the conceit of sentient beings and are adept at transforming the mentalities of sentient beings regarding their conceit.

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—all such merits are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the bodhisattvas, mindfulness of the bodhisattva practices, mindfulness of the pāramitās, mindfulness of the ten stages, mindfulness of the indestructible powers, mindfulness of the fearlessnesses, and mindfulness of the unique buddha-dharmas, up to and including never being apart from mindfulness of all-aspect omniscience.
One should constantly give rise to this thought:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the greatest, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, the teacher, and the honored one, even unto becoming the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge."

Furthermore, from this thought, he gave rise to diligent practice; by the power of such diligence, in a single moment of thought, he attained hundreds of thousands of billions of samādhis, beheld hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas, and came to know the spiritual powers of hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas. He was able to shake hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-worlds, enter hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-worlds, illuminate hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-worlds, and teach and transform the sentient beings of hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-worlds. He was able to abide for a lifespan of hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, know the events of each of the past and future hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, skillfully enter hundreds of thousands of billions of Dharma-gates, and manifest himself as hundreds of thousands of billions of bodies, with each body displaying hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas as its retinue.
If one considers the sovereign excellence of the power of their vows, the bodhisattvas’ power of vows exceeds these numbers.

They manifest various kinds of supernormal powers—whether through their bodies, or light, or supernormal faculties, or eyes, or spheres of experience, or voices, or conduct, or adornments, or empowerments, or faith, or karma.
These supernormal powers (abhijñā) are such that they cannot be fully enumerated even throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
The Commentary states:

For one who, having heard and received [the teaching], attains the light of wisdom of the samādhi of reality and practices in accordance with it, they attain the dhāraṇī of meaning; this phrase demonstrates that point.
On account of that matter, it is said that by relying on the supreme samādhi, one attains the superior practice of the light of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
"Having practiced and retained" means being able to maintain that practice.

That "the bodhisattva’s wisdom becomes increasingly superior, and even those roots of goodness become increasingly superior and luminously pure" means that he has liberated himself from those obstacles and realized their meaning.
The analogy of beryl polished to reveal true gold illustrates the manifestation of the increasingly superior, predominant radiance of supramundane wisdom within this stage.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "O Sons of the Buddha!
It is like pure gold that, when polished with lapis lazuli, becomes increasingly brilliant and pure; even so, through the observation of skillful wisdom, it becomes increasingly brilliant and pure."
Because unobstructed wisdom manifests before one and the light of the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* manifests before one, it is called the "Manifesting Stage" (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
Regarding the observation through the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), it refers to the clear wisdom encompassed by the practice of the path that does not abide [in extremes].
Regarding the analogy of the moon’s luminous orb: it demonstrates that the wisdom of this stage surpasses that of the preceding stages, as the orb is small while its light is vast.
As the sutra states: "O Sons of the Buddha!
It is, for example, like the moon’s luminous orb, which cannot be destroyed by the four kinds of māras. Thus it is said.
"Māra-path" refers to following after the activities and conduct of Māra.
The remainder is as explained previously.

7. The Stage of Far-Reaching (*Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*). The treatise says:
Within the seventh stage, there are five kinds of distinctions in characteristics:
first, the distinction of the counteractive measure (*pratipakṣa*) for the practice of effortless spontaneity (*anabhisaṃskāra-vihāra*).
2. The distinction of the remedies for those obstacles;
3. The distinction of their simultaneous practice;
4. The distinction of the superiority of the preceding higher stages.
V. The Differentiation of Their Results.
What is the antidote to the practice of effortless ease?
The Sūtra says:
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva, having fully perfected the practices of the sixth stage, wishes to enter the seventh bodhisattva stage, that bodhisattva should initiate superior conduct by means of ten kinds of skillful wisdom."
What are these ten? They are:
skillfully cultivating emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, while accumulating great merit as an aid to the path;
entering into the selflessness of all phenomena, the absence of a life-span, and the absence of a sentient being, yet not abandoning the arousal of the four immeasurables;
They give rise to dharmas of merit and perform the practices of the supreme pāramitās, yet there is no dharma to be grasped;
they attain transcendence from the triple world, yet are able to manifest transformations to initiate practices that adorn the triple world;

they have utterly extinguished the flames of all afflictions, yet are able to initiate for all sentient beings the practice of extinguishing the flames of the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.

While conforming to the non-dual nature of illusions, dreams, shadows, echoes, transformations, the moon in water, and reflections in a mirror, they give rise to minds of infinite differentiation in performing activities;
they thoroughly know that the paths of all lands are like space, yet they give rise to practices for adorning and purifying Buddha-lands;
they know that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is by nature bodiless, yet they give rise to practices for adorning the physical body with the marks and signs of excellence.

They know that the voices of all Buddhas are voiceless, primordially quiescent, and of an ineffable nature, yet they manifest various distinct and adorned vocal activities in accordance with all sentient beings;

they enter into the Buddhas' instantaneous penetration of the three periods of time, yet they are able to discern various characteristics and eons of practice, because they contemplate according to the differences in the minds of all sentient beings.
O Sons of the Buddha!

When these bodhisattvas have thus employed these ten kinds of skillful wisdom to initiate sublime practices and have fulfilled the practices of the sixth stage, they enter the seventh bodhisattva stage.
O Sons of the Buddha!
When these Bodhisattvas, through these ten kinds of skillful wisdom, initiate superior practices and manifest present activities, it is called entering the seventh Bodhisattva stage.
The Commentary states:
Regarding the antidote to the practice of effortless ease, it is the wisdom of skillful means that initiates ten kinds of sublime practices. As the Sūtra says: "O Sons of the Buddha!

If a Bodhisattva, having fully perfected the practices of the sixth stage, wishes to enter the seventh Bodhisattva stage, that Bodhisattva should enter by initiating sublime practices through ten kinds of wisdom of skillful means."

When that bodhisattva’s unobstructed wisdom manifests and the practice of the perfection of wisdom manifests, they immediately give rise to a mind of joy within the practice of non-action, rather than giving rise to a mind of superior exertion.
These ten kinds of dharmas are manifested as the antidotes to that attachment to pleasure.

As for the wisdom of skillful means, it is the antidote to the lack of wisdom regarding the non-self of sentient beings, because it does not abandon them. As for the wisdom of selflessness, it is the antidote [to the lack of wisdom regarding the non-self of phenomena].

One embraces the practice of increasing excellence and initiates the sublime practice; this sublime practice is unsurpassed among all mundane and supramundane practices of increasing excellence because it possesses four kinds of merit.

First, the matter of the superior causes for wealth and the body: because one gathers the merit that serves as the superior cause for obtaining whatever wealth and body one requires according to one's wishes, as the Sūtra says: "That is to say, by skillfully cultivating emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one gathers great merit that aids the Path."

Second, regarding the matter of guarding against unwholesome conduct: one thus attains superior and immeasurable practice because one does not give rise to deluded actions toward any sentient being. As the sutra states: "Entering into the selflessness of all phenomena, the absence of a life-principle, and the absence of a sentient being, yet not abandoning the arousal of the four immeasurables."

Third, regarding the matter of protecting the roots of goodness: because one attains the superior cause and its predominance, there is the practice of the increase of meritorious qualities through the practice of the *pāramitās*. As the sūtra says: "One gives rise to meritorious qualities, performs the predominant practice of the *pāramitās*, yet there is no dharma that can be grasped."
Fourth, the matter of the causes for gathering sentient beings; herein there are seven gates:
first, taking birth through the power of vows to act as a leader in order to teach and transform other sentient beings.
Regarding "foremost," it is because sentient beings follow after them.
As the sutra says: "Having attained detachment from the three realms, they are nevertheless able to manifest transformative emanations to initiate practices that adorn the three realms."

Second, because it teaches the remedies: in order to extinguish the afflictions (*kleśa*), the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one remains eternally self-quiescent.

As the Sūtra says: "Having ultimately extinguished the flames of all afflictions, one is nevertheless able to initiate the practice of extinguishing the flames of the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion for the sake of all sentient beings."
Third, for the purpose of extinguishing all hindrances.
There are four kinds of hindrances, as explained in the context of the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*). As the Sūtra states:

"In accordance with the non-dual nature of illusions, dreams, reflections, echoes, transformations, the moon in water, and images in a mirror, one gives rise to a mind of immeasurable differentiation in performing activities."

Fourth, because of the gathering of the great assembly of the Dharma, as the Sūtra says: "Skillfully knowing that the paths of all lands are like space, yet initiating the practice of adorning and purifying Buddha-lands."

Fifth, because merit arises from seeing, hearing, drawing near to, making offerings to, and practicing [the teachings], as the sutra states: "Knowing that the nature of the dharmakāya of all buddhas is bodiless, one initiates the practice of adorning the rūpakāya with the marks and signs."

Sixth, because of turning the wheel of Dharma, as the sutra says: "Knowing that the voices of all Buddhas are voiceless, originally quiescent, and possess the characteristic of being inexpressible, yet they give rise to various distinct and adorned vocal activities in accordance with all sentient beings."

Seventh, because of skillfully explaining whatever is asked, as the Sūtra says: "Entering into all Buddhas, they penetrate the events of the three periods of time in a single thought-moment, yet are able to discern various characteristics, eons, and numbers of practices, observing according to the differences in the minds of all sentient beings."

These ten kinds of initiations of sublime practice collectively involve the grasping of what is to be countered and the grasping of the antidotes; they consist of the well-cultivated practices of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), whereby one enters into the selflessness of all phenomena, the absence of a life-principle (*jīva*), and the absence of a sentient being (*sattva*). This sequence should be understood in this way.
These ten kinds of dharmas are attained through manifestation while dwelling in the seventh stage, as the sutra states: "O Sons of the Buddha!
When this bodhisattva’s ten kinds of skillful means and wisdom give rise to and manifest these sublime practices, it is called 'entering the seventh bodhisattva stage.'"
Thus, the distinctions in the remedies for the practice of delighting in non-action have been explained up to the seventh stage.
Next, the remedies for those obstacles are explained, which consist of two aspects:
first, the cultivation of immeasurable kinds; and second, [the cultivation of] the path of the antidote.
2. Cultivating Effortless Practice (*anābhoga-caryā*).
The Sūtra says:
"When this bodhisattva dwells in the seventh bodhisattva stage, he enters the realms of immeasurable sentient beings and enters all..."
The Buddha’s immeasurable karma of teaching and transforming sentient beings; his entry into the immeasurable net of worlds; his entry into the immeasurable pure lands of all Buddhas;
his entry into the immeasurable distinctions among all phenomena; his entry into the immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas through which he attains the Unsurpassed Way;
his entry into immeasurable kalpas; and his entry into the immeasurable Buddhas who have attained mastery over the three periods of time.
Entering into the distinctions of the superior matters that inspire faith and joy in immeasurable sentient beings;

entering into the various manifestations of the names and form-bodies of immeasurable Buddhas; entering into the various distinctions of the mental activities, faculties, and inclinations of immeasurable sentient beings;
entering into the immeasurable voices and languages of the Buddhas that cause sentient beings to rejoice; entering into immeasurable assemblies...
They enter into the various distinctions of the arising of mind and mental factors; they enter into the immeasurable practices of wisdom that follow all Buddhas;

they enter into the immeasurable vehicles of the Śrāvakas and their respective inclinations; they enter into the immeasurable teachings on the path proclaimed by all Buddhas to inspire faith and understanding in sentient beings;
they enter into the accumulation of the immeasurable vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas; and they enter into the immeasurable profound wisdom of all Buddhas.
The gate of wisdom, the entry into what has been taught, the entry into the immeasurable paths of practice of all bodhisattvas,
and the entry into the immeasurable matters of the Great Vehicle compendium taught by all Buddhas, which enable bodhisattvas to attain entry.
The Treatise says:
Regarding those who practice immeasurable kinds [of deeds], according to what they do, which sentient beings are benefited?
In what places do those sentient beings dwell?
By means of what wisdom, by means of what mind, by means of what practice, and by placing [beings] in what vehicle?
Through these distinctions, there are ten kinds of cultivation.

Regarding "the benefit accorded to which sentient beings according to their needs": because immeasurable sentient beings are taught through immeasurable karmic activities, as the Sūtra says: "When this bodhisattva dwells in the seventh bodhisattva stage, he enters the realm of immeasurable sentient beings and enters the immeasurable karmic activities of the Buddhas for teaching and transforming sentient beings."

Regarding where sentient beings abide: it is so that they may cause them to rely upon pure Buddha-lands within immeasurable worlds, as the sutra says: "Entering the net of immeasurable worlds; entering the immeasurable pure lands of all Buddhas."

Regarding "by what kind of wisdom": it is because of awakening to the wisdom of the immeasurable and manifold *dharmadhātu*, as the sutra states: "Entering the distinctions of immeasurable phenomena and entering the wisdom of immeasurable Buddhas to attain the unsurpassed path."

They penetrate immeasurable kalpas and enter the awakening of wisdom regarding the three periods of time, as the sutra states: "Entering immeasurable kalpas, they enter the penetration of the affairs of the three periods of time of immeasurable Buddhas."
Regarding the question of "by what kind of mind," there are three matters:

first, there are sentient beings who have faith in various celestial bodies and minds; [the Buddha] acts in accordance with them and speaks according to their faith. As the sutra says: "He enters into the distinctions of the superior matters of the faith and delight of immeasurable sentient beings, and he enters into the various manifestations of the names and form-bodies of immeasurable Buddhas."

Second, knowing the past mental habits and whether the faculties are dull, medium, or sharp, one preaches the Dharma accordingly, as the Sūtra states: "Entering into the various distinctions of the mental activities, faculties, and inclinations of immeasurable sentient beings; entering into the voices and languages of immeasurable Buddhas to cause sentient beings to rejoice."

Third, as for the practice by which one teaches remedies in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, it is as the sutra says: "Entering the various distinctions of the mental activities of immeasurable sentient beings, and entering the wisdom-conduct of immeasurable Buddhas."

Regarding "placing them in which vehicle": placing them within the Śrāvaka vehicle among the three vehicles is as stated in the sūtra: "Entering the immeasurable Śrāvaka vehicle of faith and understanding, and entering the immeasurable paths of teaching of all Buddhas to cause sentient beings to have faith and understanding."

Regarding those established in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, it is as the sutra says: "They enter the accumulation of the immeasurable vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas; they enter the gate of the immeasurable, profound wisdom of all buddhas; and they enter what has been taught."

Regarding "establishing them within the Mahāyāna," it is as the sūtra states: "Entering the immeasurable paths practiced by all bodhisattvas, and entering the matters of the integration of the Mahāyāna taught by all Buddhas, so that bodhisattvas may attain entry."
Thus, the ten kinds of cultivation of the various distinctions of the remedies for those obstacles have been explained. Next, the cultivation of effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) is explained.
The Sūtra says:
This Bodhisattva forms this thought:

These Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess infinite and boundless realms; these realms cannot be encompassed even in several hundred billion kalpas, a thousand billion kalpas, or a hundred thousand billion kalpas, nor even after exceeding such numbers for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas that are beyond calculation—I must gather all such Buddha-realms.
This is spontaneously accomplished not through discrimination, but through non-discrimination and the non-apprehension of signs.

Thus, this bodhisattva, having skillfully observed the supernormal power of wisdom, constantly cultivates the wisdom of skillful means day and night; he perfumes and gives rise to sublime practices, abiding well in firmness by virtue of the immovable dharma.
The Commentary states:

Herein, "spontaneous" (svayambhū) refers to the excellence of its own nature because it is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*). As the Sūtra says: "Spontaneity is not accomplished through conceptualization; it is accomplished by being non-conceptual and by not grasping at signs."

This sentence demonstrates that this bodhisattva possesses such wisdom of skillful observation and supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*); by constantly practicing the wisdom of skillful means day and night, they perfume and give rise to sublime conduct, abiding well in firmness through the dharma of immovability, because it serves as the antidote to those obstacles.
Thus, the distinctions regarding the remedies for those obstacles have been explained in this stage.
Next, the section on simultaneous practice is explained, which has four aspects:
first, the uninterrupted succession of the two practices;
2. Superiority of faith;
3. Ability to accomplish great purpose;
4. Distinctions among the factors of enlightenment.
The Sūtra says:
"When this bodhisattva gives rise to the Path, not a single thought-moment is abandoned.

This bodhisattva cultivates wisdom; it arises when coming, it arises when going, it arises when standing, it arises when sitting, and it arises even when lying down. Even in sleep and dreams, they are able to give rise to the Path."
Free from all hindrances and obscurations, they abide in the various modes of deportment, never departing from such mindfulness of these characteristics.
In every moment of thought, these bodhisattvas fully accomplish the ten pāramitās of a bodhisattva.

Why is this? Because such bodhisattvas give rise to all thoughts with great compassion as their foremost priority in every moment of mind, cultivating all Buddha-dharmas and dedicating them all toward the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
When this bodhisattva, while seeking the Buddha-way, cultivates roots of goodness and relinquishes them to all sentient beings, this is the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).
That he is able to extinguish the heat of all afflictions is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
To have compassion as one's foremost priority and to be able to endure all sentient beings is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
To seek ever-superior roots of goodness with a mind that never tires or finds satisfaction is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).

When the mind does not wander during the practice of various deeds, but constantly directs itself toward the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), this is the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*).
To manifest patience regarding the fact that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-arising is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The ability to give rise to immeasurable gateways of wisdom is the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*).
The aspiration for ever-higher, superior wisdom is the perfection of vow (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).
The fact that all heterodox arguments of external paths and the hosts of Māras cannot obstruct or destroy the bodhisattva path is the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).
To contemplate and know the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Thus, O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā*), in every thought-moment they are fully endowed with the ten perfections; they are also fully endowed with the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*); they are also fully endowed with the four foundations, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the three gates of liberation; in brief, they are fully endowed with all factors of enlightenment in every thought-moment.
The Treatise says:
This is because within a single moment of thought, the two practices of śamatha and vipaśyanā manifest simultaneously.
Regarding "abiding in all modes of deportment," it means that during the performance of all activities, those practices proceed without interval, without interruption, and without cessation.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "When this bodhisattva gives rise to the path, he does not abandon it for even a single thought-moment, because he abides in all modes of deportment and remains far removed from all hindrances of affliction."
Regarding "the excellence of faith": it refers to the manifestation of the signs of adornment through focused mindfulness upon the extraordinary meaning within that immeasurable wisdom.
As the Sūtra says: "One is never separated from such mindfulness of the signs."
"One who can accomplish the great purpose" means that in every thought-moment they are fully endowed with the great purpose of the ten *pāramitās*.
As the Sūtra says: "This bodhisattva, in every thought-moment, is fully endowed with the ten bodhisattva *pāramitās*, up to and including the *jñāna-pāramitā*."

Among these, the perfection of skillful means consists in initiating immeasurable activities of wisdom; by virtue of this wisdom, one initiates immeasurable practices such as giving, because they are embraced by the power of aspiration.

The perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā) gives rise to the highest of all wisdoms; by means of this wisdom, one initiates the superior practices of giving and so forth, because it brings about the excellence of gathering [beings].

The perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) means that one's practice cannot be destroyed by any heterodox doctrines or hosts of Māras; because of this practice, one remains far removed from the obstacles to giving and the other perfections.

The perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) consists in observing and knowing the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are. By means of this wisdom, one understands the distinctions among all varieties of practices, such as giving (*dāna*), for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Regarding the distinctions among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), there are four aspects:

first, because they rely on the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*) according to the Mahāyāna, as the Sūtra says: "In this way, O Sons of the Buddha!"... [text continues] ...because they rely on the practice of the perfections according to the Mahāyāna. Thus, the Sūtra states: "O Sons of the Buddha! In this way... [and so forth].
This is because "this bodhisattva, dwelling in this Bodhisattva Ground of Far-Going, fulfills the ten pāramitās in every thought-moment.

Second, it is because they practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, as the sutra says: "They also fulfill the four means of attraction."
Third, because it is supremely pure in reliance upon the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the "gate of liberation through the factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣadharmavimokṣamukha*): in what place does one abide?
By means of which gate does one practice to attain purity?

As it is said in the Sūtra: "Furthermore, they are fully endowed with the four families (*kula*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).

As for the "families," these are the family of Prajñā, the family of the Truths (*satya*), the family of abandoning afflictions (*kleśa*), and the family of the purification of suffering (*duḥkha-viśuddhi*).

Fourth, based on the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as the sūtra states: "In brief, all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) are fully present in every moment of thought."
Thus, the distinctions regarding the practice of the two together have been explained.

Next, the distinctions regarding the superiority of the higher stages will be explained; because the superior skillful means of the lower stages reach fulfillment, this is taught within the context of the seven stages.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
Does a bodhisattva fulfill all the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) solely within the seventh bodhisattva stage,
or do they fulfill them throughout all the bodhisattva stages?
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!

Within the ten bodhisattva stages, a bodhisattva fully possesses all the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma); however, it is because the seventh stage is preeminent that it receives this name."
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha!
It is because in this bodhisattva stage, these bodhisattvas fulfill the practice of skillful means and thereby attain entry into the superknowledges of wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!
Because a bodhisattva in the first stage (bhūmi) makes the vow to contemplate all Buddha-dharmas, they fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma).
In the second stage, because they eliminate the defilements of the mind, they fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment.
In the third stage, because the aspiration increases further and one attains the light of the Dharma, one is fully endowed with the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
In the fourth stage, because one enters the Path, one is fully endowed with the factors conducive to enlightenment.
In the fifth stage, because one practices in accordance with worldly dharmas, one fulfills the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
In the sixth stage, because one enters the profound gateway of dharmas, one fulfills the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Because all Buddha-dharmas arise within this seventh Bodhisattva stage, it is fully endowed with all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
The treatise asks:
How is the practice of superior skillful means fulfilled in the lower stages?
Because they are fulfilled, they enter the practice of great wisdom; as the *Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said:
'O Son of the Buddha!

Although Bodhisattvas fully possess all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) throughout the ten Bodhisattva stages, it is only because the seventh stage is preeminent that it receives this name.'"
Why is this? O Son of the Buddha,
it is because these Bodhisattvas, within this Bodhisattva stage, have fulfilled the practice of skillful means and thereby attained entry into the superknowledges of wisdom."
Among these, "the supernormal powers" refers to the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
"Wisdom" is as previously explained.
What is the fulfillment of the practice of skillful means within this stage?

Within those other mundane and supramundane practices, he further gives rise to superior practices; therefore, because he gives rise to all Buddha-dharmas within these seven stages, he is able to fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
As it is said in the Sūtra: "O Son of the Buddha!
Because a bodhisattva in the first stage (bhūmi) makes a vow to contemplate all Buddha-dharmas, they fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
... [omitted] ... up until this seventh bodhisattva stage, because they give rise to all Buddha-dharmas, they fulfill all factors conducive to enlightenment. Thus it is taught.
Thus, the excellence of the higher stages and the fulfillment of the superior practice of skillful means in the lower stages have already been explained.
How, then, is there the fulfillment of the practice of the factors conducive to enlightenment through the application of wisdom and skillful means in the higher stages?
The Sūtra says:
"For what reason?
O Son of the Buddha!"
From the first stage up to the seventh stage, the bodhisattva attains the paths of practice of all wisdoms.
By the power of this, from the eighth bodhisattva stage up to the tenth stage, their effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) is spontaneously fulfilled.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like two worlds:
first, a defiled and pure world; [second, a purely pure world].
2. The World of Pure Radiance (*Śuddhāvāsa*).
Between these two worlds, it is difficult to pass through.
To wish to cross this realm, one must employ great supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*).
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path of defilement and purity in this way, it is difficult to pass beyond; one can only pass beyond it by means of the power of great vows, the power of great skillful means and wisdom, and the power of great supernormal faculties.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
Are these seven bodhisattva stages characterized by defiled conduct or by pure conduct?"
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
From the first bhūmi onward, all that the bodhisattvas practice is free from the defilement of afflictions and karma."
Why is this? Because it is dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Since it accords with the practice of the Path through impartiality according to its respective portion, it is not called "transgressing the afflictive conduct of the seven stages."
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a universal monarch who, riding upon a supreme jewel elephant, travels through the four continents; though he perceives those who are impoverished, suffering, and defiled by transgressions, he is not himself defiled by their faults.

Nevertheless, the King has not yet escaped the human condition; yet, if he were to relinquish this human body and be born in the Brahma-world, dwelling in a Brahma palace, he would behold a thousand worlds and manifest the radiant power and majesty of a Brahma King.
At that time, they are not yet called "human beings.
Son of the Buddha!

It is the same for the bodhisattva: from the first stage onward, they ride upon the vehicle of the various pāramitās and traverse all worlds; though they know the faults of being defiled by worldly afflictions, they are not stained by those faults of affliction.
Because they ride upon the true path, they are not said to be defiled by the afflictions of the seven stages.
When a bodhisattva relinquishes all effortful practices and enters the eighth stage from the seventh, at that time they are said to ride the pure vehicle of the bodhisattvas throughout all worlds.
Knowing as it truly is the faults of defilement by all afflictions (*kleśa*), yet not being defiled by those faults of affliction because one has transcended them—
O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva dwells in this seventh bodhisattva stage, they transcend the multitude of afflictions such as excessive desire and the rest.
When this bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Ground of Far-Going, they are neither called one who has afflictions nor called one who is free from afflictions. Why is this?
Because all afflictions do not manifest, they are not called those who possess afflictions;
because their seeking of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is not yet fulfilled, they are not called those who are free from afflictions.
The Treatise says:
Why is it that the application of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) through the practice of superior wisdom and skillful means is fulfilled in the higher stages?
As the Sūtra asks: "For what reason?"
"O Son of the Buddha!

From the first stage up to the seventh stage, a bodhisattva attains the paths of practice characterized by various wisdoms; however, it is only by means of the power of great vows, the power of great skillful means and wisdom, and the power of great supernormal faculties that one can finally transcend them. Thus it is said.
From the first stage onward, one has already distanced oneself from all afflictions; this is what is demonstrated here.
This stage is called "defiled and pure," yet it is not a practice of defilement, because it is the path of equanimity that proceeds according to its own nature.
In this stage, that Bodhisattva, according to their capacity, relinquishes the path of effortful application, as illustrated by the analogy of the universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

In the eighth stage, they spontaneously attain the fruition of practice that transcends both afflictions and defilements, manifesting like one born in the Brahma-world, having relinquished the human body of a universal monarch.
As the sutra says: "O Sons of the Buddha!
It is, for example, like a Wheel-Turning Sage King... [he] is not defiled by the faults of afflictions, because he has transcended them.
O Sons of the Buddha!"
When a bodhisattva dwells in this seventh bodhisattva stage, they have transcended the multitude of afflictions such as excessive desire and so forth;
however, because they have not yet reached the stage of fruition (*vipākabhūmi*), this stage is not called "conduct free from afflictions," for it still involves effortful application (*sābhoga*).
"When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Far-Reaching (dūramgamā), they are not called one who possesses afflictions because [the qualities] have not yet been fulfilled;
nor are they called one free from afflictions. This has already been explained in the preceding section on the distinctions of excellence in the higher stages.
Next, the distinctions among the fruits of the two concurrent practices are explained.
These consist of four aspects:
first, the purification of karma;
2. Attaining superior samādhi;
3. Transcending the stages;
4. Attaining superior practice.
What is the purity of action?
The Sūtra says:

"When this Bodhisattva dwells in this seventh Bodhisattva stage, the Far-Reaching (dūraṃgamā), they ultimately accomplish profoundly pure bodily action, ultimately accomplish profoundly pure verbal action, and ultimately accomplish profoundly pure mental action."
This Bodhisattva has already abandoned all unwholesome courses of action that are censured by the Buddhas;
as for all wholesome courses of action praised by the Buddhas, these he constantly practices.
All the scriptures and technical arts existing in the world proceed spontaneously for this bodhisattva, as described in the context of the fifth stage.

Within the trichiliocosm, this bodhisattva becomes a great master; with the exception of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the eighth stage, there is no sentient being whose profound resolve or sublime practice can equal theirs.
All the dhyānas, samādhis, samāpattis, superknowledges (abhijñā), and liberations belonging to this bodhisattva manifest before him;
yet within the gateway of practice, they are not yet fully perfected through the power of karmic fruition, as is the case in the eighth bodhisattva stage.

When this bodhisattva dwells in this seventh bodhisattva stage, the Far-Reaching (dūraṃgamā), in every moment of thought they fully cultivate and accumulate the power of skillful means and wisdom, as well as all the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma), attaining a progressively superior degree of fulfillment.
The treatise states:
There are four characteristics of the purity of karma.

First is the excellence of purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*), as the sūtra says: "When this bodhisattva dwells in this seventh bodhisattva stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā*), they ultimately accomplish profoundly pure bodily action, and so forth, up to 'this is then constant practice.'"
2. The excellence of the purification of mundane knowledge, as stated in the sutra: "All worldly scriptures and arts, even those performed spontaneously. 3.

The excellence of attaining the equality of one's own body and mental conduct such that there is no equal, as stated in the sutra: "This bodhisattva, within the trichiliocosm, has no equal in terms of profound resolve and sublime practice."

Fourth, the excellence of the manifestation of superior powers such as dhyāna; as the sūtra states: "This bodhisattva’s all dhyānas, samādhis, and so forth, even up to their attainment of further superior fulfillment."

Within this, based on dhyāna, there arise samādhi, samāpatti, supernormal powers (abhijñā), and liberation, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings and for the practice of the bliss of quiescence.
The samāpatti of the cessation of perception and feeling follows such a sequence; such is the fruit of these paired practices.
The four aspects of the purification of karma have already been explained.
Next, the attainment of supreme samādhi is explained.
The Sūtra says:

When this bodhisattva dwells in this seventh bodhisattva stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā), they enter the bodhisattva samādhi named "Wisdom of Excellent Discernment," the samādhi "Excellent Contemplation of Meaning," the samādhi "Benefiting the Mind," the samādhi "Discerning the Treasury of Meanings," the samādhi "Discerning All Meanings," the samādhi "Firmly Abiding in the Deep Root," the samādhi "Gate of Wisdom and Supernatural Powers," the samādhi "Activity of the Dharma Realm," the samādhi "Benefit of the Tathāgatas," and the bodhisattva samādhi named "The Gate of the World and Nirvāṇa as Various Treasuries of Meaning."

By means of such a gate of great wisdom and supernormal power, the bodhisattva fulfills the thirteen foremost samādhis and is able to enter hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva samādhi-gates, thereby purifying this stage.
The Commentary states:
There are ten characteristics of one who has attained superior samādhi:

first, based on meanings not yet contemplated; second, based on meanings already contemplated, as the Sūtra says: "Because this Bodhisattva, dwelling in this seventh Bodhisattva stage, the Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching), enters the Bodhisattva samādhi named 'Skillful Selection of Wisdom' and the 'Samādhi of Skillfully Contemplating Meanings.'"

Third, the superiority of immeasurable meanings based on a single phrase; fourth, the teaching of immeasurable names based on a single meaning, as in the sūtra: "Because of the Samādhi of Beneficial Intention" and "Because of the Samādhi of Discerning the Treasury of Meanings."
Fifth, based on the wisdom that penetrates all five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), as stated in the sūtra: "the samādhi that discerns all meanings.

Sixth, based on the purification of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) through the firm root of the contemplation of *tathatā*, as stated in the sūtra: "the samādhi of abiding well in the firm root."
Seventh, regarding the purification of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), there are four kinds of purification of hindrances.
First, the hindrance to supreme merit; its antidote is as stated in the sutra: "the samādhi of the gate of wisdom and supernormal powers."
2. The obstacle of the hindrance of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); its antidote is as stated in the sutra: "the *dharmadhātu-karma-samādhi*. 3.
The obstacle of weak capacity regarding the profound and supreme Buddha-dharmas; its antidote is as stated in the sutra: "the *tathāgata-hitānuśamsa-samādhi*."

Fourth, the obstacle of non-abiding in practice and its remedy, as stated in the sutra: "Because of entering the Bodhisattva samādhi called 'The Door to the World and Nirvāṇa, Which is a Treasury of Various Meanings.'"
The treasury of various meanings refers to the various roots of goodness.

Thus, through these thirteen foremost samādhis that fulfill the gateway of great wisdom-penetration, one is able to enter hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattva samādhi-gateways, thereby purifying this stage.
Having already explained the attainment of the supreme samādhi,
the text next explains the transcendence of the stages (*bhūmi*).
The Sūtra says:

Because this bodhisattva has attained the wisdom and skillful means of this samādhi in a state of perfect purity, and because he has attained the power of great compassion, he transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and directly contemplates the progression toward the stage of wisdom.
The treatise states:
There are two kinds of characteristics for one who has transcended the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas:
first, the power of wisdom in the skillful means of practice; [and second, the power of wisdom in the maturation of the roots of goodness].
Second, by the power of great compassion.
As for "that which appears," it refers to being able to enter the stream of the Dharma.

Regarding "the stage of wisdom through deliberation," it should be understood that the wisdom of the eighth stage consists solely in observing the path of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, because these are perfected at that level.
Furthermore, as for "transcendence," it is manifested through the superiority of karma.
The Sūtra says:

"When this Bodhisattva dwells in this seventh Bodhisattva stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā), there are immeasurable bodily actions of signless practice, immeasurable verbal actions of signless practice, and immeasurable mental actions of signless practice. Because these are the Bodhisattva’s well-purified practices, they attain the radiance of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the first bodhisattva stage, they possess immeasurable physical actions, immeasurable verbal actions, and immeasurable mental actions, which have already surpassed the conduct of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
This transcendence is due to contemplating the Great Dharma; it is not through the power of one's own intellectual practice."
This seventh bodhisattva stage, because it is attained through the power of observing the practice of one's own wisdom, cannot be destroyed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!

For example, it is like a prince born into a royal family who possesses the marks of royalty and surpasses all his ministers; this is due to the power of his noble status, not due to the power of his own wisdom or conduct.
When his body has grown large, he naturally possesses the power of wisdom such that the tasks he undertakes are accomplished, surpassing all the assembly of ministers.
In the same way, O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva first resolves their mind on enlightenment, they have already surpassed all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas because the depth of their resolve is so great.
Now, by abiding in this seventh bodhisattva stage, because one dwells in the practice of self-knowledge, one transcends all the activities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Commentary says:
"The practitioner of the signless who performs immeasurable acts of the three karmas" refers to entering meditative concentration and remaining far removed from signs.

There are also immeasurable śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who possess pure karma and are free from signs; however, they do not possess immeasurable signs, and thus they cannot benefit all sentient beings.
Furthermore, this immeasurability surpasses the matters of the lower stages.
It is because the practitioner of pure conduct has fulfilled the practice of skillful means.
It is the radiance of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), because its signs manifest before one.
The parable of the prince illustrates the manifestation of superiority within this stage, because the cultivation of skillful means has been brought to fulfillment.
"Abiding in the practice of one's own wisdom" refers to dwelling in mindfulness and contemplation once the practice of skillful means is complete.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, as when a prince is born into a royal family... because he acts and abides by his own wisdom, he surpasses all the affairs of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Thus it is said.
The supreme activities of the immeasurable bodies and so forth have already been explained;
for it is not merely that there are many immeasurable supernormal powers, but also because they manifest immeasurable ultimate meanings.
As the Sūtra says:
O Sons of the Buddha!

When these Bodhisattvas dwell in this seventh Bodhisattva stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā), they attain profound detachment and non-action; yet, their physical, verbal, and mental activities continue to seek superior practices without ever abandoning them.
The Commentary states:
"Profound" means because it penetrates far;
"remote" means because those obstacles have been extinguished.
Regarding "no practice": it is because those other mundane and supramundane stages cannot be practiced [by him].

As for "the turning toward and seeking of superior practice through the actions of body, speech, and mind without abandoning them": although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have departed from those [mundane] signs, their karma is not like this, because they consider what little they have attained to be sufficient and do not seek higher practices.
Thus, the fruits of practicing these two together have already been explained as transcending the stages of the Two Vehicles.
How does one attain superior practice?
The Sūtra says:
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
From what stage does a bodhisattva come to be able to enter the samādhi of cessation?"
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!

From the sixth stage onward, bodhisattvas are able to enter the samādhi of cessation. Now, abiding in the seventh bodhisattva stage, they are able to enter the samādhi of cessation in every thought-moment, yet they do not realize final cessation. These bodhisattvas have ultimately accomplished inconceivable actions of body, speech, and mind."
O Son of the Buddha!
These bodhisattvas practice the practice of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), yet they do not realize the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
O Son of the Buddha!

For example, it is like a person who boards a great vessel and enters the great ocean; being skilled in navigating the ship and skilled in the characteristics of the water, they are not harmed by the perils of the ocean waters.
In this way, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this seventh bodhisattva stage, they board the vessel of the various pāramitās and practice the conduct of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), yet they do not realize the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
The treatise says:
