One practices the practice of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) without realizing the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because one does not abandon existence (*bhava*).
As the *Sūtra* states: "Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:"
"O Son of the Buddha!
From the sixth stage onward, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to enter the samādhi of cessation, yet they do not realize the state of cessation."
Thus, the superior practice of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) has been explained.
Next, the superior practice of arousal (*samutthāna*) is explained.
The Sūtra says:

When a bodhisattva thus practices by penetrating the power of samādhi and wisdom, they give rise to the power of great skillful means and wisdom; therefore, while manifesting their body within the gateway of the mundane world, their deep mind remains in nirvāṇa. Though surrounded by a retinue, their mind is always detached; through the power of their vows, they take birth within the triple world yet remain unstained by the mundane world.
The mind is constantly in a state of quiescent extinction, yet through the power of skillful means it is made to blaze forth again, even though it is not burned.
In accordance with the Buddha-wisdom, one transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
They penetrate the treasury of the realm of all Buddhas while manifesting the realm of Māra;
they transcend the paths of the four Māras while manifesting the practice of the realm of Māra;
they manifest the practices of various non-Buddhists while, in their profound mind, never abandoning the Buddha’s salvation.
He thoroughly understands all worldly affairs, yet his mind always dwells upon the supramundane path of the Dharma.

Regarding all matters of adornment, he excels those of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, the four heavenly kings, Śakra-devendra, and Brahmā-devaputra, yet he never abandons his mindfulness of the joy of the Dharma.
The Commentary states:
For one who initiates the sublime practice, there are eight types of practices subsumed under their respective antidotes:

first, the practice of generating merit that accords with the gateway of the world, as the Sūtra says: "When a Bodhisattva thus penetrates the power of the wisdom of samādhi and practices, because they give rise to the power of great skillful means and wisdom, they manifest within the gateway of the world while their profound mind dwells in nirvāṇa."
2. The practice of subsuming other practices through the primary [virtue], as the sūtra says: "Though surrounded by a retinue, his mind is always detached. 3.
The practice of taking birth through the power of aspiration, as the sūtra says: "By the power of his vows, he takes birth within the three realms, yet is not defiled by the world."

Fourth, the practice of not severing the household life: while remaining far removed from the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the secondary affliction of greed, they manifest the activities of greed. As the Sūtra says: "The mind is constantly in a state of quiescent extinction, yet through the power of skillful means it blazes forth again; nevertheless, it does not burn."
5. The practice of entry, as stated in the sūtra: "In accordance with the Buddha’s wisdom, one transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

6. The practice of sustaining life, which pertains to the spheres of Māra such as food, drink, sleep, and dreams, as stated in the sūtra: "Having attained mastery over the treasury of the Buddhas’ spheres, one manifests the spheres of Māra."

Seventh, there is retrogression, because he demonstrates these three realms of Māra—old age, sickness, and death—as shown by the sūtra: "He transcends the paths of the four Māras, yet manifests within the realms of Māra."
8. Transformation of Practice has three types of transformation:
first, the transformation of seeing desire, as the sutra says, "manifesting the practices of various non-Buddhists while in their deep heart not abandoning the Buddha's salvation."
2. The transformation of obstacles (*āvaraṇa-parāvṛtti*): As the sūtra says, "While penetrating all worldly affairs, the mind always abides in the supramundane path of the Dharma.

3. The transformation of craving (*tṛṣṇā-parāvṛtti*): Being embraced by the respectful minds of devas, nāgas, and others, one transforms their craving; as the sūtra says, "Regarding all matters of adornment that surpass those of devas and nāgas, he does not abandon his joyful mindfulness of the Dharma."
The Sūtra says:

"When a Bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom and dwells in this Bodhisattva stage of Far-Going (dūraṃgamā), they see many Buddhas by virtue of the power of great supernormal faculties and the power of great vows."

They see many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, many billions of Buddhas, many hundreds of billions of Buddhas, many thousands of billions of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, by virtue of their great power of supernatural faculties and the power of their great vows.

When this bodhisattva sees the Buddhas, he makes offerings, pays homage, respects, honors, and praises them with a superior mind and a profound mind; he presents them with all requisites, including robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal elixirs, and every other article of offering. He also provides the Sangha with the most excellent and delightful articles of enjoyment belonging to bodhisattvas. By means of these roots of goodness, he dedicates them all toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Toward all Buddhas, they give rise to supreme reverence; with single-minded devotion, they listen to the Dharma, and having heard it, they receive and uphold it. Having heard and upheld it, they attain the light of wisdom of the samādhi of suchness; they practice in accordance with it, and having practiced, they maintain it in memory. Thus they protect the true Dharma of all Buddhas, which cannot be destroyed by the wisdom or the challenges of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Because this bodhisattva is further able to benefit sentient beings, their patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) becomes increasingly pure.

Abiding in this Bodhisattva Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā*), over immeasurable eons, those roots of goodness become increasingly superior, clear, pure, pliant, and perfected; they further reach complete perfection. Over immeasurable hundreds of eons, immeasurable thousands of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *nayuta* eons, immeasurable billions of eons, immeasurable hundreds of billions of eons, immeasurable trillions of eons, immeasurable hundreds of trillions of eons, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* eons, those roots of goodness become increasingly superior, clear, pure, pliant, and perfected; they further reach complete perfection.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like pure, refined gold that has been fully adorned with all manner of precious jewels; its radiance and color become increasingly superior, brilliant, and pure, such that no other ornaments can equal it.
In this way, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this seventh bodhisattva stage, the Far-Reaching (dūraṃgamā), those roots of goodness arising from the wisdom of skillful means become increasingly brilliant and pure, such that they cannot be destroyed by any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the light of the sun, which cannot be eclipsed by all the stars or the moonlight, and which can completely dry up all the mud and water within Jambudvīpa.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this seventh bodhisattva stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā), those roots of goodness cannot be destroyed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and they can further dry up the mire of afflictions of all sentient beings.

Among these ten pāramitās of the bodhisattva, the pāramitā of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā) is predominant; yet it is not that the remaining pāramitās are not practiced, for they are cultivated according to his strength and capacity.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the seventh Bodhisattva stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin). Their sovereign actions skillfully cause sentient beings to give rise to right wisdom, and they also cause sentient beings to cross over the ocean of afflictions.

All the merits from the wholesome deeds one performs—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the bodhisattvas, mindfulness of the bodhisattva practices, mindfulness of the pāramitās, mindfulness of the ten stages, mindfulness of the indestructible powers, mindfulness of the fearlessnesses, and mindfulness of the unique buddha-dharmas, up to and including being never apart from mindfulness of all-aspect omniscience.
One should constantly give rise to this thought:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the greatest, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, the teacher, the honored one, and even the one upon whom the knowledge of all-knowledge relies."
Furthermore, from this thought, he gave rise to diligent practice; by the power of that diligence, in a single moment of thought,
he attained hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of samādhis, beheld hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas,
knew the spiritual powers of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, and was able to shake hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds.
...able to enter hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds; able to illuminate hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds;
able to transform sentient beings in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds;
able to abide for a lifespan of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas; and able to know each of the past and future worlds throughout hundreds of thousands [of kalpas].
They can skillfully enter into events spanning billions of nayutas of kalpas; they can skillfully enter into hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of dharma-gates;

they can manifest their bodies as hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of forms, and within each individual body, they can manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas as their retinue.
If one considers the sovereign supremacy of their power of aspiration, the bodhisattvas' power of aspiration exceeds these numbers.

They manifest various kinds of supernormal powers—whether through the body, or light, or supernormal faculties, or the eyes, or spheres of experience, or voice, or conduct, or adornment, or empowerment, or faith, or karma.
These supernormal powers (abhijñā) are such that they cannot be calculated or known even throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
The Commentary says:
Those who protect the True Dharma of all Buddhas become great teachers within the trichiliocosm because they have fulfilled their practice of skillful means (upāya).
Because he is the foremost protector and because he benefits sentient beings, the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) becomes further manifest.
One should know that this is the etymological explanation of this stage.

As the Sūtra says: "Because this Bodhisattva is further able to benefit sentient beings, because his patience regarding phenomena becomes increasingly pure, and because the power of his cultivation reaches its ultimate limit, it is called the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*), fully adorned with all manner of jewels."

The simile of refined gold demonstrates that because the skillful means, practices, and efforts regarding all factors conducive to enlightenment have reached fulfillment, the various roots of goodness within this stage are shown to become increasingly superior, brilliant, and pure.
As the sutra states: "For example, it is like primordial pure gold, which cannot be destroyed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding the analogy of the sun's rays, as explained previously in the [First] Bhūmi, because this stage is superior, as the sutra says: "O Son of the Buddha!..."
"Just as the light of the sun can even dry up the mire of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all sentient beings.
The remainder is as previously stated.
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Chapter Seven, "The Far-Reaching Stage" (*Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*), Part Nine.
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*, Chapter Eight, "The Immovable Ground" (*Acalā-bhūmi*), Part Ten.
Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Northern Wei dynasty.
8. The Treatise on the Immovable Ground states:
Within the eighth ground, there are seven distinct characteristics:
first, the section on the general elucidation of the application for the accumulation of the ground;
2. The section on attaining pure patience;
3. The section on attaining superior practice;
4. The section on purifying Buddha-fields.
5. The Section on Attaining Mastery;
6. The Section on Great Excellence;
7. The Section on Explaining the Names.
What is the section on the general clarification of the stage of the accumulation of skillful means?
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said:
O Sons of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva, within the seventh stage, has well accumulated wisdom and skillful means, has well purified all practices, has well accumulated the factors conducive to enlightenment, has well aroused the power of great vows, and has been well empowered by the empowerment of the Tathāgatas; because they have attained the power of their own roots of goodness, because they constantly mindfully accord with the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of a Buddha of the Tathāgata, because they have well purified the awakening of the profound mind, because they have accomplished the power of merit and knowledge, because they practice great compassion and so forth without abandoning any sentient beings, and because they have thoroughly penetrated the path of immeasurable wisdom.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the section on the "General Clarification of the Collection of Expedient Means" (*upāya-saṃgraha-bhūmi*), because it pertains to the seven stages as a whole, there are both common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
What are the common characteristics?
There are three kinds of common characteristics:
first, because of the progressively higher realization of the two kinds of selflessness;
second, because of the purity of the path of non-abiding.
Third, because they are encompassed by the practice of skillful means and wisdom, thereby fulfilling the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
As the Sūtra says: "O Sons of the Buddha!
If a Bodhisattva, within the seventh stage, has well accumulated wisdom and skillful means, has well purified all practices, and has well accumulated the factors that assist the Path."
What are the distinct characteristics?
They include the skillful arousal of the power of great vows and so forth.
Regarding the various stages such as the first bhūmi, it is as the sūtra states: "skillfully arousing the power of great vows."

In the second stage, for this reason, I should practice the ten paths of wholesome action equally, cultivating all their aspects to bring them to complete purity; because of the power of the Tathāgatas in that stage, as it is said in the sutra: "well-empowered by the empowerment of the Tathāgata's power."

In the third stage, because one attains non-retrogressive meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and so forth through the power of one's own roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), one achieves penetration; as the sūtra says, "one attains power through the power of one's own roots of goodness."

In the fourth stage, one attains the superior mindfulness that penetrates the Buddha-dharma through the wisdom that discerns the teachings and the wisdom that transforms the cognitive hindrances; as the sutra states: "Constantly mindful of and conforming to the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and unique Buddha-dharmas."
In the fifth stage, there is the profound purity of mind, the equanimity of the well-purified deep mind, and so forth, as the sutra states: "Awakening to the well-purified deep mind.

In the sixth stage, with sovereign great compassion as the primary focus, one achieves the power of merit and wisdom through the superior contemplation of the accumulation of causes and conditions, as the sutra states: "Achieving the power of merit and wisdom."

In the seventh stage, one initiates the sublime path through skillful means and wisdom, never abandoning the practice of benefiting all sentient beings, as the sutra states: "Because of great compassion and so forth, one does not abandon the practice of benefiting all sentient beings."
Because of the immeasurable realms of sentient beings, one enters the path of immeasurable wisdom, as the sūtra states: "Because of penetrating the path of immeasurable wisdom.
Thus, the eighth stage, which generally clarifies the section on the accumulation of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-sambhāra*), has been explained.
How does one attain the stage of pure patience?
By attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
It should be understood that this is the naturally pure, effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*).
The Sūtra says:

"One enters into all phenomena as being originally unborn, unformed, signless, non-emergent, indestructible, inexhaustible, and non-active; they do not possess the nature of existence, and are equal in the beginning, middle, and end. Thus, through the non-discriminative true suchness, one enters into the wisdom of all-knowledge."
This bodhisattva is far removed from all mind, mentation, consciousness, recollection, and conceptual discrimination; being without attachment, they are equal to space.
Entering into all phenomena as having the nature of space, this is called attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, that patience should be understood in terms of four kinds of non-arising.
As for the four kinds of non-arising:
First, the non-arising of phenomena;
second, the non-arising of intrinsic nature;
third, the non-arising of numerical distinctions.
Fourth, the non-arising of the differentiation of activities.
Regarding this, as for the non-arising of phenomena (*vastu*), there are actually seven kinds of phenomena:

first, the reality that exists primordially within the factors of the pure division (*śukla-pakṣa*); this is its antidote, as the Sūtra says: "Entering into the fact that all phenomena are originally unarisen."
2. The reality of new production; its antidote is as stated in the sūtra:
"because there is no arising. 3. The reality of characteristics; its antidote is as stated in the sūtra: "because there are no characteristics."
4. The reality of the posterior limit (*aparānta*); its antidote is as stated in the sūtra: "because there is no emergence. 5.

The reality of the anterior limit (*pūrvānta*); because it consists of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within the defiled portion, its antidote is as stated in the sūtra: "because there is no loss."
Sixth, the reality of exhaustion (*kṣaya-tattva*): this is the antidote for all sentient beings, as the sūtra says, "because it is inexhaustible" (*akṣaya*).
Seventh, the reality of affliction (*saṃkleśa-tattva*): this is the antidote within the purified portion (*vyavadāna-pakṣa*), as the sūtra says, "because of non-engagement" (*apravṛtti*).

That which is "unborn by nature" refers to the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya); because those phenomena lack an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) in their own-being, as the Sūtra states: "There is no existence of an existent nature."
Because it observes phenomena, this is "patience" (kṣānti); one cannot say it is an observation of nothingness, for dharmas lack selfhood and are non-dual in character.

Regarding the distinction of enumeration as "non-arising," it is because defiled and pure dharmas neither increase nor decrease throughout the three periods of time, as the Sūtra says: "They are equal in the beginning, middle, and end."

Regarding the non-arising of the differentiation of activities: because within *tathatā* there is pure, non-conceptual Buddha-wisdom, as the Sūtra says, "Tathatā is non-conceptual and enters into the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*)," thus the contemplation of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is manifested.

Next, it is shown that he practices the distancing from the conceptualization of objects as results of retribution, because he embraces the conceptualization of their nature; as the sūtra says: "This bodhisattva distances himself from all mind, mentation, consciousness, recollection, and conceptual discrimination."
Regarding "perception" (saṃjñā): it is the perception that is free from obstructive phenomena, yet not the absence of the perception of remedial phenomena.
That remedial perception possesses three kinds of excellence within the lower stages:
first, effortless spontaneity, as the sūtra says, "because there is no attachment."
2. The characteristic of pervading all phenomena, as the sūtra says: "Because it is equal to space. 3.

The spontaneous practice of entering into the immovability of true suchness (*tathatā*), as the sūtra says: "To enter into the nature of all phenomena as being like space is called attaining the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
Thus, the section on attaining pure patience in the eighth stage has been explained.
Next, the section on attaining superior practice is explained.
The Sūtra says:
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

Having thus accomplished the patience of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*), the bodhisattva immediately attains this eighth bodhisattva stage, the Immovable (*acalā bhūmi*). He becomes a bodhisattva of profound practice, one who is difficult to know, incapable of being differentiated, free from all signs (*nimitta*), free from all conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*), and free from all craving and attachment. He is an immeasurable and boundless tranquility that cannot be destroyed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; and all forms of tranquility manifest before him.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a bhikṣu who has attained the perfection of supernormal powers and mastery over the mind, entering successively into the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), wherein all stirring thoughts, recollections, and conceptual discriminations are entirely extinguished.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is the same for the bodhisattva: dwelling in this eighth bodhisattva stage, the Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*), they immediately depart from all effortful practices and all recollections, attaining the state of effortless dharma (*anābhoga-dharma*). Free from the activities of body, speech, and mind, they dwell in the perfection of fruition-born conduct (*vipākaja-caryā*).
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a person who, in a dream, sees his own body fallen into a great river; at that moment, this person exerts great courage and employs great skillful means, desiring to emerge from this river.
At the moment he exerts such vigor, he suddenly awakens; having awakened, he immediately leaves behind all vigorous expedients and anxious activities.
Son of the Buddha!

It is the same for the Bodhisattva: from the very beginning, seeing sentient beings fallen into the four great rivers, he exerts the power of great diligence and extensively practices the Path until reaching the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), whereupon he leaves behind all conceptualizations and all conditioned efforts (*sābhoga-prayoga*).
This Bodhisattva does not engage in dualistic thoughts at all, and none of their recollections or conceptualizations manifest before them again.
Son of the Buddha!
It is like one born in the Brahma Heaven, for whom the afflictions of the desire realm no longer function at all.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), all mental activities of mind, intellect, and consciousness cease to function; even the minds of all Buddhas, the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), the mind of a bodhisattva, and the mind of nirvāṇa do not function, let alone the functioning of worldly minds.
The Commentary states:
Regarding "attaining superior practice" herein, it refers to attaining profound practice.
There are seven kinds of profound practice:
First, it is difficult to enter because of its profundity, as the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva who has thus accomplished the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) immediately attains this eighth Bodhisattva stage, the Immovable (*Acalā*), he becomes a Bodhisattva of profound practice, whose state is difficult to comprehend."

2. Profundity of shared practice (*samānācāra-gāmbhīrya*): Because [this stage] is shared by Bodhisattvas of all pure stages (*śuddhabhūmi*), as the sūtra says, "incapable of conceptual discrimination.

3. Profundity of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-gāmbhīrya*): Because neither the grasper (*grāhaka*) nor the grasped (*grāhya*) appear before one, as the sūtra says, "free from all marks (*nimitta*), free from all conceptions (*saṃjñā*), and free from all craving attachments (*abhiniveśa*)."
Because it involves the contemplation of protecting against all obstacles, it is said to be free from all attachment.
Fourth, its practice is profound because it consists of practices for both self-benefit and the benefit of others, as the sutra states: "immeasurable and boundless."
5. Depth of non-retrogression, as the sūtra says: "That which cannot be destroyed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
6. Depth of freedom from hindrances, as the sūtra says: "Quiescent."
Seventh, the depth of the manifestation of the remedy: as the sūtra states, "all things are quiescent and manifest before one," because true suchness is entirely quiescent.
The analogy for the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is intended to demonstrate the stillness of those formations, as stated in the sutra: "O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, as when a bhikṣu, having even left behind the activities of body, speech, and mind, abides in the accomplishment of retributive action."
The phrase "all stirring of the mind, recollection, thought, and discrimination are entirely extinguished" means that there is no longer any basis for them.
"That is, one is detached from all practices involving effort" means that one has transcended the stage of effortful practice.
One who attains the state of effortlessness (anābhoga) does so by attaining its counteractive method (*pratipakṣa-dharma*), because the state of effortlessness functions spontaneously.
This abiding in the perfection of retributive conduct (*vipākacaryā*) manifests as the attainment of that which is contrary to the characteristics of effortful practice (*sābhoga-caryā*).
Furthermore, "abiding in the accomplishment of retributive practice" means dwelling well within the *tathatā* (suchness) of the *ālayavijñāna*.

The analogy of dreaming and waking demonstrates that within this practice, one guards against the perception of faults while maintaining the perception of right knowledge, because this practice is characterized by quiescence.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, as if a person in a dream sees his own body, such that even all those things he previously recollected and imagined no longer appear before him.

In this context, it is because the two minds of pure worldly existence and nirvāṇa do not function, and because the mental recollections and conceptualizations regarding the enjoyment of objects do not function.

The analogy of being born in the Brahma-heaven refers to the fact that the mind of the lower stages no longer functions at all, because one has attained the ground of retribution; this explains the excellence of detachment, as the Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!..."
For example, it is said: "How much less would one who is born in the Brahma-heaven ever give rise to a worldly mind?

In this context, because Buddhas and others do not engage in the two types of mental states—those that are conformable and those that are non-conformable—and because of the distinction between the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.

Because there are distinctions between the dharmas of sentient beings within the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, there are distinctions between those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
One should understand that the distinctions in *nirvāṇa* regarding the Buddha and others are likewise taught herein.
Among these, "conformable practice" refers to the stage of conformable practice where the mind and so forth do not function; as the Sūtra says, "all mind, thought, and consciousness do not function."

Regarding "not practicing in accordance with this": because the Buddha and others do not practice within the category of non-conformity, as the sūtra states, "The mind of the Buddha, up to the mind of nirvāṇa, does not function."
Regarding the distinction between the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna: within the Mahāyāna, the distinction lies in the differences between the *nirvāṇa* of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
within the Hīnayāna, the distinction lies in the differences between the *nirvāṇa* of Śrāvakas, Arhats, and so forth.
Regarding the distinctions between sentient beings and phenomena within the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: the distinction between sentient beings is due to the difference between Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The distinction between phenomena is due to the difference between *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, as well as the distinction between those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and those still in training (*śaikṣa*) among sentient beings in the Hīnayāna.
Among these, the distinction of phenomena (*dharma*) is due to the distinction of *nirvāṇa*.
The distinction of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is due to the distinction of the Arhats;
the distinction of those in training (*śaikṣa*) is due to the distinction of the Anāgāmins and so forth.
Because all such practices are entirely non-practiced.
The Sūtra says:
"O Son of the Buddha!"

Once this bodhisattva has attained this Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi) and abides therein by the power of their original vows, at that time all Buddhas bestow upon them the wisdom of the Tathāgata through the gateway of the flowing stream of that Dharma.
He further spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
"You have attained this ultimate patience (*kṣānti*) because it accords with all the teachings of the Buddhas.
Son of good family!

We have achieved the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), which you have not yet attained. For the sake of accomplishing these Buddha-qualities, you should strive with diligent energy and must not abandon this gate of patience."
The Commentary states:

This is because [the bodhisattva] turns away from that mind which delights in profound practices and contentment by means of the Tathāgata’s power of wisdom; because they praise the attainment of the supreme Dharma; and because they have not yet obtained the cultivation of instruction.
If one does not relinquish this practice of patience, one will not fail to accomplish all Buddha-dharmas, because by relying on that power one is able to act.
As the Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!"
"Once this Bodhisattva has attained this Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), by the power of his original vow he abides therein, even to the point of not abandoning this gate of patience.
Thus the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, O son of good family!"

Although you have attained this liberation of quiescence, these ordinary beings are neither virtuous nor tranquil; they constantly dwell amidst various accumulations of afflictions and are harmed by various divergent thoughts, perceptions, and reflections.
"You should take pity on such sentient beings.
The Commentary says:

This is based on the fact that for those sentient beings, there is no great benefit; they manifest active afflictions (*kleśa*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and because these sentient beings revolve within the states of both householders and renunciants, they are deeply attached to afflictions.
As it says in the sutra: "O son of good family!
Although you have attained this liberation of quiescence... [and so forth]... you should take pity upon such sentient beings.
"Unwholesome" refers to the manifestation of afflictions that defile the mind.
"Not pacified" means not being free from those underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
"Constantly dwelling amidst various collections of afflictions" refers to the state of householders.
"Harmed by various divergent thoughts, reflections, and investigations" refers to the state of renunciants.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, son of good family!
You should recollect your original vow, desiring to bring great benefit to sentient beings and desiring to attain the inconceivable gate of wisdom."
The Commentary states:
Relying on vows to transform sentient beings, one’s wisdom and conduct are extensively capable of turning [the wheel of Dharma]. As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, son of good family!
You should recollect your original vow, up to the desire to attain the inconceivable gate of wisdom."
The Sūtra says:
Furthermore, son of good family!
Within all these phenomena (dharmas), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains eternally present as the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), whether a Buddha appears or not.
The Tathāgatas do not become called "Buddhas" merely by attaining this dharma; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas also attain this non-conceptual dharma.
The Commentary says:

This is based on the meaning of the "unshared" (āveṇika) qualities, because their afflictions are transformed through the exhaustion of their arduous practices. As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, son of good family..."
"Because within all these phenomena, one even attains this non-conceptual nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, son of good family!"

Observe our immeasurable pure bodies, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable Buddha-lands, immeasurable circles of light, immeasurable arisings of knowledge, and immeasurable pure sounds; you should now likewise give rise to such things as these.
The treatise says:
The immeasurable pure bodies and so forth are manifestations of the power achieved through those Buddha-dharmas, based on the purpose of benefiting sentient beings.
By what kind of body is this activity of benefiting sentient beings performed?
As it says in the Sūtra: "Furthermore, son of good family!
Observe our immeasurable pure bodies.
By what kind of wisdom?
The wisdom of conventional truth and the wisdom of ultimate truth, as stated in the sutra: "immeasurable wisdom.
By what kind of land?
Pure lands, as stated in the sutra: "immeasurable Buddha-lands."
By what means are they subdued?
As the sutra says, "immeasurable circles of light.
They exercise wisdom according to the conduct of the sentient beings to be saved, as the sutra says, "immeasurable arising of wisdom."

In accordance with what has been spoken, as stated in the sutra regarding "immeasurable pure sounds," the Tathāgata brings about immeasurable benefit for sentient beings; you should now likewise manifest such deeds.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, son of good family!
You have now just attained this one illumination of the Dharma, namely, the illumination of the Dharma of the quiescence and non-differentiation of all phenomena."
Thus it is, noble son!
The Tathāgata’s illumination of the Dharma has immeasurable entries, immeasurable functions, and immeasurable transformations.
For the sake of attaining these, you should give rise to this Dharma.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, it demonstrates the immeasurable and supreme practices of all Buddhas, as the Sūtra states: "Moreover, son of good family!
You have now just attained this one illumination of the Dharma... up to 'you should give rise to this Dharma.'"
"Immeasurable entry" refers to the differentiation of the gateways of the Dharma (*dharmaparyāya*).
"Immeasurable activity" refers to the differentiation of the performance of deeds.
"Immeasurable transformation" refers to the differentiation of the uninterrupted progression from stage to higher stage.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, son of good family!

You should observe the infinite lands, the infinite sentient beings, and the infinite distinctions among phenomena in the ten directions; you should thoroughly penetrate all those matters exactly as they are."
In this way, O Son of the Buddha!

The Buddhas provide this Bodhisattva with such immeasurable and boundless gateways for the arising of wisdom. By means of these immeasurable gateways of wisdom, this Bodhisattva is able to give rise to immeasurable varieties of karmic activities, all of which he fully accomplishes.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, because one can achieve the transformation by means of a slight contemplation upon the distinctions among the immeasurable worlds, sentient beings, and phenomena as they appear, as the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, good son!"
"Observe that the immeasurable lands of the ten directions have all been fully accomplished.
Thus the Sūtra says:
Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying:
O Son of the Buddha!
If the Buddhas did not grant this Bodhisattva the gateway to the arising of wisdom, that Bodhisattva would at that moment enter nirvana, thereby abandoning the benefit of all sentient beings.

Because the Buddhas have bestowed upon this Bodhisattva immeasurable and boundless gateways for the arising of wisdom, the activity of wisdom produced in a single thought-moment is such that, compared to all the activity of wisdom from the first production of the thought of enlightenment up until the completion of the seventh stage, it exceeds it; the former does not equal even one-hundredth part of the latter, nor one-thousandth, nor one-hundred-thousandth, nor one-hundred-thousand-nayuta-th part, nor one-billionth, nor one-hundred-billionth, nor one-trillionth, nor one-hundred-thousand-billionth, nor one-hundred-thousand-billion-nayuta-th part. It does not equal even one part out of an immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable number of *asaṃkhyeya* parts, nor can it even be reached by calculation or metaphor.

Why is this so? O Son of the Buddha, whereas previously one initiated practice with a single body, now, within these bodhisattva stages, one attains the differentiation of a bodhisattva’s immeasurable bodies; accumulates the power of immeasurable practices; gives rise to immeasurable voices; gives rise to immeasurable wisdom; manifests immeasurable births; [purifies] immeasurable pure lands; teaches and transforms immeasurable sentient beings; makes offerings to and reveres immeasurable Buddhas; accords with the awakening to immeasurable dharmas; and gives rise to the attainment of immeasurable supernormal powers. Furthermore, because of the quality of immovability, one gathers the power of all bodhisattva practices through immeasurable distinctions of assemblies and through immeasurable actions of body, speech, and mind.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like one who boards a ship intending to enter the great ocean: before reaching the great ocean, much effort and labor are required; once the great ocean is reached, no further exertion is needed, for one proceeds solely by the power of the wind.
If one were to travel across the great ocean for a single day, it would not equal the power of one's original effort even after a hundred years.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva has well accumulated the provisions of roots of goodness and boards the ship of the Mahāyāna, they reach the ocean of great wisdom where bodhisattvas practice; in a single thought-moment, through effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), they are able to enter the state of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajña-jñāna*). What was previously achieved through effortful practice—even over an eon or hundreds of thousands of millions of eons—cannot equal this.
The Commentary states:

Regarding "entering nirvana therein," this refers to the manifestation of wisdom, as the Sūtra says: "Because all Buddhas grant this bodhisattva immeasurable and boundless gateways for the arising of knowledge... up to: because of the quality of immovability."

Because the Buddhas provide this bodhisattva with immeasurable and boundless gateways for the arising of wisdom, they excel as causes for gathering merit within those practices, as they provide instruction by teaching in common.
One should understand that this is explained in sequence up to calculation and so forth.
As for numerical division (*saṃkhyā-bhāga*), it refers to making one into two, and two times two into four, and so on.
Even a metaphor cannot reach it, for this matter is beyond the scope of analogy or comparison.
Regarding the differentiation of immeasurable bodies: it is because all bodhisattvas’ bodies are perceived with the same conviction as their own body.
In this way, it should be understood that the arising of immeasurable sounds and so forth are likewise immeasurable.

These ten phrases should be understood as being based upon the transformation of sentient beings, based upon the accumulation of practices conducive to the path, and based upon the purification of hindrances.

It abides with the person; it follows what is taught; it relies upon wisdom; it arises according to what is grasped; it accords with whichever land one uses to transform sentient beings; and it accords with the accumulation of the aids to the path of merit and the accumulation of the aids to the path of wisdom, because of making offerings to and revering immeasurable Buddhas.
Because it accords with the awakening to immeasurable dharmas, and because it accords with the purification of the obstacles to supernormal powers and the obstacles to perfect enlightenment.
It should be understood that in all these instances, there is an immeasurable karma of body, speech, and mind that accords [with this].
Regarding those who possess the quality of immovability, it is because they have accumulated [merit] without interruption or cessation.

Son of the Buddha, it is as if one were traveling by boat; even after hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, others cannot catch up. The boat is a metaphor for the swiftness of that practice, demonstrating the superiority of the cause.
"Having well accumulated the provisions of the roots of goodness" refers to practicing the bodhisattva conduct within the seven stages.
"Riding the great vehicle of the ship to reach the ocean of great wisdom where bodhisattvas practice" should be understood as the ocean of wisdom in the eighth stage.
Thus, the section on attaining superior practice in the eighth stage has been explained.
Next, the purification of the Buddha-field is discussed.
This purification of the Buddha-field consists of three kinds of sovereign practices:
1. Mastery over the receptacle world;
2. Mastery over the world of sentient beings;
3. Mastery over the perfect awakening of wisdom.
What is the sovereign practice regarding the vessel world?
The Sūtra says:
"O Son of the Buddha!"

When this bodhisattva attains the eighth bodhisattva stage, they give rise to effortlessness from great skillful means and wisdom; abiding in the bodhisattva path, they contemplate the power of the knowledge of all modes, namely, contemplating the formation of world-systems and contemplating the destruction of world-systems.
This bodhisattva knows, as it truly is, the formation of the world;
he knows, as it truly is, the destruction of the world.
He also knows that the world forms due to the accumulation of karmic causes and conditions.
He also knows that the world perishes when the causes and conditions of karma are exhausted;
he also knows for how long the world remains formed,
and he also knows for how long the world remains in a state of destruction.
He knows for how long the world remains in its formation;
he also knows for how long the world remains in its destruction.

This bodhisattva knows the minor characteristics of the earth element, knows the major characteristics of the earth element, knows the immeasurable characteristics of the earth element, and knows the differentiated characteristics of the earth element.

This bodhisattva knows the minor characteristics of the water element, knows the major characteristics of the water element, knows the immeasurable characteristics of the water element, and knows the differentiated characteristics of the water element.

This bodhisattva knows the minor characteristics of the fire element, knows the major characteristics of the fire element, knows the immeasurable characteristics of the fire element, and knows the differentiated characteristics of the fire element.

This bodhisattva knows the small characteristics of the wind element, knows the large characteristics of the wind element, knows the immeasurable characteristics of the wind element, and knows the differentiated characteristics of the wind element.
This bodhisattva knows the subtle characteristics of minute particles, their coarse characteristics, their immeasurable characteristics, and their differentiated characteristics.
In whatever world-system there may be, they are able to know all the accumulation and dispersion of atoms, as well as every distinction among those atoms.

In whatever world-system there may be, they are able to know the exact number of atoms in the earth element; they are able to know the exact number of atoms in the water element; they are able to know the exact number of atoms in the fire element; they are able to know the exact number of atoms in the wind element; they are able to know the exact number of atoms in the bodies of all sentient beings; and they are able to know the exact number of atoms in the bodies of all lands.

This bodhisattva knows that the coarse bodies and subtle bodies of sentient beings are composed of various numbers of atoms; he knows that the bodies of hell-beings are composed of a certain number of atoms, the bodies of animals are composed of a certain number of atoms, the bodies of hungry ghosts are composed of a certain number of atoms, the bodies of asuras are composed of a certain number of atoms, the bodies of devas are composed of a certain number of atoms, and the bodies of humans are composed of a certain number of atoms.

Once this bodhisattva has attained mastery through entering such wisdom that analyzes atoms, they know the formation of the desire realm, the formation of the form realm, and the formation of the formless realm; they know the destruction of the desire realm, the destruction of the form realm, and the destruction of the formless realm; they know the small characteristics of the desire realm, the great characteristics of the desire realm, the immeasurable characteristics of the desire realm, and the distinct characteristics of the desire realm; they know the small characteristics of the form realm, the great characteristics of the form realm, the immeasurable characteristics of the form realm, and the distinct characteristics of the form realm; they know the small characteristics of the formless realm, the great characteristics of the formless realm, the immeasurable characteristics of the formless realm, and the distinct characteristics of the formless realm. In this way, they enter into the wisdom that contemplates the three realms.

This bodhisattva further skillfully gives rise to the light of wisdom, skillfully knowing the differences among the bodies of sentient beings, skillfully knowing how to distinguish the bodies of sentient beings, and skillfully observing the places where they are to be born.

This bodhisattva assumes a body in accordance with the place where sentient beings are born and in accordance with the karma accumulated by the bodies of sentient beings, for the purpose of teaching and transforming them.

This Bodhisattva manifests his body pervading the trichiliocosm, appearing in accordance with the various differences of the bodies of sentient beings. Thus, in conformity with their places of birth, he gives rise to manifest radiance. Whether it be two or three trichiliocosms, or four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty; whether it be a hundred trichiliocosms, or a thousand, ten thousand, a million, ten million, a hundred million, or a billion; whether it be ten billion, or a hundred thousand million, a billion, ten billion, nayuta, up to immeasurable, boundless, and unspeakably unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosms—his body pervades them all. In accordance with the differences in the bodies of sentient beings and their faith in such places of birth, he gives rise to manifest radiance, because his wisdom acts in conformity with them.

This bodhisattva, having accomplished such wisdom, remains unmoved within a single buddha-field, yet causes the light of presence to arise before the assemblies in as many unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields.
The Treatise says:
Regarding mastery over the receptacle world, there are five kinds of mastery:
first, according to one's desire, one can cause it to appear or not appear.
2. It can manifest according to whatever one desires;
3. It manifests immediately at whatever time one desires;
4. It can manifest according to whatever extent of breadth or narrowness one desires.
Fifth, he can manifest whatever he desires according to his mind.
As the Sūtra says: “O Son of the Buddha!

When this Bodhisattva attains the eighth Bodhisattva stage, he gives rise to effortlessness from great skillful means and wisdom; dwelling on the Bodhisattva path, he contemplates the power of the knowledge of all modes, even down to the destruction of the world, knowing them as they truly are. Thus it is said.

Regarding the formation and destruction of this world: within the initial stage of the mastery over the receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*), because he can manifest or non-manifest it according to his will, he knows the formation of the world through the accumulation of karmic causes and conditions;

and because he knows the destruction of the world through the exhaustion of karmic causes and conditions, he possesses the knowledge of the accumulation and exhaustion of karma. This is the second [mastery], because he can manifest whatever he desires.
He knows for how long the world endures from its formation until the fourth stage, its destruction;
he possesses the knowledge of how long the world remains formed, because whatever he desires for that duration immediately manifests before him.
This bodhisattva knows the minor characteristics of the earth element, up to knowing that the human body is composed of a certain number of atoms.

This is because, through the wisdom that discerns the specific differences between the characteristics of the earth and other elements, he is able to manifest them according to his desire for their breadth or narrowness; this is the fourth [power].

This bodhisattva enters into such wisdom that discerns subtle atoms, up to the wisdom that perceives the manifestation, formation, and destruction of light before one’s eyes; furthermore, while remaining unmoved in body within a single buddha-field, they are able to manifest as many forms as they desire according to their will, due to this fifth [power].
Within this, the sequence of the earth element consists of the wisdom of objects and the wisdom of characteristics.
What is the wisdom of objects?

The objective sphere of the retributive consciousness of the non-concentrated stages is called the "small characteristic"; the objective sphere of the consciousness of the concentrated stages is called the "great characteristic"; and the objective sphere of the Tathāgata is called the "immeasurable characteristic."
What is the knowledge of characteristics (*lakṣaṇajñāna*)? The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) are called the differentiated characteristics.

Regarding the coarseness and subtlety of the body: for sentient beings of the form and formless realms and so forth, there is the knowledge of the objects such as the desire realm and so forth, in that successive order; this is the knowledge of characteristics.
The realm of humans in the desire realm is called the small characteristic; the realm of devas is the great characteristic.
In the form realm, the realm of applied and sustained thought is the small characteristic; the realm of neither applied nor sustained thought is the great characteristic.

Within the Buddha-dharma of the formless realm, the realm of ordinary persons is the small characteristic; that of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas is the great characteristic; and the realm of all Tathāgatas is the immeasurable characteristic.

"Skillfully knowing the differences among the bodies of sentient beings and skillfully knowing how to discern the bodies of sentient beings" means one should understand that bodies are not identical, and that there are distinctions between those born through different skillful means and those born through the same means.
Regarding the manifestation of light appearing before the assemblies in all Buddha-fields: this is the manifestation of the body of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) in each respective place.
Thus has been explained the sovereign practice regarding the vessel-world of the pure Buddha-fields.
What is the sovereign practice regarding the world of sentient beings?
The Sūtra says:

"This bodhisattva, in accordance with the differences in the bodies and faiths of sentient beings, and in accordance with the differences in their resolute faith, manifests his own body in such and such ways within various Buddha-lands and within various great assemblies."

This bodhisattva, if among the assembly of śramaṇas, manifests the form and appearance of a śramaṇa; among the assembly of brahmins, manifests the form and appearance of a brahmin; among the assembly of kṣatriyas, manifests the form and appearance of a kṣatriya; among the assembly of vaiśyas, manifests the form and appearance of a vaiśya; among the assembly of śūdras, manifests the form and appearance of a śūdra; among the assembly of householders, manifests the form and appearance of a householder; among the assembly of elders, manifests the form and appearance of an elder; among the assembly of the Four Heavenly Kings, manifests the form and appearance of the Four Heavenly Kings; and among the assembly of Śakra, manifests the form and appearance of Śakra.

In this way, among the hosts of Yama, the hosts of Tuṣita, the hosts of Nirmāṇarati, the hosts of Paranirmita-vaśavartin, the hosts of Māra, and the hosts of Brahmā, he manifests the form and color of a Brahmā; even among the hosts of Akaniṣṭha Heaven, he manifests the form and color of an Akaniṣṭha deva.

This bodhisattva should manifest the form and color of a śrāvaka for those who are to be delivered by means of a śrāvaka’s body; he should manifest the form and color of a pratyekabuddha for those who are to be delivered by means of a pratyekabuddha’s body; he should manifest the form and color of a bodhisattva for those who are to be delivered by means of a bodhisattva’s body; and he should manifest the form and color of a Buddha for those who are to be delivered by means of a Buddha’s body.
O Son of the Buddha!

In all these unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands, according to the differences in the bodies and inclinations of sentient beings, such various manifestations of their own bodies are displayed within each respective Buddha-land.
The treatise says:

Regarding those who exercise mastery over the world of sentient beings, because they possess mastery over their subduing [of others], they manifest in a manner identical to the body and mind of the sentient beings they transform, acting in concert with them and appearing as an equal portion of their own body and mind.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "This Bodhisattva manifests his own body in various ways according to the differences in the bodies and inclinations of sentient beings, even unto those various Buddha-lands."
Thus, the sovereign activity regarding the world of sentient beings has been explained.
What is the sovereign activity of the Perfectly Enlightened One’s wisdom?
It consists of the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the wisdom of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and so forth.
The Sūtra says:
This Bodhisattva, having distanced himself from all conceptualizations of bodily characteristics, attains the equality of the body.

This Bodhisattva knows the bodies of sentient beings, knows the bodies of lands, knows the bodies of karmic retribution, knows the bodies of śrāvakas, knows the bodies of pratyekabuddhas, knows the bodies of bodhisattvas, knows the bodies of Tathāgatas, knows the body of wisdom, knows the dharma-body, and knows the body of space.

This bodhisattva thus knows the joy arising from the profound intentions of sentient beings; whether taking the bodies of sentient beings as his own body, or likewise taking the body of a land, the body of karmic retribution, the body of a śrāvaka, the body of a pratyekabuddha, the body of a bodhisattva, the body of a tathāgata, the body of wisdom, the body of dharma, or the body of space as his own body.

This bodhisattva thus knows how the deep minds of sentient beings give rise to delight; whether by taking his own body to become the body of a sentient being, or likewise by becoming the body of a land, the body of karmic retribution, the body of a śrāvaka, the body of a pratyekabuddha, the body of a bodhisattva, the body of a Tathāgata, the body of wisdom, the body of Dharma, or the body of space, he makes it the body of a sentient being.
This bodhisattva thus knows the inclinations arising from the deep minds of sentient beings, and how they can exercise mastery in creating various kinds of bodies within various kinds of bodies.
This bodhisattva knows the body of sentient beings, the body of accumulated karma, the body of retribution, the body of afflictions, and the body of form; he also knows the formless body.

This bodhisattva knows the small characteristics, the large characteristics, the immeasurable characteristics, the defiled characteristics, the pure characteristics, the expansive characteristics, the disordered characteristics, the inverted characteristics, and the level and upright characteristics of the bodies of lands; he knows the distinctions of the characteristics of the square lattice, and he knows the conventional designations for the bodies of karmic retribution, the conventional designations for the bodies of śrāvakas, the conventional designations for the bodies of pratyekabuddhas, and the conventional designations for the bodies of bodhisattvas.

This bodhisattva knows the Tathāgata-body, the Bodhi-body, the vow-body, the transformation-body, the body that receives supernatural powers, the body adorned with marks and signs, the radiance-body, the mind-made-body, the merit-body, and the dharma-body; he knows the wisdom-body.

This bodhisattva skillfully knows the characteristics of the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*), the characteristics of skillful reflection, the characteristics of being subsumed within the practice of the fruit, the characteristics of the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane, the characteristics of the distinctions among the three vehicles, the characteristics of the common and the uncommon, the characteristics of the vehicle and the non-vehicle, and skillfully knows the characteristics of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This bodhisattva knows the mark of equality of the dharma-body; knows the indestructible mark; knows the mark of conventional distinctions during the process of transformation; knows the mark of the distinction between the dharmas of sentient beings and non-sentient beings; and knows the mark of the distinction between the dharmas of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha.

This bodhisattva knows that the body of space has immeasurable characteristics, pervasive characteristics, formless characteristics, non-differentiated characteristics, and boundless characteristics; he also knows the distinct characteristics of the manifest-colored body.
The Treatise says:

The wisdom of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is far removed from all conceptualization of bodily characteristics, as it demonstrates the attainment of the equality of the body; for it does not differentiate between one's own body and the bodies of others.
As the sutra states: "This bodhisattva, being far removed from all conceptualization of bodily characteristics, attains the equality of the body.
This demonstrates the ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*) that distinguishes [the bodhisattva] from śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

The wisdom of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) consists in skillfully knowing the defiled portion, the purified portion, and the non-dual portion of the bodies and so forth of sentient beings, because it is characterized by skillful discernment.
As the Sūtra says: "This Bodhisattva knows the body of sentient beings, up to knowing the body of space."
Within this, the sentient world and the vessel world—these two are the causes for birth. Karmic afflictions constitute the defiled portion, while the three vehicles constitute the purified portion.
As for these three vehicles, by what wisdom do they follow, and by what dharma?
That purity reveals that space is non-dual.

Thus, this bodhisattva knows how to give rise to joy from the deep minds of sentient beings, such as taking the bodies of sentient beings as one’s own body, and even taking the body of space as one’s own body, and so forth.

This bodhisattva thus knows how the deep minds of sentient beings give rise to joy, such as by taking his own body to become the body of a sentient being, and even by taking his own body to become the body of empty space, and so forth.
In this context, regarding "making the bodies of sentient beings one's own body," it refers to the various manifestations of the practices of appropriation performed within that sovereignty.

Herein, "the bodies of sentient beings" means knowing as they truly are the distinctions of karma-born afflictions and conceptual constructions, as well as the distinctions between the realms of form and formlessness.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "This bodhisattva knows the body of sentient beings, the body of accumulated karma, the body of retribution, the body of afflictions, and the form-body; he knows the formless body."

Regarding the body of the land (*kṣetraprabheda-kāya*), one should know the distinctions among thousands of worlds; one should skillfully discern and know the distinctions between pure and impure worlds, as well as the distinctions among vast and other types of worlds.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "This bodhisattva knows the body of the buddha-field, up to knowing the characteristics of the distinctions of the network of directions.
The meaning of the various phrases, such as "extensive characteristics" and so forth, is as explained in the First Ground.

Regarding the conventional designations for the distinctions between the bodies of karmic retribution, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas: these are conventional designations based on the differentiation of specific and general characteristics; they are devoid of a self or a person.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "This bodhisattva knows the conventional designations for the distinctions of the body of karmic retribution, up to knowing the conventional designations for the distinctions of the bodhisattva body.

This bodhisattva knows the Tathāgata’s body by way of: manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment for the sake of awakening; making the vow to be born in Tuṣita Heaven; all the Buddha’s emanations and transformations; the preservation of his own bodily relics; all the bodies of actual recompense; all the radiances that subdue and gather sentient beings; the mastery and liberation of all mundane and supramundane minds, whether common or uncommon; all the uncommon qualities that act as causes for vast benefit; the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) of the Tathāgata; and all unobstructed wisdom.
Therefore, this wisdom is capable of performing all activities and can fully know the distinctions among those activities.
As the Sūtra says: "This Bodhisattva knows the Tathāgata-body, the Bodhi-body, and so forth, up to knowing the Wisdom-body."

This bodhisattva, as one who knows the body of wisdom, knows as they truly are the distinctions between the wisdoms of hearing and reflection, the distinctions of the wisdom of cultivation, the distinctions of the wisdom of the fruit and its practice, and the distinctions between mundane and supramundane wisdom.
As the sutra states: "This bodhisattva skillfully knows the body of wisdom, up to knowing the characteristics of those in training and those beyond training.

This bodhisattva knows the equal characteristic of the dharma-body because all immeasurable dharma-gates are the illumination of a single dharma-body; because he grasps them as they were heard; because he teaches distinctions at times corresponding to the faculties and dispositions of the beings to be converted; and because there are distinctions between those with faculties and those without faculties. Thus, he knows the distinctions of the primary characteristic and is able to know them all.
As the Sūtra says: "This bodhisattva knows the mark of equality of the Dharma-body, up to knowing the distinct marks of the Buddhas, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha.

Regarding this bodhisattva’s knowledge of the space-body (*ākāśakāya*), he knows its inexhaustible mark, its pervasive mark, its invisible mark, its unobstructed mark, and its unconditioned mark; he is able to thoroughly comprehend the causes of material forms and all their various distinctions.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "This bodhisattva knows the immeasurable characteristics of the space-body, up to knowing the distinct characteristics of the manifest-form body.
Thus, the three types of sovereign practice for purifying the Buddha-land in the eighth stage have been explained.
Next, the attainment of the ten masteries (*vaśitā*) is explained.
The Sūtra says:

"When this Bodhisattva skillfully knows how to manifest such various bodies, he attains mastery over life (*āyur-vaśitā*), because he can maintain his life for unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas."
They attain mastery over the mind, because they have entered the wisdom of immeasurable, incalculable samādhis.
They attain mastery over material things, because they manifest the maintenance and adornment of all worlds with immeasurable arrays of ornaments.
They attain mastery over karma, because they manifest the sustaining of karmic retribution as it appears in the present, future, and past lives.
They attain mastery over birth, because they manifest birth in all worlds.
They attain mastery over vows, because they manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) in buddha-fields at times according to their heart's desire.
They attain mastery over faith and understanding, because they manifest the presence of Buddhas filling all worlds.
They attain mastery over will (*vaśitā*), because they manifest miraculous transformations at will within all Buddha-fields.
They attain mastery over phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*), because they clearly manifest boundless and centerless Dharma-gates.

One attains mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*) because of the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), the adornments of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), and the three types of awakening (*bodhi*).
The Commentary says:

Regarding the attainment of mastery, it is because the Bodhisattva practices in this way—through the three kinds of sovereign conduct regarding the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*), the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), and the world of the perfect awakening of wisdom (*jñāna-sambodhi-loka*)—that they attain the ten masteries (*daśa-vaśitā*).
As the Sūtra states: "This bodhisattva, through skillfully knowing how to manifest such bodies, attains mastery over life, and so forth, up to mastery over wisdom.
One should understand that these ten masteries correspond to the antidotes for the ten kinds of fear in this specific order.
What are these ten kinds of fear?
First, the fear of death;
second, the fear of the defilements of affliction.
Third, the fear of poverty;
fourth, the fear of evil karma;
fifth, the fear of the miserable realms.
Sixth, the fear of being unable to obtain what one seeks;
seventh, the fear of the karmic retribution for slandering the Dharma;
eighth, the fear of being unable to sustain oneself due to the constraints of seeking a livelihood.
9. Fear of "how" and "what";
10. Fear of the majestic power of the great assembly.
Thus, the attainment of the tenfold mastery in the eighth stage has been explained.
Next, the section on the Great Victorious Division is explained.
The Sūtra says:
"When this bodhisattva has attained these ten masteries of a bodhisattva, he is immediately named one of inconceivable wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, vast wisdom, and indestructible wisdom."

When the bodhisattva has thus arrived and has thus accomplished such wisdom, they constantly cultivate pure physical action, constantly cultivate pure verbal action, and constantly cultivate pure mental action. With wisdom as the foremost, they proceed in accordance with wisdom, and their *prajñāpāramitā* becomes preeminent;
with great compassion as the foremost, they are skillfully able to discern through their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

Having personally aroused the power of aspiration and being well-empowered by the empowerment of all Buddhas, they never abandon the practice of benefiting sentient beings and universally know the diverse affairs of boundless worlds.
O Son of the Buddha!

Briefly stated, when a bodhisattva attains this Bodhisattva Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), all actions performed through body, speech, and mind are capable of gathering and giving rise to all Buddha-dharmas.
When this bodhisattva attains this Bodhisattva Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), they dwell securely within the power of the pure mind, because they are free from the accumulation of all afflictions;
they dwell securely within the power of the profound mind, because they are never separated from the Path.
They abide well within the power of great compassion, because they do not abandon the benefit of sentient beings;
they abide well within the power of great loving-kindness, because they rescue all the world;
they abide well within the power of dhāraṇī, because they do not forget the Dharma.
They are well-established in the power of eloquence, because their wisdom skillfully discriminates all Buddha-dharmas;
they are well-established in the power of supernormal faculties, because they traverse the distinctions of infinite worlds.
They are well-established in the power of their vows, because they do not abandon any of the practices of a bodhisattva;
they are well-established in the power of the perfections, because they cultivate and accumulate all the Buddha-dharmas.
Because, through the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment, all modes of omniscience manifest before them.
Having attained such power of wisdom, these bodhisattvas demonstrate all their activities, for they are free from fault in every undertaking.
The Commentary says:
"Greatly Victorious" refers to three kinds of greatness:
first, the greatness of wisdom;...
2. The greatness of karma;
3. The greatness of the qualities of abiding in those two.
What is the greatness of wisdom?
The one of inconceivable wisdom does not abide in the world, nor does he abide in nirvāṇa.
As the sūtra states: "When this bodhisattva has attained these ten masteries of a bodhisattva, he is immediately called 'the one of inconceivable wisdom.'"
This inconceivability should be understood as being of three kinds:
first, the inconceivability of the ultimate limit of cultivation;
second, the inconceivability of the objects of knowledge; [and third, the inconceivability of the nature of reality].
Third, the inconceivable wisdom that eliminates hindrances.
As the Sūtra states: "Because it is immeasurable wisdom, because it is vast wisdom, because it is indestructible wisdom"—this is called the greatness of wisdom.
When the bodhisattva has thus arrived, it is for the purpose of gathering and giving rise to all Buddha-dharmas.
"When the bodhisattva has thus arrived" is as explained above.
"Thus accomplishing wisdom" is also as explained above.
"Constantly gathering and initiating pure actions of body, speech, and mind" refers to the greatness of action (*karmamahattva*).
There are four characteristics of those pure actions:
first, the arising [of the action] occurs simultaneously with the arising of that which causes it, as the Sūtra says: "Because wisdom is foremost, and because wisdom follows along."

Second, the practice of benefiting sentient beings through non-attachment, which is encompassed by wisdom, as stated in the sūtra: "Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is predominant, with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as the foremost, one is skillfully able to discern through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)."

The third [category] comprises the causes for one’s own practice and the practice of others, as stated in the sutra: "Because they skillfully give rise to the power of aspiration, and because they are well-empowered by the empowerment of all Buddhas.

Fourth, there is the arising of benefit for sentient beings through their activities, which consists of purifying buddha-fields and accomplishing all Buddha-dharmas, as stated in the sutra: "Because they never abandon the practice of benefiting sentient beings, and because they universally know the distinctions among boundless worlds."
O Son of the Buddha!

To speak briefly, when a bodhisattva attains this Bodhisattva Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), all actions performed through body, speech, and mind are able to gather and give rise to all Buddha-dharmas.
This is called the greatness of karma.
Regarding the greatness of the qualities of those two abodes, it is manifested through the power of the mind of purity and so forth, based on seven kinds of qualities:

first, the quality of being well-established in the path, as the sūtra says: "When this bodhisattva attains this Immovable Bodhisattva Stage, they are well-established in the power of the mind of purity, because they are free from all accumulation of afflictions."
They abide well within the power of profound resolve, for they are never separated from the Path;
they abide well within the power of great compassion, for they do not abandon the task of benefiting sentient beings;
they abide well within the power of great kindness, for they rescue all the world."
Furthermore, regarding the merit of being well-established in the path: the first two [stages] are so because they distance one from obstacles and because their remedies are firm;
the next two are so because they do not abandon sentient beings.
These constitute the two merits of non-forgetfulness.
As the sutra states: "Because of dwelling well within the power of dhāraṇī, one does not forget the Dharma.
Third, the merit of accomplishing verbal karma: as the sutra states, "Because of dwelling well within the power of eloquence, one skillfully employs wisdom to discern all Buddha-dharmas."

Fourth, the merit of accomplishing mastery over the mind, as stated in the sutra: "Because they dwell well within the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and traverse the distinctions of infinite worlds."
Fifth, the merit of accomplishing the power of vows, as the sūtra says: “Because they dwell well within the power of vows, they do not abandon any of the practices of bodhisattvas.
Sixth, the merit of accomplishing spiritual practice, as the sūtra says: “Because they dwell well within the power of the pāramitās, they gather all the Buddha-dharmas.”

Seventh, the merit of bestowing wisdom, as stated in the sutra: "Because, while well-abiding within the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment, the knowledge of all modes and the knowledge of all-knowledge manifest before one."

When this Bodhisattva attains such power of wisdom to manifest all that is to be done, they attain freedom from both hatred and love; they do not discriminate between sentient beings who have afflictions and those who are free from them, because they perform their activities with equanimity.
Regarding the fact that there is no fault in any activity whatsoever, it is because one has attained these seven kinds of merit.
Thus, the section on the Great Excellence of the Eighth Ground has been explained.
Next, the section on the Explanation of the Name is taught.
The Sūtra says:
"O Son of the Buddha!
This stage of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is called the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), because it cannot be destroyed."
It is called the "Non-regressive Ground" because wisdom does not decline;
it is called the "Hard-to-Attain Ground" because it is difficult for all the world to know;
it is called the "Prince’s Ground" because it is free from the faults of a household.
It is called the Ground of Birth because one possesses mastery according to one's will;
it is called the Ground of Accomplishment because there is nothing further to be done;
it is called the Ground of Culmination because wisdom skillfully discerns all things.
It is called the stage of nirvāṇa, because it skillfully gives rise to the power of great vows.
It is called the stage of empowerment, because others cannot move it.
It is called the stage of effortlessness, because it skillfully gives rise to the prior path.
The Treatise says:
There are two ways of explaining names:
first, explaining names according to their stage (*bhūmi*).
2. The wise explain the etymology of "ground" (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the explanation of the term "ground," there are six characteristics:
first, the antidote to defilement; as for this defilement, it is of two kinds: [text continues].
1. The practice of effort on the lower stages and the vows of the Hīnayāna are various demonic activities;
2. the practice regarding the habitual tendencies of afflictions is their antidote.
As the Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!..."
