Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions between all phenomena; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions between the meanings of all phenomena; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma according to various languages and sounds; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma according to what is desired and understood.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the characteristics explained herein, there are four kinds:
first, the characteristic of the Sūtra explanation; [and so forth].
2. The characteristic of explanatory exposition;
3. The characteristic of conforming exposition;
4. The characteristic of analogous exposition.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid), one knows the distinctions among all phenomena; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid), one knows the distinctions among the meanings of all phenomena; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (niruktipratisaṃvid), one preaches the Dharma in accordance with various languages and sounds; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (pratibhānapratisaṃvid), one preaches the Dharma according to what is desired and understood."
Regarding "speaking in accordance with various words and sounds," this means speaking in accordance with the words and sounds of those sentient beings.

Regarding "speaking in accordance with what is desired," this means speaking in accordance with all the mental inclinations of sentient beings, even down to employing various kinds of analogies as appropriate.
What is the characteristic of wisdom?
The Sūtra says:

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one uses the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) to know the distinctions among all phenomena through unimpaired skillful means; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one uses inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) to know the distinctions among all phenomena as they truly are; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma through right view by means of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma through the skillful means of the knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārthajñāna*).
The treatise says:
Among these, the characteristics of wisdom are fourfold:
first, the wisdom of direct perception;
2. Inferential knowledge;
3. Knowledge of the means for attainment;
4. Knowledge of attainment.

As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions among all phenomena through the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) because of the non-disruption of skillful means; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions among all phenomena as they truly are through inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*); by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma through correct view by means of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma through the skillful means of the knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārthajñāna*)."

Among these, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) consists in knowing the distinctions among the truths as not different from the skillful means (*upāya*), because it does not undermine those skillful means.
Inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) likewise distinguishes things according to reality; the same applies to the others.
Because conventional knowledge knows the distinctions of the truths as they truly are,
one should understand that the skillful means of ultimate knowledge are not erroneous or divergent explanations.
What is the characteristic of being without the conceit of "I"?
The Sūtra says:

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that all phenomena possess a single characteristic that is indestructible; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), truths (*satya*), causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), and the skillful means of their accumulation; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one knows how to preach the Dharma using excellent sounds, syllables, and phrases that are honored and revered by all the world; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma with an ever-increasing, immeasurable illumination of the Dharma.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the absence of the characteristic of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") herein, there are four kinds:
first, the absence of the characteristic of *asmimāna* in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
2. The characteristic of being without the conceit of "I" regarding conventional truth;
3. The characteristic of being without the conceit of "I" when speaking of what is beautiful and sublime;
4. The characteristic of being without the conceit of "I" when speaking of the unsurpassed.

As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that all phenomena possess a single, indestructible characteristic; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the aggregates, elements, bases, truths, causes, conditions, and the skillful means of their accumulation; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma with excellent sounds, syllables, and phrases that are honored and revered by all the world; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma through an ever-increasing, immeasurable illumination of the teachings."
Among these, "the non-destruction of the single characteristic" means that the non-self is indestructible.

Because one knows non-self, realizes non-self, and so forth—entering non-self through such skillful means as the destruction of the aggregates—the cognitive domain of that bodhisattva is thus established.
First, attachment to the accumulation of a self;
second, attachment to a distinct cause;
third, attachment to desire.
Fourth, the attachment to activity.
One should understand that the skillful means regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth follow this sequence as their respective remedies.
What are the characteristics of the Hīnayāna and the Mahāyāna?
The Sūtra says:

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that all phenomena are without distinction and are subsumed within the One Vehicle; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the various gates of differentiation among the vehicles; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one is able to explain the non-destruction of the various vehicles; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one expounds the immeasurable light of the Dharma for each and every vehicle.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the characteristics of the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna herein, there are four kinds:
first, the characteristic of contemplation;
2. the characteristic of nature;
3. the characteristic of liberation;
4. the characteristic of mindfulness.

As the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that all phenomena are without distinction and are subsumed within the One Vehicle; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the various gates of differentiation among the vehicles; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one is able to expound the vehicles without impairment; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one speaks the immeasurable light of the Dharma for each and every vehicle."

In this context, knowing that all phenomena are without distinction and are subsumed within the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) should be understood as being based on the non-differentiation of the single contemplation.
As for being able to explain the various vehicles without undermining them, it is because one relies on the commonality of liberation and thus has no fear.
"Proclaiming the immeasurable light of the Dharma" means that one explains and distinguishes the various lights of the Dharma;
according to those who can be guided, one provides liberation in accordance with their various modes of thought and practice.
What are the characteristics of the bodhisattva stages?
The Sūtra says:

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows all bodhisattva practices, the practice of the Dharma, the practice of wisdom, and entry in accordance with wisdom; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the entry into the distinctions of the meanings of the ten stages as they are analytically explained; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one explains the paths of the various stages without impairment and in accordance with them; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one explains the immeasurable characteristics of each individual stage.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the characteristics of the bodhisattva stages herein, there are four kinds:
first, the characteristic of wisdom;
Second, the characteristic of exposition;
third, the characteristic of skillful means;
fourth, the characteristic of entering immeasurable gates.

As the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows the entry into all bodhisattva practices through the practice of the Dharma and the practice of wisdom; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the entry into the distinctions of the meanings of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) through their analytical exposition; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one knows the indestructible exposition that accords with the paths of the various stages; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one explains the immeasurable characteristics of each individual stage."
Among these, all practitioners of the bodhisattva path—whether practicing through the Dharma or practicing through wisdom—are explained by means of manifesting the wisdom of contemplation.
Regarding the distinctions of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it should be understood that what is referred to as "mind" is actually spoken of through verbal expression.
Regarding the teaching that is non-disruptive and conforms to the paths of the various stages, it is because it provides instruction free from inversion.
What are the characteristics of the Tathāgata stage?
The Sūtra says:

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that all Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment in a single thought-moment; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions between the various characteristics of events and times; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one explains according to the distinctions of perfect enlightenment; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one can explain each and every phrase of the Dharma for immeasurable eons without exhaustion.
The treatise says:
Regarding the characteristics of the Tathāgata stage herein, there are four kinds:
first, the characteristic of the Dharmakāya;
2. the marks of the form body;
3. the marks of perfect enlightenment;
4. the marks of teaching.

As the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that all Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment in a single thought-moment; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions between the various characteristics of events and things; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one explains according to the distinctions of perfect enlightenment; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one can explain each and every phrase of the Dharma for immeasurable eons without exhaustion."

Regarding "time" herein: it refers to whichever eon; regarding "accomplishing what kind of Buddha-work": it refers to whichever Buddha-land; regarding "which Buddha-body and marks": it refers to whatever is recorded by name that may be seen or heard.
Regarding the "Conformity with Perfect Enlightenment," it should be understood that there are ten aspects through which a Buddha conforms to perfect enlightenment.
What is the characteristic of his sustaining presence (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*)?
The Sūtra says:

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows all the Buddha’s words—the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), great compassion, and the practice of unimpeded wisdom—and turns the wheel of Dharma in accordance with the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*). By means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows how to accord with the Tathāgata’s voice to produce eighty-four thousand [teachings], according to the differences in the minds, faculties, and inclinations of sentient beings. By means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one explains the conduct of all sentient beings through the Tathāgata’s voice without impairment. By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma according to inclinations, with the practices of the Buddhas’ wisdom and the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The Commentary states:
Among these, there are four kinds of characteristics that constitute the manifestation of abiding and sustaining:
first, the characteristic of awakening; [and so forth].
2. The characteristic of differentiation;
3. The characteristic of exposition;
4. The characteristic of its immeasurability.

As the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows all the Buddha’s words—his powers, fearlessnesses, unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), and great compassion—and through the practice of unimpeded knowledge, one turns the wheel of Dharma in accordance with the wisdom of all-knowledge. By means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows how to accord with the Tathāgata’s voice to produce eighty-four thousand [teachings] according to the differences in the minds, faculties, and inclinations of sentient beings. By means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one explains the practices of all sentient beings through the Tathāgata’s voice without impairment. By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma according to their inclinations, with the practices of the Buddhas’ wisdom and the perfection of supernormal powers."
Among these, "the words of the Buddha" refers to his ability to expound the Dharma;
"powers" refers to his ability to shatter the arrogance of sentient beings;
and "fearlessnesses" refers to his ability to subdue non-Buddhists.
The "unshared Buddha-dharmas" are so called because they are not common to śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Great Compassion" is so called because it constantly enables the preaching of the Dharma.
"Unimpeded Wisdom-Practice" is so called because it relies upon that preaching of the Dharma.
Turning the wheel of Dharma means teaching the Dharma in accordance with [the needs of beings].
All these matters are known through the penetration of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
"In accordance with the mind" should be understood as being in accordance with the nature of the mind.

Regarding "the perfection of the wisdom, conduct, and supernormal powers of all Buddhas": this refers to the Dharma-body of all Buddhas, for this conduct is an indestructible practice for the benefit of sentient beings.
It is called "perfection" because, in accordance with their faith, it manifests the inexhaustible eloquence of the Bodhisattvas.
Thus, the accomplishment of verbal karma has been explained.
What is the accomplishment of mastery by the Dharma Master?
It is demonstrated through four matters:
First, accomplishment through upholding;
second, accomplishment through exposition;
third, accomplishment through question and answer.
4. Accomplishment through Upholding.
What is accomplishment through upholding?
The Sūtra says:
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva thus well understands unimpeded wisdom and dwells securely in the ninth bodhisattva stage, they are said to have attained the treasury of all buddha-dharmas and become a great Dharma teacher.

They attain the dhāraṇī of manifold meanings, the dhāraṇī of manifold dharmas, the dhāraṇī of the arising of wisdom, the dhāraṇī of radiance, the dhāraṇī of noble intention, the dhāraṇī of manifold wealth, the dhāraṇī of majestic power, the dhāraṇī of the gate of non-obstruction, and the immeasurable dhāraṇī; they attain these various kinds of dhāraṇīs of meaning.
Having attained such dharani-doors as these, they fulfill one hundred thousand dharani-doors of ten asaṃkhyeyas.

Likewise, they employ one hundred thousand skillful means of vocal expression of ten asaṃkhyeyas, and thus preach the Dharma through the distinctions of one hundred thousand doors of immeasurable faith and joy of ten asaṃkhyeyas.

This bodhisattva attains such ten hundred-thousand *asaṃkhyeya* gateways of immeasurable *dhāraṇīs*, enabling them to hear the Dharma from immeasurable Buddhas and never forget it once heard; furthermore, they are able to expound the Dharma as they have heard it for others through immeasurable methods of differentiation.
The Commentary says:
Regarding the accomplishment of retention (*dhāraṇī*), there are ten kinds of *dhāraṇīs*:
first, the *dhāraṇī* of meaning (*artha-dhāraṇī*), as stated in the Sūtra: "attaining the *dhāraṇī* of manifold meanings."
Second, the dhāraṇī of hearing, as stated in the sūtra: "attaining the dhāraṇī of all dharmas.
Third, the dhāraṇī of wisdom, as stated in the sūtra: "arousing the dhāraṇī of wisdom."
Fourth is the *raśmipramokṣa* dhāraṇī, as in the sūtra’s “*prabhāsa* dhāraṇī.
Fifth is the *paravijaya* dhāraṇī, as in the sūtra’s “*sumati* dhāraṇī.”

Sixth, the dhāraṇī for making offerings to the Tathāgata and gathering in impoverished sentient beings through giving, as indicated by the passage in the sūtra: "attaining the dhāraṇī of manifold wealth."
7. The dhāraṇī that instructs and benefits beings of narrow and inferior capacity within the Mahāyāna, as indicated by the "Dhāraṇī of Majestic Power" in the sūtra;
8. The dhāraṇī of uninterrupted eloquence, as indicated by the "Dhāraṇī of Attaining the Gate of Non-obstruction" in the sūtra.
9. The dhāraṇī of inexhaustible eloquence, as stated in the sūtra: "Because one attains immeasurable dhāraṇīs. 10.
The dhāraṇī of eloquence regarding various meanings, as stated in the sūtra: "Because one attains the dhāraṇī of various meanings."

Furthermore, regarding the various other scriptural passages—such as those concerning immeasurable distinctions heard according to one's capacity—that speak of accomplishment, the accomplishment of questions and answers, and the accomplishment of upholding, these should be understood as they are explained in the sūtras; since they are easy to understand, they are not annotated here.
The rest is as previously explained.
The Sūtra says:
"This bodhisattva, in the presence of a single Buddha, listens to and receives the Dharma through ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates."
Just as they hear the Dharma from one Buddha, so it is likewise with all other immeasurable and boundless Buddhas.

When these Bodhisattvas pay homage to the Buddhas, they are able to receive the gateways of the illumination of the Dharma; this is not something that even highly learned Śrāvakas, despite possessing the power of great dhāraṇīs, could receive and uphold in a hundred thousand kalpas.
This bodhisattva, having attained such power of dhāraṇī as well as the power of unhindered wisdom and eloquence, preaches the Dharma.
When preaching the Dharma while seated upon the Dharma-throne, he pervades the entire trichiliocosm, preaching the Dharma according to the differences in the mental dispositions of sentient beings.

This Dharma seat of the Bodhisattva is the most preeminent among all, with the sole exception of the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas who have received their office; it has attained immeasurable illumination of the Dharma.
This bodhisattva, seated upon the Dharma-seat, may preach with a single voice, causing the entire great assembly to fully understand and immediately comprehend;
or he may preach with various voices, causing each member of the entire great assembly to attain individual understanding and immediate comprehension.
Or he may simply emit light and teach, causing the entire great assembly to each understand the Dharma and immediately attain realization of the Dharma.

Or he may cause the sounds of the Dharma to emerge from every single pore; or he may cause the sounds of the Dharma to emerge from all material objects throughout the trichiliocosm; or he may use a single voice to pervade the entire Dharma-realm, causing all to attain understanding; or he may maintain all sounds as the sound of the Dharma; or he may cause the sounds of songs, music, and all vocalizations in all worlds to emerge as the sounds of the Dharma; or within the sound of a single syllable, he may distinguish and explain the sounds of the words and phrases of all dharmas; or within each and every subtle atom of the unspeakably many atoms of earth, water, fire, and wind gathered in unspeakable worlds, he is able to expound unspeakable gateways of the Dharma.

If all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm were to simultaneously pose difficult questions in a single moment—each individual being asking with immeasurable variations of voice, such that what one person asks differs from what another asks—this Bodhisattva would receive all such questions in a single moment and, using but a single voice, cause them all to attain understanding and liberation.

In this way, whether it be two or three *trichiliocosms*, or four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty; whether it be a hundred *trichiliocosms*, or a thousand, or ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million, or a billion *trichiliocosms*; or even ten billion, a hundred thousand, ten million, a billion, or a *nayuta* of them, up to immeasurable, boundless, and unspeakably unspeakable numbers of *trichiliocosms*—if all the sentient beings therein were to simultaneously pose difficult questions in a single moment of thought, and each individual being were to question with immeasurable variations of voice such that what one person asked was different from what another asked, this Bodhisattva would receive all such questions and difficulties in a single moment of thought and, using but a single voice, cause them all to attain understanding and liberation.

This bodhisattva pervades unspeakably unspeakable worlds, preaching the Dharma to sentient beings according to their minds, faculties, and inclinations, because they have attained the illumination of the Dharma.
Seeking to fulfill the Buddha-work through the powers of a Tathāgata and to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings,
this bodhisattva redoubles their diligence and grasps such luminous wisdom.

If, upon each and every pore, there were great assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable worlds, with a Buddha dwelling therein preaching the Dharma; and if each and every Tathāgata were preaching the Dharma for sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable worlds; and if within the mind of each and every sentient being, mental states arose as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable worlds—then the Tathāgata would thus accord with the minds of those sentient beings and bestow upon them the Dharma-gates.
As it is with one Buddha, so it is with all Buddhas in every single pore.

Thus, throughout the entire dharma-realm, he generates a great power of mindfulness; in a single thought-moment, he receives from all Buddhas the illumination of all dharmas without losing even a single phrase, let alone the teachings for all sentient beings in all worlds.

This bodhisattva, dwelling in this Bodhisattva Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), becomes increasingly superior; day and night, they have no other thoughts but enter the realm of the Buddhas, constantly gaining proximity to all Buddhas and attaining mastery over the profound liberation of bodhisattvas.

This bodhisattva, conforming to such wisdom, constantly enters samādhi and never ceases to attend upon the Buddhas; within each and every kalpa, they behold immeasurable Buddhas—immeasurable hundreds, immeasurable thousands, immeasurable hundreds of thousands, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas, immeasurable billions, immeasurable hundreds of billions, immeasurable thousands of billions, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas. With supreme and exquisite offerings, they honor, revere, respect, praise, and attend upon these Buddhas, and in the presence of these Buddhas, they pose various questions and inquiries, thereby attaining mastery over the dhāraṇī of the Dharma-exposition.
The roots of goodness of these Bodhisattvas become increasingly superior, bright, and pure.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like, for example, when gold of the finest quality is fashioned into an ornament and fastened upon the neck or the crown of a Wheel-Turning Sage King; none of the ornaments possessed by all the minor kings or all the people of the four continents can equal it.
In this way, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), those roots of goodness become increasingly superior, luminous, and pure, such that they cannot be destroyed by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas of the lower grounds.

The roots of goodness of this bodhisattva become increasingly radiant, able to illuminate the dense thickets of the afflictions within the minds of sentient beings; having illuminated them, they draw them back in.
Son of the Buddha!
It is like the Great Brahma King, who can illuminate all the deep and dense thickets within the two-thousandfold world system.
In this way, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Ground of Excellent Intelligence, the radiance of those roots of goodness illuminates the dense forests of the afflictions within the minds of all sentient beings; having illuminated them, it draws them back in.

Among these ten pāramitās of the bodhisattva, the pāramitā of power (bala-pāramitā) is predominant; yet it is not that the remaining pāramitās are not practiced, for they are cultivated according to his strength and capacity.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the ninth Bodhisattva stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*).
Were it to be explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even in immeasurable eons.

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become a Great Brahmā King, attaining great power as the lord of two thousand worlds; they attain mastery within mastery, their authentic and correct understanding is most preeminent, and they are well-able to proclaim the *pāramitās* of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas, such that no one can exhaust them when questioned by sentient beings.

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—all such merits never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the bodhisattvas, mindfulness of the bodhisattva practices, mindfulness of the pāramitās, mindfulness of the ten stages, mindfulness of the indestructible powers, mindfulness of the fearlessnesses, and mindfulness of the unique buddha-dharmas, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of all-aspect omniscience.
One should constantly give rise to this thought:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the greatest, the sublime, the most subtle, the highest, the unsurpassed, the guide, the general, the teacher, and the honored one, even unto becoming the one upon whom the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) relies."
Furthermore, from this reflection, he gave rise to diligent practice; by the power of that diligence, in a single thought-moment,
he attained as many samādhis as there are atoms in ten hundred-thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-lands,
beheld as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten hundred-thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-lands, and came to know ten hundred-thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-lands.
Through the spiritual power of Buddhas as numerous as atoms, one can shake worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten hundred-thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-lands,
enter worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten hundred-thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-lands,
illuminate worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten hundred-thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-lands, and manifest emanations.
They are able to sustain their lives for as many eons as there are atoms in ten hundred thousand buddha-fields of *asaṃkhyeya* worlds;
they are able to know the events of ten hundred thousand buddha-fields of *asaṃkhyeya* eons each in both the past and future worlds; and they are able to skillfully enter [into these realms].
There are dharma-gates as numerous as the atoms in ten hundred-thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-lands;
one can manifest bodies as numerous as the atoms in ten hundred-thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-lands, and from each individual body,
one can manifest ten hundred-thousand *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-land atoms of bodhisattvas as one's retinue.
If one considers the sovereign supremacy of the power of their vows, the bodhisattvas' power of vows exceeds these numbers.

They manifest various kinds of supernormal powers—whether through their bodies, or light, or supernatural faculties, or eyes, or spheres of experience, or voices, or conduct, or adornments, or empowerments, or faith, or karma.
These supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are such that they cannot be calculated or known even throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* eons.
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Chapter Nine, "The Stage of Excellent Intelligence" (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*), Part Eleven;
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Chapter Ten, "The Stage of the Cloud of Dharma" (*Dharmameghā-bhūmi*), Part Twelve.
Composed by Bodhisattva Maitreya;
translated by Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Later Wei Dynasty. Chapter Ten:
The Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi). The Treatise says:

The Bodhisattva has already purified Buddha-fields and transformed sentient beings during the nine stages; in the tenth stage, he practices to bring the awakening of wisdom to fulfillment, for this is supreme.
This stage consists of eight distinct divisions:
first, the division of fulfilling the preparatory practices;
second, the division of attaining the fulfillment of samādhi.
3. The section on attaining the stage of consecration;
4. The section on entering great perfection;
5. The section on explaining the names of the stages.
Sixth, the section on the supreme and non-supreme aspects of supernormal powers;
seventh, the section on the images of the stages;
eighth, the section on the benefits of the stages.
What is the section on fulfilling the stage through skillful means?
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said:
O Son of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva possesses such immeasurable wisdom and skillfully investigative wisdom, up to the skillfully discerning wisdom of the ninth bodhisattva stage; if they have well fulfilled the pure dharmas, accumulated immeasurable factors conducive to enlightenment, skillfully mastered great merit and wisdom, extensively practiced the increase of great compassion, broadly known the distinctions of world-systems, deeply entered the dense forest of practices within the realm of sentient beings, mindfully followed and entered the sphere of the Tathāgata’s conduct, and deeply penetrated toward the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and unique buddha-dharmas—this is called attaining the stage of being enthroned in the knowledge of all modes of omniscience.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the section on "fulfilling the stages through the skillful means of those stages," one should understand that this refers to the activity of wisdom that skillfully discriminates throughout the first through the ninth stages.
As the Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!..."
"If a bodhisattva possesses such immeasurable wisdom, well-observed wisdom, and even the well-discriminating wisdom up to the ninth bodhisattva stage.
This well-discriminating wisdom has seven aspects:

first, because of its excellent practice, there are three phrases, as stated in the sūtra: "excellently fulfilling pure dharmas, accumulating immeasurable factors conducive to enlightenment, and excellently gathering great merit and wisdom."
One should understand that these phrases explain one another in successive order.
Second, because it universally accords with both self-benefit and the benefit of others, as the sūtra says: "Extensively practicing superior great compassion."
3. Purifying the Buddha-fields, as the sūtra says: "extensively knowing the distinctions between worlds.
4. Teaching and transforming sentient beings, as the sūtra says: "profoundly entering the dense forest of the realms of sentient beings."
Fifth, skillful understanding, as the sūtra states: "Mindfulness enters in accordance with the sphere of the Tathāgata’s activity.
The sphere of the Tathāgata refers to the dharma of true suchness (*tathatā*).
Sixth, insatiability, as the sūtra says: "Because they have deeply entered and are directed toward the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata.

Seventh, the exhaustion of stages and entry [into the result], as the sūtra says: "It is called the stage of attaining the position of the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all-knowledge."
Thus, the section on the fulfillment of the stages through skillful means has been explained.
How is the fulfillment of the samādhis attained?
The Sūtra says:

O Son of the Buddha! When a Bodhisattva practices in accordance with such wisdom, they attain entry into the Stage of Receiving the Empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). Thereupon, the Bodhisattva’s samādhi called "Free from Defilement" (*vimala*) manifests before them; the samādhi called "Entry into the Differentiations of the Dharma Realm" (*dharmadhātu-praveśa-viśeṣa*); the samādhi called "Adornment of the Site of Enlightenment" (*maṇḍala-vyūha*); the samādhi called "Flower-Light of All Kinds" (*sarvākāra-puṣpa-prabhā*); the samādhi called "Ocean Treasury" (*sāgara-garbha*); the samādhi called "Ocean Accomplishment" (*sāgara-samudāgama*); the samādhi called "Vastness of the Space Realm" (*ākāśa-dhātu-vipula*); the samādhi called "Thoroughly Discerning the Nature of All Dharmas" (*sarva-dharma-svabhāva-su-vicaya*); the samādhi called "Following the Mental Activities of All Sentient Beings" (*sarva-sattva-citta-carita-anuvartana*); and the samādhi called "Manifesting All Buddhas Abiding Before One" (*sarva-buddha-abhimukha-sthiti*). Such leading samādhi-doors, numbering ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands, all manifest before them.
These bodhisattvas all enter into this entirety of samādhis, skillfully knowing the expedient means of samādhi, up to the correct attainment (*samāpatti*) produced by samādhi.

For these bodhisattvas, even up to ten hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis, the final samādhi—named the "Bodhisattva Samādhi of Attaining the Supreme Rank of All-Knowledge Wisdom" (*sarvajñajñāna-vara-sthāna-pratilambha-bodhisattva-samādhi*)—manifests before them.
The Treatise says:
One who attains the fulfillment of samādhi does so because the *vimala-samādhi* (stainless samādhi) and its associated retinue manifest before them.
As for the *vimala-samādhi*, it is so called because it is free from the defilements of affliction (*kleśa*).
That which manifests before one does so spontaneously without the application of effort.
Furthermore, this stainless samādhi consists of nine types of samādhi; it should be understood as being free from eight kinds of defilements.
First, entry into the stainless, as the sūtra says: "It is called the samādhi of the differentiation of the dharmadhātu.
Second, proximity to the stainless, as the sūtra says: "It is called the samādhi of adorning the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)."
Third, the stainlessness of emitting light, as the sūtra says: "It is named the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of All Kinds.
Fourth, the stainlessness of dhāraṇī, as the sūtra says: "It is named the Samādhi of the Ocean-Treasury."
Fifth, the stainless arising of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), as stated in the sūtra: "named the Samādhi of Accomplishing the Ocean.

Sixth, the stainless purification of the Buddha-field, which consists of two phrases: because of immeasurable right contemplation, as stated in the sūtra: "named the Samādhi of the Vastness of the Space-Element" and "named the Samādhi of Thoroughly Discerning the Nature of All Dharmas."
7. The stainlessness of transforming sentient beings, as the sutra says: "It is named the samādhi that accords with the mental activities of all sentient beings. 8.

The stainlessness of perfect awakening, because at the time of attaining bodhi, all Buddhas mutually appear before one’s eyes and are known; as the sutra says: "The samādhi of the Bodhisattva who dwells with all Buddhas appearing before him manifests before one."

As for the manifestation before one of the Bodhisattva Samādhi that receives the supreme station of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), it is because the knowledge of all modes is non-conceptual and because one receives the station of equality within the knowledge of all modes.
"Skillfully knowing the skillful means of samādhi, up to the meditative attainments produced by samādhi," thus is the manifestation of the fulfillment of the matters of samādhi.
The section on the fulfillment of the attainment of samādhi in the Ten Grounds has already been explained.
How does one attain the stage of receiving empowerment?
The Sūtra says:

"When this samādhi manifests before one, there immediately appears a great king of precious lotuses, its circumference equal to ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems. It is adorned with an intermingling of all kinds of jewels, surpassing the spheres of all worlds; it is born from supramundane roots of goodness and is accomplished through the sphere of the practice of the illusory nature of all phenomena."
Its light universally illumines all dharma-realms, surpassing all the spheres of the various devas.
A great lapis lazuli maṇi-jewel forms its stalk; an immeasurable king of sandalwood forms its calyx; a great agate jewel forms its filaments; and Jāmbūnada gold forms its petals.
The flower-body possesses immeasurable radiance, with all manner of precious jewels interspersed within it.
Immeasurable nets of jewels cover its surface, and it is accompanied by a retinue of lotuses equal in number to the atoms within thirteen thousandfold great trichiliocosms.
When he had thus achieved and perfected all the marks, the Bodhisattva’s body was then exquisite and perfectly proportioned to the flower seat.
By the power of the Samādhi of Receiving the Supreme Position through the Wisdom of All-Knowledge, the Bodhisattva immediately sat upon the throne of the Great Jewel Lotus King.

When this bodhisattva sat upon the throne of the great jewel lotus king, at that time there were bodhisattvas upon each of the lotus thrones belonging to the retinue of the great jewel lotus king; every one of these bodhisattvas sat upon a lotus throne, surrounding that bodhisattva.
Each and every bodhisattva attains ten times ten hundred thousand samādhis, and all with single-minded reverence gaze up at the Great Bodhisattva.
The Commentary states:

Regarding those who receive their consecration within this [assembly], one should understand six matters according to the following: the seat they occupy, the dimensions of their body, their retinue, their physical marks, their place of origin, and the rank they attain; it is according to these that they are thus described.
Regarding the "place of the middle seat," there are ten characteristics:
first, the characteristic of arising, as the sūtra states: "When this samādhi manifests before one, a great king of precious lotuses immediately emerges."
2. The characteristic of measurement, as stated in the sūtra: "It is circular, equal in circumference to ten hundred thousand asaṃkhyeya trichiliocosms.
3. The characteristic of excellence, as stated in the sūtra: "It is adorned with all manner of various jewels interspersed."
4. The characteristic of the ground (*bhūmi-lakṣaṇa*), as stated in the sūtra: "because it transcends all worldly spheres. 5.
The characteristic of the cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), as stated in the sūtra: "because it is produced by supramundane roots of goodness."
Sixth is the characteristic of accomplishment, as the sutra says: "It is accomplished through the sphere of the illusory nature of all phenomena.
Seventh is the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), as the sutra says: "Its radiance excellently illuminates the entire *dharmadhātu*."
"Skillfully illuminating" means it is called right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
Eighth is the characteristic of merit, because it surpasses all devas, as the sutra says: "surpassing all the spheres of experience belonging to all devas."
9. The characteristic of the essential body (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), such as the stalk and pedestal, as stated in the sūtra: "The great lapis lazuli maṇi-jewel forms the stalk," and so forth. 10.

The characteristic of the perfection of adornments (*alaṃkāra-saṃpad-lakṣaṇa*), as stated in the sūtra: "The body of the flower possesses immeasurable radiance; within it, all kinds of jewels are interspersed, and immeasurable jewel nets cover it from above."

Regarding "according to the dimensions of the body": the body corresponds in size to the flower seat, as stated in the sutra: "At that time, the Bodhisattva’s body was exquisite and beautiful, corresponding in size to the flower seat," and so forth.

Regarding "according to whichever retinue": this refers to the Bodhisattvas who constitute the retinue of the Great Jewel Lotus King Throne seated therein, as stated in the sutra: "At that time, the retinue of the Great Jewel Lotus King," and so forth.
The Sūtra says:

When this Bodhisattva ascends the throne of the Great Jewel Lotus King, and the attendant Bodhisattvas have likewise sat upon their lotus thrones and entered samādhi, at that time all worlds in the ten directions tremble greatly, and all evil realms of existence are completely stilled.
The light shines universally throughout all dharma-realms; all worlds are entirely adorned and purified, and all are able to see and hear the great assemblies of all Buddhas. Why is this?
O Son of the Buddha!

When this Bodhisattva sits upon the throne of the Great Jewel Lotus King, ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of rays of light immediately issue from his two feet. Having emerged, they completely illuminate the immeasurable Avīci hells and other realms throughout the ten directions, extinguishing the suffering and affliction of sentient beings.

From his two knees, he emitted ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of rays of light; once emitted, they completely illuminated the infinite animals of the ten directions, extinguishing their suffering and affliction.

From his navel wheel, he emitted ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of rays of light; once emitted, they completely illuminated the infinite hungry ghosts of the ten directions, extinguishing their suffering and affliction.

From his left and right flanks, he emitted ten hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light; once they had issued forth, they completely illuminated the bodies of immeasurable people throughout the ten directions, extinguishing their suffering and affliction.

From his two hands, he emitted ten hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light; once they had issued forth, they completely illuminated the palaces of immeasurable devas and asuras throughout the ten directions.
From his two shoulders, he emitted ten hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light; once they had issued forth, they completely illuminated the infinite *śrāvakas* of the ten directions.

From the back of his neck, he emitted ten hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light; once they had issued forth, they completely illuminated the bodies of the infinite *pratyekabuddhas* of the ten directions.

From his face, he emitted ten hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light; once they had issued forth, they completely illuminated the infinite Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, from those who first resolved their minds for enlightenment up to those who have attained the ninth stage.

From the mark of the white tuft between his brows, he emitted hundreds of thousands of light rays as numerous as ten asaṃkhyeyas; once they had issued forth, they completely illuminated the bodies of immeasurable bodhisattvas who had attained their stations throughout the ten directions and remained there, while all the palaces of Māra were eclipsed and rendered invisible.

From the crown of his head, he emitted light rays as numerous as the atoms in ten hundred-thousand *asaṃkhyeya* trichiliocosms. Once emitted, they illuminated all the great assemblies of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions and circled all worlds ten times. Abiding in the midst of space, they formed a great wheel-net terrace of radiant light called "Lofty Great Radiance," performing a grand offering to all the Buddhas.

Such offerings as these do not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousand-nayuta-th part, nor one hundred-millionth part, nor one ten-billionth part, nor one hundred-billionth part, nor one ten-trillionth part, nor one hundred-trillion-nayuta-th part of the offerings made by Bodhisattvas from their first aspiration until they attain the ninth stage; indeed, they cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy.

This great luminous wheel-net terrace surpasses all the offerings found throughout the worlds of the ten directions—such as flowers, incense, powdered incense, burning incense, unguents, scattered perfumes, floral garlands, robes, precious parasols, banners, pennants, various jewel necklaces, and mani-gems—for it transcends all worldly realms, having arisen from supramundane roots of goodness.
In each of the great assemblies of the Buddhas, a rain of various jewels falls like a heavy downpour.
If there are sentient beings who perceive and understand such offerings, you should know that they are all certain not to regress from the unsurpassed Great Way.

After these various radiances had rained down such great offerings, all those radiances illuminated the great assemblies of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, circled all worlds ten times, and entered beneath the feet of the Buddhas.

At that time, those Buddhas and those great Bodhisattvas know that in a certain world, a certain Bodhisattva is practicing such a Bodhisattva path and has achieved the stage of attaining the Bodhisattva position.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

At that moment, Bodhisattvas from the ten directions, including those dwelling in the ninth stage, all came to surround him and present great offerings, gazing upon him with single-minded devotion, each attaining ten times ten, a hundred thousand samādhis.

When Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages and grounds [of realization] produce from the *vajra-svastika* upon their chests—which are adorned with merit—a great light named "Destroyer of Māra’s Enmity," accompanied by a retinue of ten hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* lights; once emitted, it illuminates all the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and displays immeasurable spiritual powers, and then returns to enter the *vajra-svastika* upon the chests of these great Bodhisattvas, which are likewise adorned with merit.
Once this radiance has vanished, this bodhisattva immediately attains hundreds of thousands of superior powers of merit and wisdom that manifest before him.
The Commentary says:

"Regarding whatever signs" refers to the signs of the movement of all worlds and so forth, as stated in the Sūtra: "This bodhisattva ascends the throne of the great precious lotus-king, and so on, until he is able to see and hear all the great assemblies of all Buddhas."
Regarding "from whatever source it emerges," this refers to the fact that it emits light.
Furthermore, one should know that light has three kinds of activity: first, the activity of benefiting others; [the second is the activity of maturing, and the third is the activity of manifesting].
2. The activity of awakening;
3. The activity of subduing.
As the sūtra says: "For what reason?"
"O Son of the Buddha!

When this Bodhisattva sits upon the throne of the Great Lotus King, ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of rays of light immediately issue from his two feet, and even his merit and wisdom manifest before him. Thus it is said.
One will certainly not regress from the unsurpassed Great Way, because of the definitive meaning within the stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, there is another sense of certainty: one will certainly not be negligent, because of the resolute mind regarding the tasks to be performed.

Regarding "the one whose chest bears the *vajra-svastika* adorned with merit": on the chest of this bodhisattva there is the mark of a *vajra-svastika* adorned with merit, which is called "Incomparable."
The Sūtra says:
"Thus, O Son of the Buddha!

At that time, all the Buddhas emitted from the white tuft between their eyebrows a light called 'Augmenting All-Knowledge-Penetration,' accompanied by an incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) retinue of rays. It illuminated all worlds in the ten directions without exception, circling all worlds ten times and manifesting the great supernormal powers of all Buddhas, thereby exhorting and inspiring immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas."

All the Buddha-lands of the ten directions shook in six ways; all the sufferings and afflictions of the evil realms were extinguished; all the palaces of Māra were obscured and vanished from sight; the places where all Buddhas attain Bodhi were revealed, as were the miraculous adornments of the great assemblies of all Buddhas. Illuminating the limits of all dharma-realms and the entire realm of empty space, they returned from throughout all worlds and gathered together, surrounding the great assembly of bodhisattvas on every side, manifesting the majestic adornment of great supernatural powers and radiance.
This light entered the crown of that great bodhisattva’s head, and the lights of his various retinues entered the lotus seats of their respective retinues.
When the light from the bodhisattva’s crown entered the body of this bodhisattva, each of those bodhisattvas attained ten times ten hundred thousand samādhis, such as they had never before obtained.

When those rays of light simultaneously enter the crown of that bodhisattva’s head, that bodhisattva is said to have attained the stage; he enters the realm of all Buddhas, becomes endowed with the ten powers of a Buddha, and is reckoned among the ranks of the Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, like the eldest son of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, born of the Jewel of the Noble Woman and endowed with the marks of royalty.

The Wheel-Turning Sage King places his son upon a seat of Jāmbūnada gold atop the White Elephant Jewel; he takes water from the four great oceans and, having spread out a canopy of nets, banners, flowers, and various precious pennants as adornments, takes a golden pitcher of fragrant water in his hand and pours it over the crown of the son’s head. Thereupon, he is reckoned among the number of consecrated Kṣatriya kings; because he fully possesses and turns the ten paths of wholesome action, he receives the name "Wheel-Turning Sage King."
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!
Once that bodhisattva has received the consecration from the Tathāgatas, they are said to have attained the stage of wisdom; endowed with the ten powers, they are reckoned among the Buddhas.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is called the stage of the Great Vehicle for Bodhisattvas.
For the sake of this stage, Bodhisattvas undergo immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of hardships and difficult practices.
Once this bodhisattva has attained this stage, immeasurable merit and wisdom further increase; he is said to be "securely dwelling in the Bodhisattva Ground of the Cloud of Dharma.
The Commentary states:
Regarding "attaining the stage accordingly," it is because the light of all Tathāgatas mutually knows and equally embraces that bodhisattva.
As it is said in the sutra: "In this way, O Son of the Buddha!
At that time, all Buddhas emitted from the mark of the white tuft between their eyebrows a light named 'Benefiting All Wisdom-Penetration' (sarvajñānābhijñānuvartana)," and so forth.
How does one attain a status like that of the eldest son of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*)?
As the sutra states: "For example, it is like the eldest son of a universal monarch," and so forth.

When this bodhisattva attains such a status, he is said to be "well-established" in this stage, as the sutra says: "Once this bodhisattva has attained this status, his immeasurable merit and wisdom increase further; he is called 'one who dwells securely in the Bodhisattva Stage of the Cloud of Dharma' (*dharmameghā bhūmi*)."
Thus, the section on attaining the stage of consecration has been explained.
What is the entry into the section on the great perfections?
There are five kinds of entry into the section on the great perfections:
First, greatness of wisdom;
second, greatness of liberation;
third, greatness of samādhi.
Fourth, the greatness of dhāraṇī;
fifth, the greatness of supernormal powers.
These matters should be understood through their analysis according to these five meanings.
1. Based on the meaning of the true wisdom of perfect enlightenment;
2. Based on the meaning of mastery over the mind;
3. Based on the meaning that all matters are accomplished as soon as the mind is resolved.
Fourth, based on the meaning of benefiting sentient beings in accordance with all worldly needs;
fifth, based on the meaning of being capable of delivering sentient beings.
What is the accomplishment of wisdom?
The Sūtra says:
"O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva, dwelling in this Bodhisattva stage of the Cloud of Dharma, knows, as they truly are, the origin of the desire realm, the origin of the form realm, and the origin of the formless realm."

He knows, as they truly are, the arising of the realm of sentient beings, the arising of the realm of consciousness, the arising of the conditioned realm, the arising of the unconditioned realm, the arising of the realm of space, and the arising of the realm of phenomena; he knows, as it truly is, the arising of the realm of nirvana.

He knows, as they truly are, the accumulation of the realm of afflictions of false views; the accumulation of the formation and destruction of worlds; the accumulation of the practices of śrāvakas; the accumulation of the practices of pratyekabuddhas; the accumulation of the practices of bodhisattvas; the accumulation of the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique buddha-dharmas of all buddhas, as well as their form bodies and dharma bodies; the accumulation of the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all-knowledge; the accumulation of attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and manifesting parinirvāṇa; and, in brief, he knows, as they truly are, the accumulation of the distinctions of the wisdom that enters into the accomplishment of all dharmas.

By means of such wisdom and penetrating superior insight, this bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the transformations of the karma of sentient beings, the transformations of afflictions, the transformations of views and actions, the transformations of world-systems, the transformations of the dharma-realm, the transformations of śrāvakas, the transformations of pratyekabuddhas, the transformations of bodhisattvas, and the transformations of tathāgatas; he knows, as they truly are, all transformations of conceptualization and non-conceptualization.

This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the sustaining power of the Buddha, the sustaining power of the Dharma, the sustaining power of the Saṅgha, the sustaining power of karma, the sustaining power of afflictions, the sustaining power of time, the sustaining power of vows, the sustaining power of offerings, the sustaining power of practice, and the sustaining power of eons; he knows, as they truly are, the sustaining power of wisdom.

This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, all the subtle modes of entry of the Buddhas, namely: the subtle mode of entry into activity; the subtle mode of entry into withdrawal; the subtle mode of entry into entering the womb; the subtle mode of entry into birth; the subtle mode of entry into prowess; the subtle mode of entry into leaving the household life; the subtle mode of entry into attaining enlightenment; the subtle mode of entry into turning the wheel of Dharma; the subtle mode of entry into sustaining the lifespan; the subtle mode of entry into manifesting parinirvāṇa; and the subtle mode of entry into the long endurance of the Dharma. He knows these, exactly as they are.

This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, all the secret domains of the Buddhas: namely, the secrets of body, speech, and mind; the secret of deliberating upon the appropriate and inappropriate times; the secret of bestowing predictions upon bodhisattvas; the secret of gathering and subduing sentient beings; the secret of the various vehicles; the secret of the distinctions among all faculties and practices; the secret of acting in accordance with reality based on all inclinations; and the secret of knowing that practice leads to the attainment of enlightenment.
This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, all the Buddhas' wisdom regarding the entry into eons (*kalpa*), namely:
one eon entering incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), and incalculable eons entering one eon; numbered eons entering unnumbered eons, and unnumbered eons entering numbered eons;
a single thought-moment eon entering immeasurable eons, and immeasurable eons entering [a single thought-moment eon].
In a single thought-moment, eons enter non-eons and non-eons enter eons;
eons with Buddhas enter eons without Buddhas, eons without Buddhas enter eons with Buddhas, eons with Buddhas enter eons with Buddhas, and eons without Buddhas enter eons without Buddhas;
past and future eons enter the present eon, and the present eon enters [past and future eons].
Past and future kalpas enter the present kalpa; the present kalpa enters future and past kalpas;
long kalpas enter short kalpas; short kalpas enter long kalpas; short kalpas enter short kalpas;
and long kalpas enter long kalpas—thus one knows, as they truly are, the mutual entry of all the characteristics of the kalpas.

This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, all the wisdoms of entry possessed by the Buddhas; that is to say: the wisdom of entering the path of ordinary beings; the wisdom of entering the atoms of dust; the wisdom of entering the bodies and bodhi of lands; the wisdom of entering the bodies and minds of sentient beings and their bodhi; the wisdom of entering all places in accordance with bodhi; the wisdom of entering the manifestation of erratic conduct; the wisdom of entering the manifestation of compliant conduct; the wisdom of entering the manifestation of contrary conduct; the wisdom of entering the conceivable and the inconceivable; the wisdom of entering the manifestation of the conduct of the mundane and the supramundane; and the wisdom of entering the wisdom of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas—thus knowing, as they truly are, the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s conduct and wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!
The wisdom of all Buddhas is thus vast, immeasurable, and boundless; when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are able to enter into such wisdom.
The Commentary states:
Within this, it should be understood that the greatness of wisdom further comprises seven kinds:
first, the greatness of the knowledge of accumulation;
2. The greatness of the wisdom of responding through transformation;
3. The greatness of the wisdom of empowerment;
4. The greatness of the wisdom of entering the subtle and minute;
Fifth, the greatness of wisdom regarding the secret places;
sixth, the greatness of wisdom regarding entry into eons;
seventh, the greatness of wisdom regarding entry into the paths.

Among these, the first should be understood as relying on the power of being able to sever doubt; the second relies on the power of arising within that body; the third relies on the power of proceeding in such and such a manner; the fourth relies on the performance of the non-dual wisdom well-accumulated through the empowerment of transformational manifestations; the fifth relies on protecting sentient beings with immature faculties so as not to cause them alarm; the sixth relies on the abandonment of the will for self-mastery through the empowerment of the life-force and conduct; and the seventh relies on the teaching intended as an antidote.
Regarding the knowledge of accumulation therein, one should understand it as the knowledge of the accumulation of causes and conditions.

Furthermore, it consists in knowing all aspects of defilement, purification, or cessation; all locations within the three realms; all sentient beings; all minds characterized by defilement or purification; and all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.

In whatever places there may be, such as throughout space; in whatever ways the correct or incorrect Dharma is taught; and in whatever ways realization or non-realization occurs—namely, regarding nirvāṇa, those other outsiders and the like who follow erroneous views cannot realize it.
One should understand the distinctions of their accumulation according to the destruction and formation of all vessel-worlds (*bhājana-loka*) and according to all three vehicles (*yāna*).
As the Sūtra states: "O Son of the Buddha!

When this Bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), he knows the accumulation of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as it truly is, up to knowing the accumulation of the distinctions of the wisdom that enters into the accomplishment of all phenomena as it truly is."

Regarding the wise one who should transform beings therein, one should understand the distinctions such as those between sentient beings and their transformations, as the Sūtra states: "This bodhisattva, by means of such wisdom, penetrates superior insight, and so forth, until he knows all conceptualization and non-conceptualization as they truly are."
Among these, "transformations produced by afflictions and views" refers to manifesting transformations that demonstrate the defilement of afflictions and views.
"Transformations of the dharma-realm" refers to the practice of the teachings as they are expounded; for one must know all those transformations—both conceptual and non-conceptual—as they truly are.

Regarding the wisdom of empowerment therein, it is as stated in the sutra: "This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the empowerment of the Buddha's powers, up to knowing, as they truly are, the empowerment of wisdom"; thus it should be understood according to the sutra.
Regarding "the maintenance of wisdom therein," this is because it is the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*); this wisdom is capable of accomplishing all tasks.

Regarding "entering into subtle wisdom," as the sutra states: "This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the subtle entry-wisdom of all Buddhas, up to knowing, as it truly is, the subtle entry-wisdom of the long endurance of the Dharma"; this should be understood according to the sutra.
Regarding "mastery" (*vikrīḍita*) herein, it should be understood as the manifestation of the seven steps and so forth.

Regarding "knowledge of the secret places" (*guhyasthānajñāna*) herein, it should be understood according to the sūtra, which states: "This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, all the secret places of the Buddhas, up to knowing, as they truly are, the secret of attaining enlightenment through practice. It should be understood according to the sūtra.

Regarding the wisdom of entering eons (*kalpa*) therein, "entering eons" refers to what the sutra states: "This bodhisattva knows, as it truly is, the wisdom of all Buddhas for entering eons—namely, one eon entering incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), and so on, up to knowing, as it truly is, that the characteristics of all eons mutually enter one another. This should be understood according to the sutra.
Regarding "entering therein," it refers to the equal liberation that allows all eons to enter into one another.

Regarding "the wisdom of entering the path therein," this refers to those who rely on the stage of ordinary beings, those who act out of pride, those who seek birth in heaven through faith, and those who rely on applied and sustained thought. As the sutra states: "This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the wisdom of entry possessed by all Buddhas—namely, the wisdom of entering the path of ordinary beings, up to and including the ability to enter such wisdom."
Thus, the seven kinds of greatness of wisdom have been explained.
What is the greatness of liberation?
The Sūtra says:
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva thus penetrates the practice of this stage, they are said to have attained the bodhisattva’s inconceivable gate of liberation, the unobstructed liberation, the liberation of the differentiation of pure wisdom, the liberation of the light of universal gates, the liberation of the *tathāgatagarbha*, the liberation of conforming to the non-retrogressive wheel, the liberation of entering into the penetration of the three periods of time, the liberation of the treasury of the dharma-realm, and the liberation of the circle of light of liberation; this is called attaining the bodhisattva’s liberation that leaves no remainder regarding all spheres of experience.
O Son of the Buddha!

With these ten bodhisattva gates of liberation as the foremost, this bodhisattva attains immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* bodhisattva gates of liberation, all of which are attained within the tenth bodhisattva stage.

Likewise, there are likewise immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis, immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* dhāraṇīs, and immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The Commentary states:
Regarding the greatness of liberation herein, first, it relies upon the sphere of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). As the Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!
When a Bodhisattva thus penetrates the practice of this stage, they are named a Bodhisattva who has attained the gate of inconceivable liberation."
2. The unimpeded power of the vow-knowledge (*praṇidhijñāna*) that can reach immeasurable worlds, as stated in the sūtra: "unobstructed liberation" (*anāvaraṇavimokṣa*). 3.

The knowledge of the liberations and wisdoms of those in the world and those transcending the world—namely, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas, whether they are in training (*śaikṣa*) or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—as stated in the sūtra: "liberation through the differentiation of pure wisdom" (*viśuddhajñānaprabhedavimokṣa*).
4. The matter of turning according to one's will, as in the sūtra’s “Universal Gate Radiance Liberation.
5. The dharma-dhāraṇī, as in the sūtra’s “Tathāgatagarbha Liberation.”
Sixth, the ability to refute the arguments of others, as stated in the sutra: "Because of the liberation that accords with the non-retrogressive wheel.

Seventh, the ability to abide for as long as one intends throughout the kalpas of the three periods of time, as stated in the sutra: "Because of entering the liberation of penetrating the three periods of time."
8. The wisdom that understands the collection of causes and conditions for all phenomena in all their aspects, as stated in the sūtra:

“the liberation of the treasury of the dharma-realm. 9. The light that can illuminate everywhere without departing from the body, as stated in the sūtra: “the liberation of the circle of light of liberation.”

Tenth, by knowing the minds of all sentient beings in immeasurable worlds simultaneously, as stated in the sutra: "This is called attaining the bodhisattva’s liberation that is exhaustive regarding all spheres of experience."
Regarding the greatness of the samādhis therein, it is as the sūtra says: "In this way, up to immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of asaṃkhyeya samādhis.
Regarding the greatness of the dhāraṇīs therein, it is as the sūtra says: "Immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of asaṃkhyeya dhāraṇīs."

Regarding the greatness of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) therein, it is as the Sūtra states: "The immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of *asaṃkhyeya* supernormal powers are likewise so.
Thus has the section on the Great Perfection (*mahāparyanta*) within the ten stages (*bhūmi*) been explained.
What is the section on the etymological explanation of the stages?
The Sūtra says:

"This bodhisattva penetrates such wisdom that accords with enlightenment; having perfected immeasurable power of mindfulness and skillful means, this bodhisattva, in a single moment of thought, is able to receive, endure, contemplate, and uphold the immeasurable light of the Dharma, the immeasurable illumination of the Dharma, and the immeasurable rain of the Dharma from the presence of immeasurable Buddhas throughout the ten directions."
O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, like a mass of great rain poured down by the clouds of the Sāgara; no other land can receive it, endure it, conceive of it, or sustain it, except for the great ocean.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

Regarding the secret realm of all Tathāgatas—namely, the great illumination of the Dharma, the great radiance of the Dharma, and the great rain of the Dharma—all sentient beings, as well as all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, are unable to receive, endure, contemplate, or uphold them. Even Bodhisattvas from the first stage up to those dwelling in the ninth stage are likewise unable to receive, endure, contemplate, or uphold them. Only these Bodhisattvas who dwell in the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma are able to receive, endure, contemplate, and uphold them all.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the great ocean, which can receive, endure, contemplate, and sustain the great clouds and rain raised by a single great nāga king.

Whether it be two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred nāga kings, or a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a billion, ten billion, or a hundred thousand billion nayutas of nāga kings—even up to immeasurable, boundless, and inexpressible numbers of great nāga kings who raise great clouds and rain, pouring them down all at once in a single moment—he is able to receive, endure, contemplate, and sustain it all.
Why is this? Because the great ocean is an immeasurably vast vessel.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Ground of the Cloud of Dharma, they are able to receive, endure, contemplate, and maintain the great illumination of the Dharma, the great radiance of the Dharma, and the great rain of the Dharma from a single Buddha.

Whether it be two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred Buddhas; whether it be a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a billion, ten billion, or a hundred thousand billion nayutas of Buddhas—even unto the presence of immeasurable, boundless, and ineffable numbers of Buddhas—the great illumination of the Dharma, the great radiance of the Dharma, and the great rain of the Dharma, they are all able in a single thought-moment to receive, endure, contemplate, and uphold them. For this reason, this stage is called the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmiḥ*).
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Dharma-cloud stage (dharmameghā bhūmi), how many great illuminations of the Dharma, great radiances of the Dharma, and great rains of the Dharma from as many Buddhas can they receive, endure, contemplate, and uphold within a single moment?"
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Dharma-cloud stage (dharmameghā-bhūmi), they are able, within a single moment of thought, to receive, endure, contemplate, and uphold all the great dharma-illuminations, great dharma-luminosities, and great dharma-rains from incalculable and ineffable numbers of Buddhas."
O Son of the Buddha!

Suppose there were as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions; and suppose that among all the sentient beings in those worlds, a single sentient being were to attain the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining, becoming the attendant of the Buddha and the foremost among the great śrāvakas in the mastery of the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining.

For example, when the Buddha Vajrapadma was present, there was a bhikṣu named Mahājayin who was foremost in the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining; a single sentient being [there] achieved such power of the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining.

Suppose that one sentient being, as well as every other sentient being in all worlds, were likewise endowed with the power of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining; yet the Dharma received by one person would not be received again by a second person, such that all of them would each be distinct from one another.
O Son of the Buddha!
What do you think?
Is the power of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining possessed by all those sentient beings truly great?
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
The power of the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining possessed by all those sentient beings is exceedingly great and immeasurable."
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
I shall now explain it for you."

When this bodhisattva dwells in this stage of the Cloud of Dharma, within a single thought-moment, at the presence of a single Buddha, they are able to receive, endure, contemplate, and uphold the great dharma-illumination, the great dharma-radiance, and the great dharma-rain known as the "Treasury of the Dharma-realm of the Three Times."

That great light of Dharma, that great illumination of Dharma, and that great rain of Dharma—compared to the power of the *dhāraṇī* for hearing and retaining [the teachings] as described above regarding the skillful means of upholding them, the [power of] all sentient beings hearing and retaining it does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousand-nayuta part, nor one hundred-millionth part, nor one ten-billionth part, nor one thousand-billionth part, nor one hundred-thousand-billionth part, nor one hundred-thousand-billion-nayuta part; indeed, it cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy.

Just as was previously described regarding the presence of a single Buddha, so too at the abodes of Buddhas equal in number to the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions—and even beyond this number, at the abodes of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas—he is able, in a single moment of thought, to receive, endure, contemplate, and uphold the great Dharma-light, the great Dharma-illumination, and the great Dharma-rain known as the "Treasury of the Dharma-realm of the Three Times. For this reason, this stage is named the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (Dharmameghā-bhūmi).
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
When this Bodhisattva dwells in this Dharma-Cloud Stage (Dharmameghā-bhūmi), they arise from the power of their vows a great cloud of compassion;
they cause the great thunder of the Dharma to resound; they take penetrating clarity and fearlessness as lightning flashes; and they take the light of great wisdom as...
With swift winds, great merit and roots of goodness as thick and dense clouds, manifesting various forms of bodies as multicolored clouds,
they rain down the true Dharma to shatter all demonic adversaries; in a single thought-moment,
throughout as many worlds as there are atoms within all the aforementioned worlds, and likewise across hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of worlds.
They completely cover all of them, and furthermore, they also pervade immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of worlds beyond these numbers.

They pour down the great rain of the Dharma of roots of goodness and ambrosia, extinguishing the flames of the dust of afflictions arising from ignorance that sentient beings experience according to their inclinations; for this reason, this stage is called "Dharma."
The Cloud Ground.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

When this Bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Ground of the Cloud of Dharma, within a single world-system they manifest the descent from Tuṣita Heaven, entry into the womb, dwelling in the womb, initial birth, renunciation of the world, attainment of the Way of the Buddha, request for the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the demonstration of Great Nirvāṇa; in all these Buddha-activities, they attain mastery of wisdom according to the beings to be saved.
