Whether it be a trichiliocosm, or even as many worlds as the aforementioned number of atoms, or further beyond this count of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* worlds—from descending from Tuṣita Heaven until manifesting Great Parinirvāṇa—all these Buddha-activities are performed with mastery over wisdom according to the beings to be saved.
The treatise says:
Regarding the explanation of the name of this stage (*bhūmi*), there are three types.
First, it resembles the clouds of the Dharma because they universally cover; in this stage, the hearing of the Dharma is similar to the body of space because it universally covers.
Second, the analogy of extinguishing dust and removing defilement, because this Dharma can extinguish the dust of afflictions (*kleśa*) for sentient beings.

Third, the analogy of delivering sentient beings—from descending from Tuṣita Heaven to manifesting Great Parinirvāṇa—because it gradually transforms sentient beings, just as a great rain cloud generates and nurtures the sprouts of all vegetation.
Regarding the phrase "in this, one accomplishes the ultimate skillful means of immeasurable power of mindfulness," this is because it refers proximately to the meaning of upholding [the teaching].
As the sutra says: "This bodhisattva, having penetrated such wisdom in accordance with enlightenment, accomplishes the ultimate skillful means of immeasurable power of mindfulness."

Furthermore, because they are able to receive and uphold a multitude of subtle and secret teachings with rapidity, as the sutra says: "This bodhisattva, at the abodes of immeasurable Buddhas in the ten directions, [receives] immeasurable great illumination of the Dharma," and so forth.

Regarding "the immeasurable great Dharma-illumination of the immeasurable Buddhas therein": it is because they expound a multitude of teachings and because they enter the subtle and secret realm of the Tathāgata.
Regarding "in a single thought-moment": it is because of the swiftness of reception.
Regarding those who hear the Dharma, two matters are demonstrated: by way of their nature and by way of their activity.
What is meant by "nature"?
It is because they are the radiance of the Great Dharma and because they are embraced by the wisdom of hearing and reflection.
The Great Dharma shines because it is embraced by the wisdom of cultivated insight (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
How does it produce the great rain of Dharma?
It is like a great cloud that bestows the rain of Dharma upon others, for one gives rise to faith therein.
"Receiving" (śruta) refers to receiving the words and phrases that are spoken.
"Being capable" (dhṛti) refers to being able to grasp the meaning.
"Reflecting" (cintā) refers to the non-loss of the integration of those two.
Regarding "retaining" (*dhāraṇa*): the great ocean is likewise, because it is not turbid.
Regarding "receiving" (*pratigraha*): it is able to receive all waters.
Regarding "withstanding" (*kṣama*): other waters, upon entering in number, lose their original names [as distinct bodies].
Regarding "speech and thought," it is because their function is inexhaustible;
one should know that they are "retained. As the Sūtra says:

"The Dharma-realm treasury of the three periods of time is a great Dharma-light, a great Dharma-illumination, and a great Dharma-rain; all of these can be received, can be endured, can be contemplated, and can be retained."
"...therefore this stage is called the Dharma-Cloud Stage (dharmameghā bhūmi).

Regarding the phrase "the treasury of the dharma-realm of the three times" herein, one should understand that within the dharma-realm there are three kinds of treasuries of phenomena, which correspond to the similes of clouds, thunder, and lightning.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva, dwelling in this stage of the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā-bhūmi), [proceeds] from his own power of aspiration... for this reason this stage is called the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma."
In this context, the great light of wisdom acting as a swift wind is analogous to the nature of wind;
manifesting various forms of the physical body is analogous to the nature of variegated clouds, for it revolves according to the various bodies within the world.
Regarding the statement that "the rain of the True Dharma breaks all demonic adversaries," it is because this is analogous to the falling of rain.
Thus, the section on the etymological definition of this stage has been explained.
What, then, is the section on the supreme and non-supreme supernormal powers?
The Sūtra says:

"When this Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he attains supreme mastery over wisdom; through his skillful discernment and the supernormal power of great knowledge, he acts according to his mental intention, such that he may make a narrow land wide or a wide land narrow."
Furthermore, according to his mental inclinations, he may transform a defiled land into a pure one, or a pure land into a defiled one.
In this way, through his sovereign power, he can manifest all kinds of worlds—vast and immeasurable, whether abiding in disorder, inverted, or upright.

Furthermore, according to the bodhisattva’s mental resolve, he may manifest within a single atom all the Iron Ring Mountains and other features of an entire world-system, yet that atom does not increase in size.

Whether it be two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a billion, ten billion, a hundred thousand billion, or a hundred thousand billion nayutas of worlds, even up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds—all the Iron Ring Mountains and other such features within them enter into a single minute atom (*paramāṇu*), yet that minute atom does not increase in size.
Furthermore, according to his mental inclinations, this bodhisattva may display the adornments of one world within two worlds.
Again, according to his mental inclinations, he may display the adornments of one world even unto worlds that are immeasurable, unspeakable, and beyond description.

Furthermore, according to his mental inclinations, he may manifest the adornments of two worlds within a single world, and even manifest the adornments of immeasurable, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds within a single world.

Furthermore, according to his mental resolve, he may even place the sentient beings of immeasurable, unspeakably unspeakable worlds into a single world, yet those sentient beings feel no fear and remain unaware and unknowing of it.

Furthermore, according to his mental resolve, he may place the sentient beings of a single world-system, or even those of immeasurable, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of world-systems, yet these sentient beings feel no fear and remain unaware and unknowing of it.
Furthermore, according to his mental inclinations, he may manifest within a single pore all the matters of the adornments of the realms of all Buddhas.

Again, according to his mental inclinations, he may even manifest within a single pore all the matters of the adornments of the realms of all Buddhas—immeasurable, unspeakable, and beyond description.

Furthermore, according to his mental resolve, in a single thought-instant he manifested bodies as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable worlds; within each of these bodies, he manifested hands as numerous as those same atoms. With all these hands, he venerated the Buddhas of the ten directions with diligent devotion, and with each hand, he held flower-caskets as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to scatter over the Buddhas.

In this same way, it was also so for flower boxes, flower garlands, powdered incense, ointments, perfumes, garments, precious canopies, banners, flowers, precious standards, and all other articles of adornment.

Within each and every body, he manifests as many heads as there are atoms; within each and every head, he manifests as many tongues as there are atoms. With these tongues, he praises the deeds of the Buddhas' virtues, and such activities fill the ten directions in every moment of thought.
In every thought-moment, they manifest the attainment of Bodhi in immeasurable worlds, even manifesting the adornment, maintenance, and abiding of Great Nirvana.

Within the three periods of time, they manifest immeasurable bodies; within their own bodies, they manifest immeasurable Buddhas and manifest the matters of the adornments of immeasurable Buddha-worlds, as well as the matters of the formation and destruction of worlds. Or, from a single pore of their own body, they emit all the calamities of wind without afflicting sentient beings.

Furthermore, according to his mental resolve, he may transform immeasurable and boundless worlds into a single sea of water; within this sea of water, he creates a great lotus flower, its radiant adornments pervading and covering immeasurable and boundless worlds.
Within that, he manifests the wondrous adornments of the great Bodhi tree, even unto the manifestation of all modes of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvākāra-sarvajñajñāna*).

Or, within his own body, he manifests the radiance of the ten directions—such as the light of mani-jewels, lightning, the sun, the moon, and the stars—and even all the lights of all worlds appear within his body.
With a breath from his mouth, he can move infinite worlds throughout the ten directions without causing sentient beings to feel fear or alarm.
He manifests the exhaustion of the world-systems in the ten directions by the kalpa-ending wind-disasters, the kalpa-ending fire-disasters, and the kalpa-ending water-disasters.

In accordance with the various mental inclinations of all sentient beings, they achieve the adornment of manifesting physical bodies as appropriate; they may manifest their own bodies as the body of a Tathāgata, or manifest the body of a Tathāgata as their own body; they may manifest the body of a Tathāgata as their own Buddha-land, or manifest their own Buddha-land as the body of a Tathāgata.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!
Such are the supernatural transformations of a bodhisattva dwelling in this Bodhisattva Ground of the Cloud of Dharma.

Furthermore, there are other immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of adornments of supernormal powers that are manifested with sovereign mastery beyond these.
The treatise states:
Regarding the phrase "among these, the power of supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) is either unsurpassed or surpassable," one should understand that there are six aspects:
first, based on the internal;
2. Based on the external;
3. Its own characteristic;
4. Performing the function of maintenance.
Fifth, causing joy;
sixth, great victory.
Among these, "supreme supernormal power" refers to its comparison with the supernormal powers of other sentient beings.
Regarding "having a superior," this is because it is compared to the supernatural powers (*ṛddhibala*) of the Tathāgata.
Within this, there are four kinds based on the internal:
first, inconceivable liberation (*acintyavimokṣa*).
Second, samādhi;
third, the dhāraṇī of arising wisdom;
fourth, the supernormal powers, as previously described.
Regarding the external, there are external objects such as the earth and so forth;
furthermore, there are external objects such as one's own body and the bodies of others.
Within these, there are two kinds of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*):
First, the transformation of external phenomena and so forth;
second, the manifestation of one's own body and so forth.
Within these, there are furthermore three types of transformation:
First, transformation through brevity and extensiveness;
second, transformation through diverse activities;
third, transformation through mastery, which is able to produce all manner of adornments for all sentient beings.
What is the transformation from the narrow to the broad?

As the Sūtra states: "This bodhisattva, dwelling in this stage, attains supreme mastery over wisdom; through his skillful discernment of the great power of knowledge, he acts according to his mental intention, such that he may make a narrow land broad or a broad land narrow."
What is the transformation of diverse phenomena?

As the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, according to the mind's intention, one may transform a defiled land into a pure one, or a pure land into a defiled one, and so forth, until all worlds are accomplished in various ways through the power of mastery."
What is sovereign transformation?

It is as the sutra says: "Furthermore, this bodhisattva, according to his mental resolve, manifests a single world within a single atom, and even causes all sentient beings therein to feel neither fear nor to perceive or know [the occurrence]. Thus it is said.
How does one manifest transformations of one's own body and so forth?

As the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, according to his mental resolve, he may display within the space of a single hair-pore all the matters of the adornments of the spheres of all Buddhas; again, according to his mental resolve, he may even display within a single hair-pore the matters of the adornments of the spheres of all Buddhas, as many as are unspeakably unspeakable. Thus it is said.

Regarding those who act as sustainers within this [teaching], they achieve the gates of making offerings and so forth because they gather the factors that assist the realization of bodhi. As the sutra states: "Furthermore, in accordance with their mental intentions, in a single moment of thought, they manifest bodies as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds, even up to the manifestation of infinite, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of sovereign adornments."
How does one cause them to rejoice?
The Sūtra says:

At that time, all the assembly of Bodhisattvas, as well as all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, the four heavenly kings, Śakra-devendra, Brahmā-devaputra, Maheśvara, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, and so forth.
Each of them thought to themselves:
"If the power of the bodhisattvas' supernormal knowledges and wisdom can be thus immeasurable and boundless, what then must the Buddha be like?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the great assembly, asked the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
"O Son of the Buddha!
Now this great assembly, having heard of the power of the bodhisattva’s supernormal knowledge and wisdom, has fallen into a net of doubt.
To sever their doubts, I shall briefly demonstrate the wondrous deeds adorned by the power of the bodhisattva’s supernormal faculties."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha entered the bodhisattva samādhi called "The Essential Nature of All Buddha-lands.

When the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha entered this samādhi of the essential nature of all Buddha-lands, the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, as well as all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, the four heavenly kings, Śakra-devendra, Brahmā-devaputra, Maheśvara, and the Śuddhāvāsa devas, all saw themselves enter into the body of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha; within his body, they beheld the Buddha-lands.
The various signs and wondrous adornments within that land could not be fully described even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.

Within it stands a Bodhi tree; its trunk has a circumference of one hundred thousand trichiliocosms and a height of one million trichiliocosms, providing shade over three hundred billion trichiliocosms.
The tree was praised as being high and vast, and upon it was a lion throne. On that throne sat a Buddha named Sarvajñābhijñārāja Tathāgata.

The entire great assembly all beheld the Buddha seated beneath the bodhi-tree on the lion throne; the various marks and wondrous adornments therein could not be fully described even in hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.

After the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha had manifested such great supernormal powers, he caused all the assemblies of bodhisattvas, as well as all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, the four heavenly kings, Śakra-devendra, Brahmā-devaputra, Maheśvara, and the Śuddhāvāsa devas, each to return to their respective places.
At that time, the entire great assembly rejoiced and leaped for joy, conceiving a sense of wonder; they remained silent, gazing at the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
Then, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
This is most rare. This samādhi,
adorned with supernormal powers, possesses great power and majesty,
O Son of the Buddha!
"What is the name of this samādhi?
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replied:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
"This samādhi is named the Essential Nature of All Buddha-lands.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
"To what extent do the majestic adornments and wondrous deeds of the supernatural powers within the realm of this samādhi extend?
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replied:
"O Son of the Buddha!"

If a bodhisattva, in accordance with their mental inclinations, skillfully cultivates this power of samādhi, they are able to manifest within their own body as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in such buddha-fields, and even more than that number.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva dwells in this Bodhisattva Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), they attain hundreds of thousands of such immeasurable bodhisattva samādhis.

For this reason, this bodhisattva [surpasses] even those bodhisattvas who have attained their respective positions as well as those dwelling in the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī bhūmi*).
He cannot fathom or know it: whether it be his body or bodily karma, which is difficult to fathom; his speech or vocal karma, which is difficult to fathom;
his mind or mental karma, which is difficult to fathom; his supernormal powers, which are difficult to fathom;
his wisdom that contemplates the three periods of time, which is difficult to fathom; or the realm of his entry into samādhi, which is difficult to fathom.
It is difficult to fathom or know: whether it be the sphere of their wisdom, which is difficult to fathom; or their play in various liberations, which is difficult to fathom;

or what they perform through emanation, what they perform through empowerment, or what they perform through spiritual power, which is difficult to fathom—even down to the lifting and lowering of their feet, and even [the deeds of] Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages.
Bodhisattvas dwelling on the Stage of Excellent Intelligence cannot fathom it.
O Son of the Buddha!
Thus have these immeasurable qualities of the Bodhisattva’s Cloud of Dharma Stage been briefly explained.

If explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, nor in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads, nor in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions.
Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
"If the power of the bodhisattva’s sphere of supernormal activity is thus immeasurable, what then is the power of the Buddha’s sphere of supernormal activity?
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha replied:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, suppose a person were to take two or three grains of soil from among the four continents and say:
"Is the earth-element of the infinite worlds greater, or is this [soil] greater?
My answer to your question would be as follows.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom is immeasurable; how can you seek to fathom it with the wisdom of a bodhisattva?
Son of the Buddha!
It is like a person who takes a small portion of the earth-element from among the four continents, while the remainder remains exceedingly vast.
"Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!
Even if one were to speak for immeasurable eons, one could only describe a single fraction of the Bodhisattva’s Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā), let alone the Stage of the Tathāgata.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha to the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra.
O Son of the Buddha!
May all these Tathāgatas bear witness to my words.
O Son of the Buddha!

Suppose that in each of the ten directions, there were Buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable worlds, and these lands were entirely filled with Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, like a dense forest of sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, or hemp.

The merit, wisdom, and karmic practices cultivated by these bodhisattvas over immeasurable eons do not equal even one hundredth part of the power of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom; they do not equal one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousand-nayuta part, nor one hundred-millionth part, nor one ten-billionth part, nor one hundred-billionth part, nor one hundred-thousand-billionth part, nor one hundred-thousand-billion-nayuta part; indeed, they cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

This bodhisattva, having mastered such wisdom, accords with the body, speech, and mind activities of the Tathāgata; without relinquishing the power of bodhisattva samādhi, they are able to see all Buddhas and diligently make offerings to them. Throughout each and every kalpa, they offer the most supreme of all kinds of requisites to immeasurable Buddhas, and while receiving the empowerment of the Buddhas’ spiritual powers, they become increasingly brilliant and superior. Regarding all challenges and inquiries within the dharma-realm, there is none who can surpass this bodhisattva; they remain inexhaustible for immeasurable hundreds of kalpas, immeasurable thousands of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, immeasurable billions of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of billions of kalpas, immeasurable trillions of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of trillions of kalpas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a skillful goldsmith who, having expertly refined this gold to create an ornament, intersperses it with unsurpassed mani-jewels and fastens it upon the neck or crown of the Sovereign King of Gods (Śakra); no other ornaments of the devas can equal it.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this tenth bodhisattva stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), that bodhisattva’s inconceivable course of wisdom cannot be attained by any sentient being, nor by any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, nor even by bodhisattvas from the first stage up to those dwelling in the ninth stage.

When this bodhisattva dwells in this stage, the illumination of the light of great wisdom enables all sentient beings to reach even the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), such that it cannot be destroyed by the light of any other wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the radiance of the celestial king Maheśvara, which surpasses the radiance of all beings in every place of birth and is able to bring coolness and clarity to the bodies and minds of sentient beings.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this tenth bodhisattva stage, the Cloud of Dharma, that radiance of their wisdom cannot be equaled by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even by bodhisattvas dwelling from the first stage up to the ninth stage.
When this Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are able to cause all sentient beings to dwell within the dharma of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
O Son of the Buddha!

This Bodhisattva accords with such wisdom; the Buddhas of the ten directions preach wisdom for them, causing them to penetrate the activities of the three periods of time, to correctly know the distinctions of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), to pervade all world-realms (*lokadhātu*), and to illuminate all world-realms, so that all realms of sentient beings may realize the Dharma. Briefly stated, this continues until they accord with and attain the knowledge of all-knowledge.
Among these ten pāramitās of the bodhisattva, the pāramitā of wisdom (jñānapāramitā) is predominant.
O Son of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the tenth bodhisattva stage, the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā).
If explained in detail, it would be inexhaustible throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons.

If a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become the celestial king Maheśvara, endowed with sovereign power, skillfully bestowing upon sentient beings the practices of the perfections (*pāramitā*) of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; and regarding the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), no one is able to exhaust their responses to questions and challenges.

The wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—all these merits never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the bodhisattvas, mindfulness of the bodhisattva practices, mindfulness of the pāramitās, mindfulness of the ten stages, mindfulness of the indestructible powers, mindfulness of the fearlessnesses, and mindfulness of the unique qualities of a buddha, up to and including mindfulness of the complete possession of all aspects of the knowledge of all modes.
One should constantly give rise to this thought:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the greatest, the sublime, the most subtle, the highest, the unsurpassed, the guide, the general, the teacher, and the honored one, even unto becoming the one upon whom the knowledge of all-knowledge relies."
Furthermore, from this thought, he gave rise to diligent practice; by the power of that diligence, in a single moment of thought,
he attained as many samādhis as there are atoms in ten unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds,
and he beheld as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds.
...is able to know the spiritual powers of as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds;
is able to shake as many worlds as there are atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds;
and is able to enter ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas...
He can illuminate worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds;

he can teach and transform sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds; and he can abide for a lifespan of ten [unspeakable eons].
One may speak of eons as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds;
one can know the events of ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-world-atom eons each in the past and future worlds;
and one can skillfully enter ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.

He possesses dharma-gates as numerous as the atoms in a world-system, and is able to transform his body into as many bodies as there are atoms in ten unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds; in each and every body,
he manifests as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in ten unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-worlds to serve as his retinue.
If one considers the sovereign excellence of their power of vows, the bodhisattvas' power of vows exceeds these numbers.

They manifest various kinds of supernatural powers—whether through the body, or light, or supernormal faculties, or the eyes, or spheres of experience, or sounds, or conduct, or adornments, or empowerments, or faith, or karma.
These supernormal powers (abhijñā) cannot be fully enumerated even throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
The Commentary states:
herein, that which causes joy is so called because it is able to sever doubt.
There are two ways of severing doubt:
first, by manifesting one's own supernormal powers;
second, by teaching all dharmas.
How does he manifest his own supernatural powers?
As the sutra states: "At that time, all the assembly of bodhisattvas, as well as all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas," and so forth.
Thus, by manifesting his own power, he severs the doubts of sentient beings and causes them to rejoice.
How does he teach all dharmas? As the sutra says:
"In this way, O Son of the Buddha!"
This bodhisattva, having attained such wisdom, accords with the bodily, vocal, and mental actions of the Tathāgata, becoming even more brilliant and superior.
Regarding all challenges and inquiries within the dharma-realm, there is none who can surpass this bodhisattva. Thus it is said.
Within this, there are two kinds of supreme excellence:
first, excellence in supernormal powers;
second, excellence in calculation.

Because these two matters surpass all preceding stages, as the sūtra states: "One should know that the knowledge of the three periods of time and so forth are supernormal powers (abhijñā)," for they penetrate the three types of conduct.
First, the practice of being able to sever doubt, as the sutra states: "O Son of the Buddha!

When this bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he accords with such wisdom; the Buddhas of the ten directions preach wisdom for him, causing him to penetrate the practices of the three periods of time," and so forth.
Regarding the practitioner of the three periods of time, the meaning of the Path should be understood.

Second is the practice of swift supernatural power, because of hearing the teaching of the Tathāgata’s secret Dharma, as stated in the Sūtra: "correctly knowing the distinctions within the Dharma-realm."
Third, the auxiliary practices of equal application; herein, three kinds should be known:
first, the equality of purifying Buddha-fields for the sake of transforming sentient beings;
second, the equality of the light of the Dharma; [and third, the equality of the light of wisdom].
Third, the equality of attaining perfect enlightenment.

As the sutra states: "Because it pervades all world-realms, because it illuminates all world-realms, because it causes all realms of sentient beings to realize the Dharma, and briefly stated, up to 'conforming to the attainment of the knowledge of all-knowledge,'" and so forth.
Thus, the section on the superior and surpassable aspects of the supernormal powers of this stage has been explained.
Next, the section on the images of the stages is explained.
Within this, there are four kinds of images of the stages:
First, ponds;
second, mountains;
third, oceans.
Fourth, the maṇi jewel is used as a metaphor for four kinds of merit:
first, the merit of practice; second, the merit of supreme excellence; [third, the merit of non-retrogression; fourth, the merit of the fruit of liberation].
3. The merit of being able to cross over what is difficult to cross and attaining the great fruit;
4. The merit of transforming and exhausting that which is firm and solid.
What is the merit of spiritual practice?
The Sūtra says:
"O Son of the Buddha!
These ten stages of the bodhisattva are practiced in successive order, proceeding toward the knowledge of all aspects, the knowledge of all-knowledge."
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the four rivers flowing from the great lake Anavatapta, filling Jambudvīpa without ever being exhausted, and further increasing until they fill the great ocean.
In this way, O Son of the Buddha!

From the bodhicitta, the Bodhisattva flows forth the water of roots of goodness and great vows; through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they fill the realms of sentient beings without exhaustion, further increasing until they reach fulfillment and attain the knowledge of all modes, the omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The Commentary states:

Regarding the merit of practice herein, one should understand that it consists of the practice of benefiting others by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) based on the power of one's original vow, as well as the practice of self-benefit through the increase of one’s own roots of goodness and the attainment of *bodhi*.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, like the four rivers flowing from the great lake Anavatapta, until they reach fulfillment and attain the knowledge of all aspects, the knowledge of all-knowledge."
What are the supreme and excellent qualities?
The Sūtra says:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
These ten stages of the Bodhisattva exist with their distinctions because of the Buddha’s wisdom.
It is, for example, like the existence of the distinctions among the ten great mountain kings based upon the great earth.
What are these ten?

They are the King of Mountains, Himavat; the King of Mountains, Gandhamādana; the King of Mountains, Vidyutprabha; the King of Mountains, Ṛṣigiri; the King of Mountains, Yugandhara; the King of Mountains, Aśvakarṇa; the King of Mountains, Nimindhara; the King of Mountains, Kālaparvata; the King of Mountains, Citrakūṭa; and the King of Mountains, Sumeru.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the King of Snowy Mountains, wherein all medicinal herbs are gathered; these various medicinal herbs can never be exhausted once taken.
In the same way, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), all worldly treatises, arts, literature, recitations, and incantations are contained therein; all worldly treatises, arts, literature, recitations, and incantations are inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like Mount Gandhamādana, the king of mountains, wherein all fragrances are gathered; all these fragrances can never be exhausted by taking them.
In the same way, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the fragrances of the observance of precepts and meditative attainments practiced by all bodhisattvas are gathered therein; these fragrances of the observance of precepts and meditative attainments practiced by all bodhisattvas are inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like Mount Vidyutprabha, the king of mountains, which is of the nature of pure jewels and wherein all kinds of jewels are gathered; all these jewels can never be exhausted, no matter how much they are taken.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), all worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*) are gathered therein; the questions and answers concerning all worldly meditative concentrations, supernormal powers, liberations, samādhis, and attainments are inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like the King of Mountains, the Abode of Sages and Seers, where pure and precious beings—sages endowed with the five supernatural powers—dwell; these sages with the five supernatural powers are inexhaustible.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the bodhisattva stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), the supreme practices of wisdom among all practices are gathered therein; the various inquiries regarding these supreme practices of wisdom among all practices are inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is, for example, like Mount Yugandhara, the king of mountains, which is of the nature of pure jewels; all the yakṣas and great spirits gather therein, and these yakṣas and great spirits are inexhaustible.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva stage of Difficult to Conquer (Duranjayā), all the majestic arrays of sovereign and spontaneous supernormal powers and transformations are gathered therein; the questions and answers regarding these sovereign and spontaneous supernormal powers and transformations are inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the King of Mountains, Aśvakarṇa, which is of the nature of pure jewels; all manner of fruits gather therein, and one could never exhaust them by taking them all.
In this way, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva Ground of Presence, they teach the entry into the contemplation of the accumulation of causes and conditions; therein, the teachings on the entry into the contemplation of the accumulation of causes and conditions, as well as the questions and answers concerning the realization of the fruits of the śrāvakas, are inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like Mount Nimiṃdhara, the king of mountains, which is of the nature of pure jewels and wherein all the great powerful nāga deities gather; these all-powerful nāga deities are inexhaustible.
In this way, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva stage of Far-Reaching (dūraṃgamā), various forms of skillful means and wisdom are gathered therein; the explanations and dialogues concerning the realization of the fruit of the pratyekabuddha through these various forms of skillful means and wisdom are inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like Mount Khadiraka, the king of mountains, which is composed entirely of pure precious substances; therein dwells a multitude of those who have attained mastery, and this multitude of those who have attained mastery is inexhaustible.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), they give rise to the path of all bodhisattva masteries, which is gathered therein; they give rise to the path of all bodhisattva masteries, wherein the explanations and dialogues concerning the distinctions of all world-systems are inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the King of Mountains, Mount Viśvānara, where a multitude of great asuras of pure jewel-nature gather; that multitude of great asuras is inexhaustible.
In this way, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva stage of Good Intelligence (Sādhumatī), they know that within it are gathered all the forward and reverse movements of all sentient beings; they know all the forward and reverse movements of all sentient beings, and their explanations of the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of all worlds and their ensuing questions and answers are inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, which is of the nature of pure jewels; within it gather the great assemblies of devas, and these great assemblies of devas are inexhaustible.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Bodhisattva Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of a Tathāgata are gathered therein; the manifestation of the Buddha-activities through the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of a Tathāgata, as well as the ensuing questions and answers, are inexhaustible.
O Son of the Buddha!
These ten great kings of jewel mountains all exist within the great ocean and derive their names from it.
In the same way, O Son of the Buddha!
The ten stages of the bodhisattva are all contained within omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and they receive their names by reason of omniscience.
The treatise states:
"Among these, the superior and excellent qualities arise because they depend upon the ten stages of superior practice based on omniscience," as it says in the Sūtra: "O Son of the Buddha!"

These ten stages of the bodhisattva possess distinctions because they are based upon the Buddha’s wisdom; it is, for example, like the existence of the distinctions among the ten great mountain kings based upon the great earth.
In this context, the metaphor of the mountains composed of pure jewels represents the eight stages (*bhūmi*), because these stages are thoroughly purified through the cultivation of detachment.
Furthermore, the kings of mountains do not belong to the category of sentient beings, yet they serve as the support for those who do.
Those that do not belong to the category of sentient beings are of two kinds:
first, objects of enjoyment;
second, objects such as treasures that are guarded and accumulated.
Regarding the matters of enjoyment therein, there are two kinds:
first, the remediation of the increase and decrease of the four great elements of sentient beings;

second, the nurturing of sentient beings. Depending upon the Snowy Mountains, the Fragrant Mountains, the Vidyāla Mountains, and the Horse-Ear Mountains—since these four mountains are not included within the category of sentient beings—all medicinal herbs, various fragrances, various jewels, and all fruits are gathered therein.
Regarding "all fruits," as for those among the classes of sentient beings on the sixth mountain, there are further six kinds of difficulties that are hard to remedy.
These six kinds of difficulties are:
first, the difficulty of poverty; [and so forth].
2. The calamity of death;
3. The calamity of famine;
4. The calamity of lack of discipline;
Fifth, the hardship of evil karma; sixth, the hardship of hostile enemies.

On the fourth mountain, the field of merit possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) counteracts the hardship of poverty. On the fifth mountain, the great yakṣa deities with their supernormal transformations counteract the hardship of death. On the seventh mountain, the various great nāga kings counteract the hardship of famine. On the eighth mountain, the assembly who have attained mastery counteracts the hardship of being unsubdued. On the ninth mountain, the asuras reciting mantras counteract the hardship of evil karma. On the tenth mountain, the sovereign Four Heavenly Kings (*caturmahārāja*) counteract the hardship of hostile enemies.
That all these mountains are gathered therein means that, as described, they are able to produce all things.
That they are gathered therein and cannot be exhausted means that their continuous activity proceeds without interruption or rest.
Those ten great mountains derive their names from the great ocean, and the great ocean likewise derives its name from the great mountains.

It is the same with the ten stages of the bodhisattva: they all reside within omniscience (sarvajñatā) and derive their names from omniscience, because the characteristics of cause and effect manifest one another.
As the sutra says: "O Son of the Buddha!
These ten great kings of jewel mountains all exist within the great ocean and are named because of the great ocean.
In the same way, O Son of the Buddha!"
"Because the ten stages of the bodhisattva all reside within omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and it is by reason of omniscience that they receive their names.
What, then, are the qualities of the great fruit that is difficult to attain yet capable of being attained?
The Sūtra says:
"O Son of the Buddha!
For example, it is because of ten characteristics that the great ocean is reckoned as the 'great ocean,' and none are able to destroy it."
What are the ten?
First, it is progressively deeper;
second, it does not accept corpses.
Third, the remaining waters lose their original names;
fourth, they become of one taste;
fifth, there is an immeasurable accumulation of jewels.
Sixth, it is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom;
seventh, it is vast and immeasurable;
eighth, it is the abode where many large-bodied sentient beings dwell.
Ninth, its tides do not exceed their limits;
tenth, it can receive all great rains without ever being satiated.
Such, O Son of the Buddha! is [the ocean].
The bodhisattva practice is reckoned as such by way of ten characteristics, and it cannot be destroyed.
What are these ten? They are:
because in the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one gradually gives rise to great vows; and in the Bodhisattva Stage of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*)...

Because in the Middle [Bhūmi], one does not dwell with the corpses of those who have broken the precepts; because in the Bodhisattva’s Radiant Bhūmi (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), one abandons all worldly conventional designations and numerical categories;
because in the Bodhisattva’s Blazing Bhūmi (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), one reveres the Triple Gem and attains the undifferentiated single flavor;
and because in the Bodhisattva’s Difficult-to-Conquer Bhūmi (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), immeasurable wisdom of skillful means arises to perform manifold worldly deeds.
Because the Bodhisattva contemplates the profound dharma of the accumulation of causes and conditions in the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*);

because in the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*) he skillfully discriminates all dharmas through immeasurable wisdom of expedient means; because in the Stage of Immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*) he manifests the undertaking of great adornments;
and because in the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*) he attains profound liberation and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Because he has realized the conduct of the world as it truly is and does not transcend its limits, and because, within the Bodhisattva stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*),
he can receive the great rain of the Dharma-light from all Buddhas without ever being satiated.
The Commentary states:
Regarding the merit of being able to cross over that which is difficult to cross within this [path], it is because cause and effect accord with one another.
The ten stages (*bhūmi*) are like a great ocean, difficult to cross yet capable of being crossed, for they result in the attainment of the fruit of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
One should know that the great ocean possesses eight kinds of meritorious qualities:
first, the quality of easy entry, as the sūtra says it is "gradually deep";
second, the quality of purity, as the sūtra says it "does not receive corpses."
3. The merit of equality, as the sūtra says: "The other waters lose their original names.
4. The merit of protection, as the sūtra says: "They become of one taste."
Fifth, the merit of benefit, as stated in the sutra: "an immeasurable mass of jewels.
Sixth, the merit of inexhaustibility, meaning its profundity and vastness, etc., as stated in the sutra: "extremely deep and difficult to cross" and "vast and immeasurable."
7. The merit of being a dwelling place: because it is where great multitudes of sentient beings rely and dwell, as the sūtra says, "many large-bodied sentient beings rely and dwell [there].

8. The merit of protecting the world: the tide does not exceed its time and receives water without weariness, as the sūtra says the tide "does not exceed its limit" and "is able to receive all great rains without ever being satiated."

The analogy of the great ocean should be understood as having ten corresponding aspects regarding the practices of the ten stages of a bodhisattva, as stated in the sutra: "In this way, O Son of the Buddha!
Because the bodhisattva practice possesses ten characteristics, it is designated by the number 'ten' as the bodhisattva practice, for there is nothing that can destroy it," and so forth.
What is the transformation and exhaustion of firm and solid merit?
The Sūtra says:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, it is like a great maṇi jewel that surpasses ten types of precious substances:
first, it originates from the great ocean;
second, it is skillfully refined by a master craftsman.
3. Well-turned and exquisite;
4. Well-purified; 5. Well-cleansed and lustrous.
Sixth, it is well-bored;
seventh, it is threaded with precious thread;
eighth, it is placed upon a high pillar of lapis lazuli.
Ninth, they emit all manner of light;
tenth, they rain down various precious objects according to the king’s will, able to bestow all kinds of treasures upon all sentient beings.
Such, O Son of the Buddha! is it.
When a bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), they transcend the ten natures of the noble ones:
first, upon the initial generation of the mind, they practice giving and abandon stinginess;
second, they skillfully cultivate the precepts so that their correct conduct is bright and pure.
Third, he skillfully cultivates dhyāna, samādhi, and samāpatti, causing them to become increasingly refined and subtle;
fourth, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) are thoroughly purified;
fifth, his skillful means and supernormal powers (abhijñā) are perfectly pure and radiant.
Sixth, skillfully drilling through by means of the contemplation on the convergence of causes and conditions;
seventh, skillfully threading together with the threads of wisdom regarding various skillful means;
eighth, placing them upon the banner of sovereign supernormal powers.
Ninth, observing the conduct of sentient beings, they radiate the light of wisdom derived from extensive learning;
tenth, the Buddhas confer upon them the station of knowledge.
At that time, they are able to manifest Buddha-works for the sake of all sentient beings, which is termed the attainment of *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
The Commentary states:
Regarding the "transformation and exhaustion of firm and steadfast virtues" herein, it is illustrated by the simile of the great maṇi jewel, as the sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, like a great maṇi jewel," and so forth.

Regarding "surpassing the ten jewel natures": the maṇi jewel surpasses lapis lazuli and the like because it excels them; this is taken up [as an example] up to its emitting all radiance, as it is shown that this jewel is comprised of eight kinds of qualities.
The eight kinds of qualities are:
first, the quality of emergence, because it is selected and taken up through skillful observation;
second, the quality of color, because it has been well-finished by a skilled craftsman.
3. The merit of form and appearance, because it is skillfully transformed and exquisite;
4. The merit of stainlessness, because it is perfectly pure;
5. The merit of luminous purity, because it is perfectly refined and radiant.
Sixth, the merit of initiating practice, because it is well-pierced.
This is manifested by these three phrases: being strung with precious threads, and being placed upon a high banner of lapis lazuli.
7. The merit of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), because he emits all manner of light that universally illumines all places.
8. The merit of non-protection (*arakṣa*), because he rains down various precious objects according to the king’s intention and is able to bestow all precious objects upon all sentient beings;
because he has received the throne through right wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), and because he shares the same treasury of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) with all sentient beings.
"Transcending the nature of the ten noble ones" means transcending the natures of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth.
There are eight types of śrāvaka natures, due to the distinctions between the four practices and the four fruits.
There are two kinds of *pratyekabuddha* natures, due to the distinction between their practice and their fruit.
Thus, the section on the images of the ten stages has been explained.
What, then, is the section on the benefits of the stages?
The Sūtra says:
"O Son of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva practice is the Dharma-gate chapter on the collection of the merit of all aspects of the knowledge of all modes."
"If sentient beings have not deeply planted roots of goodness, they will be unable to hear it.
Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
If one should hear this "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Collection of All Kinds and All Aspects of the Wisdom of Omniscience," how much merit will that person accomplish?
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!

Just as the observation encompassed by the knowledge of all-knowledge gathers all merits, so too is this Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of Gathering the Merits of All Aspects of the Knowledge of All-Knowledge."
If this person hears this Dharma-gate, the merit they obtain will likewise be such as this.
Why is that? O Son of the Buddha!

If one is not a bodhisattva, they cannot even hear this "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Accumulation of All Kinds of Merits for the Wisdom of All-Knowledge"; how much less could they believe it, how much less uphold it, and how much less correctly practice it?

When this sutra was being preached, through the Buddha’s spiritual power and the power of the Dharma, worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the atoms within ten billion buddha-lands shook in six ways and eighteen modes: namely, shaking, shaking everywhere, and shaking equally everywhere; surging, surging everywhere, and surging equally everywhere; awakening, awakening everywhere, and awakening equally everywhere; rising, rising everywhere, and rising equally everywhere; trembling, trembling everywhere, and trembling equally everywhere; and roaring, roaring everywhere, and roaring equally everywhere.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power and by the power of the Dharma, various celestial flowers rained down like clouds; celestial garments rained down, celestial jewels rained down, celestial ornaments rained down, celestial parasols rained down, celestial banners rained down, celestial standards rained down, celestial music rained down, and celestial sounds rained down, praising the ground of all-knowledge and extolling the sublime excellence of the ten stages.

Just as this Dharma of the Ten Stages is being taught in the Maṇi-ratna-kośa Hall within the palace of the Sovereign Heavenly King in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven of the four continents in this world-system, so too is this Dharma of the Ten Stages being taught everywhere throughout all worlds in the ten directions.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, there came from worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields, bodhisattvas equal in number to the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields, who gathered and filled the void of the ten directions.
Having arrived, they all spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of the Buddha!"
You have excellently explained the characteristics of the bodhisattvas dwelling in the various stages.
O Son of the Buddha!
We all are also named Vajragarbha, and we have come from the presence of the Buddha Vajradhvaja in the world-realm named Vajraśrī.

All those worlds, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, expound this Dharma-gate; the assemblies therein are likewise, the words and phrases are likewise, the explanations of the names are likewise, and the underlying meanings are likewise—neither more nor less.
O Son of the Buddha!
For this reason, we have come to this assembly by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power to bear witness to this Dharma.
O Son of the Buddha!

Just as we have come to this assembly, so too in every world throughout the ten directions—in each of those worlds, within the four continents, atop the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, in the palace of the Sovereign King of Gods, in the Maṇi-jewel treasury hall—there are bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields, who have all gone there to serve as witnesses.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, spoke this sutra, the Tathāgata expressed his approval; and all those assemblies of bodhisattvas, as well as all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, the four heavenly kings, Śakra Devendra, Brahmādeva, Maheśvara, and the hosts of Śuddhāvāsa devas, were all greatly rejoiced.

Not long after the Buddha attained enlightenment in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, on the second seven-day period, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva spoke this in the Maṇi-jewel Treasury Hall of the palace of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; they rejoiced and practiced it with devotion.
The Treatise states:
Regarding the benefits of this stage, there are two kinds:
first, the merit of generating faith; [and second, the merit of practicing according to that faith].
2. The Merit of Making Offerings.
Furthermore, within this Dharma-door, the meaning of the great benefit of resolute faith is demonstrated.
As the Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!..."

"This is the chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Collection of Merits for the Cultivation of All Kinds of Omniscience by this Bodhisattva," and so forth; "The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra spoke," and so forth.
"Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said: and so forth.

For the purpose of generating faith in this sutra and thereby attaining merit, and furthermore, for the purpose of generating the conditions for the merit of faith, he manifested the six kinds of eighteen-fold earth-quakings through his supernormal powers.
As stated in the sūtra: "When this sūtra was being preached, by means of the Buddha’s spiritual power and because the power of the Dharma had been attained," and so forth.
Among these, there are six kinds of shaking:
first, shaking (*calana*);...
2. Leaping; 3. Ascending; 4. Rising;
Fifth, descending;
sixth, roaring—these are the eighteen marks.
These six types of movements and so forth should be understood according to this sequence: inferior, middling, and superior.
Within the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), there are four types of assemblies of sentient beings:
first, those based on unwholesome sentient beings;
second, those based on sentient beings who have faith in various deities.
Third, those sentient beings who rely on the conceit of "I";
fourth, those sentient beings who rely on incantations and arts.

Because there are these distinctions of lower, middle, and upper grades among these classes of beings, one should understand that there are eighteen distinct meanings corresponding to the stages from "moving" up to "roaring."
Thus, the merit of generating faith and the meaning of dependent origination have been explained.
Regarding the merit of making offerings therein, it is as stated in the Sūtra: "Various celestial flowers fell like clouds," and so forth.

This Dharma-gate is taught as a manifestation throughout all worlds, manifesting for the benefit of sentient beings through immeasurable Dharma-gates, as in the sutra passage beginning, "In this world of four continents," and so forth.
The remainder is easy to understand.
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Chapter Ten, "The Stage of the Cloud of Dharma" (*Dharmameghā-bhūmi*), Part Twelve.
